title: Individualised total knee arthroplasty results in low reintervention rates for stiffness and instability in 1000 consecutive knees, regardless of intraoperative bone recuts or polyethylene thickness.
abstract: Purpose Individualised total knee arthroplasty (TKA) aims to restore the pre-arthritic anatomy, but concerns persist regarding ligament imbalance, as only two polyethylene insert thicknesses are available. This study aimed to evaluate revision and reintervention rates, especially for stiffness and instability, after individualised TKA, and whether intraoperative adjustments influenced these outcomes. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 1000 consecutive primary TKAs implanted using a CT-based individualised system with a 1-year minimum follow-up. The primary endpoint was any revision TKA. Secondary analyses evaluated reintervention for stiffness or instability and the association between reinterventions and (1) bone recuts and (2) polyethylene thickness. Survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method. Results At a mean follow-up of 4.2 ± 1.8 years, 12 revision TKA (1.2%) and 29 reinterventions (2.9%) were recorded. All procedures were completed as planned with only two polyethylene insert thicknesses. Revision-free survival was 99.4% (95% confidence interval [CI] 98.7-99.7) at 1 year and 98.7% (95% CI 97.7-99.3) at 5 years. Reoperation-free survival was 98.1% (95% CI 97.0-98.8) and 97.0% (95% CI 95.7-97.9) at 1 and 5 years, respectively. Stiffness-related procedures occurred in nine cases (0.9%), and instability-related revision was observed in one case (0.1%). Bone recuts were performed in 42.8% of knees. No significant association was found between revision risk and bone recuts or polyethylene thickness. Conclusion In this large consecutive cohort, individualised TKA was associated with low rates of revision and of reintervention for stiffness and instability. Intraoperative adjustments (bone recuts, polyethylene thickness changes) were not associated with a higher revision rate. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Purpose Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups. Methods Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups. Results A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm 3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm 3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm 3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm 3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001). Conclusions The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR. Level of evidence Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Elective Neck Dissection in cT1-4 N0M0 Submandibular Gland Cancer.
abstract: Objective To investigate occult nodal metastasis (ONM) and overall survival (OS) in patients undergoing elective neck dissection (END) for clinically node-negative submandibular gland cancer (SMGC). Methods The 2006 to 2018 National Cancer Database was retrospectively reviewed for patients with cT1-4 N0M0 SMGC undergoing surgical resection. Linear, binary logistic, Kaplan-Meier, and Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented. Results A high proportion of patients were female (N = 710, 54.6%) and White (N = 1059, 82.5%) with adenoid cystic carcinoma histology (N = 567, 43.6%) classified as cT1 (N = 545, 41.9%). A minority of patients (N = 255, 19.6%) underwent END. Academic/research reporting facility, high grade, cT3, and cT4 classification were associated with higher odds of undergoing END; Medicare insurance was associated with lower odds (p < 0.05). ONM was identified in 63 (24.7%) patients undergoing END. The rate of ONM increased with cT classification (13.2% in cT1, 27.9% in cT2, 22.0% in cT3, and 50.0% in cT4) and grade (6.5% in well-differentiated, 9.5% in moderately differentiated, and 40.3% in poorly differentiated). END is performed frequently in SMGC but is not associated with OS. Although the rate of ONM approaches 25%, these findings suggest that END should not be routinely performed for prognostic purposes alone, especially in the absence of adverse features.

title: Regional Mitochondrial Density Maps Selective Posterior Atrophy in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Background Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in the pathobiology of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the spatial relationship between regional energetic demand and patterns of neurodegeneration remains poorly understood, limiting mechanistic insight and development of disease-modifying therapies. Objectives This study tested whether regional mitochondrial density aligns with patterns of brain atrophy in PD, how this alignment differs across genetic groups, and whether the mitochondrial-atrophy axis associates with motor and cognitive features. Methods Structural magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from 849 individuals (210 healthy controls, 639 patients with PD). Principal component analysis (PCA) identified dominant atrophy axes and tested their association with regional mitochondrial density and complex I activity. Transcriptomic validation used Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression data restricted to 924 MitoCarta-annotated genes across 31 cortical regions. Results Participants with PD exhibited higher volumetric loss in limbic and subcortical regions than controls. PCA showed a posterior cortical axis of atrophy (PC3) that correlated positively with regional mitochondrial density and was more strongly expressed in LRRK2-PD than in sporadic PD. This axis was selectively associated with visuospatial dysfunction. Transcriptomic validation confirmed that regions of greater atrophy preferentially expressed mitochondrial genes, with mitoribosome assembly, mitochondrial DNA maintenance, and coenzyme Q biosynthesis emerging as the strongest pathway-level predictors. Conclusion These findings link the brain's regional mitochondrial landscape to spatially patterned neurodegeneration in PD, with amplification in LRRK2 mutation carriers. This mitochondrial atrophy axis may provide a biologically informed marker aiding patient stratification and mitochondrial-targeted therapeutic development. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Reliability-weighted patch learning for synthetic CT reconstruction in head and neck adaptive radiotherapy: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Background Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is essential for adaptive radiotherapy (ART) but is limited by poor image quality. Existing deep learning methods for synthetic CT (sCT) generation face a critical trade-off: diffusion models offer high fidelity but are impractically slow, while fast-inference networks often lack structural accuracy and optimization stability. Purpose To develop HQ-PatchNet, a reliability-driven deep learning framework designed to improve CBCT-to-sCT image quality while maintaining rapid inference speed for online ART workflows. Methods HQ-PatchNet utilizes a vision transformer (ViT)-integrated CycleGAN architecture. It introduces a reliability-driven, SSIM-based selective patch weighting mechanism controlled by a temperature decay schedule. This dynamically suppresses artifact-dominated regions and focuses optimization on anatomically reliable structures. The model was evaluated on 304 paired head-and-neck (HN) scans against conventional networks and recent diffusion models using quantitative metrics (MAE, SSIM, NCC, PSNR), computational speed, and clinical dosimetric accuracy (3D gamma index, 2%/2 mm). Results HQ-PatchNet improved image quality, reducing Mean Absolute Error (MAE) from 44.81 ± 11.24 HU to 11.85 ± 4.31 HU and achieving an SSIM of 0.960 ± 0.055, comparable to state-of-the-art diffusion models. Inference required only 6.42 ± 1.71 s per volume, compared to > 15 min for diffusion approaches. The model reduced severe metal and truncation artifacts, and representative qualitative assessment suggested visually consistent sCT generation under interfractional anatomical variation. Dosimetric assessment of complex HN IMRT plans yielded a high average gamma passing rate of 99.32 ± 0.56%. Conclusions HQ-PatchNet provides a computationally efficient and clinically promising approach for daily CBCT-guided online ART by improving CBCT-to-sCT image quality while maintaining rapid inference speed. Further contour-based, multi-institutional, and multi-site validation remains necessary to confirm its broader clinical utility.

title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed-set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open-set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. We propose a GCD framework integrating semi-supervised contrastive learning with global-local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross-instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine-grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open-set diagnostic AI.

title: Impact of correlated PBPK parameters on intra-patient global sensitivity analysis in molecular radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models integrated into digital twins provide a robust framework for optimizing individualized molecular radiotherapy (MRT). Nevertheless, uncertainties in PBPK-model-derived dosimetry can compromise the reliability of dosimetry-guided treatment planning and individualized therapy decisions. Purpose This study employs intra-patient global sensitivity analysis (GSA) to assess the influence of uncertainty and correlations among PBPK model parameters on estimated kidney and tumor absorbed doses (ADs) in prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted theragnostics. Methods Data from 10 patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who underwent pre-therapeutic [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-I&T PET/CT and a cycle of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T therapy, followed by post-therapeutic SPECT/CT scans at Days 1 and 4 post-injection, were analyzed. A previously established whole-body PBPK model for PSMA-targeted radionuclide therapy was used as the baseline model. Fifteen model parameters, their standard errors, and inter-parameter correlations were estimated by fitting to measured time-activity data and subsequently evaluated using intra-patient GSA based on the Kucherenko method implemented in UQLab. In one approach, correlations were ignored to identify the direct influences of uncertainty in input parameters on ADs. In a second approach, correlations were included to reflect realistic parameter distributions and to capture indirect effects arising from parameter interdependencies. Pharmacokinetics were simulated to estimate therapeutic kidney and tumor ADs as well as main- and total-effect indices ( Si,SiT) . Sensitivity indices, ADs, and their associated uncertainty metrics were compared between scenarios with and without parameter correlations. Results Including parameter correlations in the GSA yielded kidney ADs of 4.2 Gy [3.0-7.2 Gy] (median [min-max]) with standard deviations (SDs) of 0.5 Gy [0.4-0.9 Gy] and tumor ADs of 10.1 Gy [2.0-26.8 Gy] with SDs of 1.7 Gy [0.6-3.4 Gy]. Neglecting correlations resulted in significantly higher uncertainties in ADs, by a factor of 1.2 [1.0-1.8] for both kidneys and tumors. Kidney ADs were most sensitive to kidney receptor density ( Si=0.3[0.1-0.6], SiT=0.7[0.6-0.8] ) and to the filtered fraction of renal blood flow (Si=0.2[0.1-0.3], SiT=0.3[0.1-0.4]) . Tumor ADs were most affected by tumor receptor density ( Si=0.7[0.1-1.0], SiT=0.8[0.3-1.0] ). The involvement of parameter correlations did not alter the identification of the parameters most influential on AD estimates and further reduced computational runtime. Conclusions Incorporating parameter correlations into intra-patient GSA reduced the estimated uncertainty associated with ADs, underscoring the importance of preserving parameter dependencies when propagating uncertainty in PBPK-based individualized MRT. The identification of key PBPK parameters governing kidney and tumor ADs remained stable when including correlation, confirming the robustness of the underlying model structure.

title: An anatomy-aware spatio-temporal generative extrapolation network for distal ascending aorta restoration in standard echocardiographic views.
abstract: Background In two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), the standard parasternal long-axis (PLAX) view enables reliable evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root. Owing to the limited field of view of the ultrasound probe and rib-window occlusion, the distal ascending aorta (AA) is frequently truncated, compromising the diagnosis of aortic aneurysm and dilation. Purpose We aim to address the incomplete visualization of the distal AA in standard PLAX views. By aggregating fragmented anatomical features intermittently visible in adjacent frames, we enhance the clarity of vessel wall edges and generate the distal AA structure, thereby completing the missing AA imagery in standard PLAX views. Materials and methods We retrospectively collected 1160 TTE videos from Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (August 2022 - December 2024), all showing complete AA anatomy. After de-identification, 1059 cases were randomly split into training/validation/test sets (6:2:2), and 101 cases were reserved for observer agreement experiments. An additional 152 videos from three different device models (EPIQ CVX, GE Voluson E10, Resona A20T) formed an external validation set. Two training data types were constructed: (i) dual-view synchronous data - a standard PLAX sequence and an AO-PLAX sequence acquired after a cranial probe shift, phase-matched at end diastole (ED); and (ii) locally masked data - the distal AA region was masked, forcing the model to infer missing anatomy from left-side context. Input sequences of five frames (ED ± 2) were extracted. The proposed Spatio-Temporal Ascending-Aorta generative adversarial network (STAA-GAN) first aligns adjacent frames using an Edge Boosted Feature Alignment (EBFA) module with multi-stage modulated deformable convolutions. A channel-wise fusion strategy then aggregates temporally aligned features. The fused representation is fed into a Swin-UNet generator enhanced with a Strip based Cross window Prediction (SCP) module to capture long-range structural dependencies. Training employs a composite loss including pixel reconstruction, feature reconstruction, texture consistency, relativistic average least-squares GAN (RaLSGAN), temporal coherence, and structure-aware terms, with data-dependent weighting. Statistical analyzes included Bland-Altman, Passing-Bablok regression, paired t-tests with Cohen's d, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and two one-sided tests (TOST, Δ=0.2cm ). Results STAA-GAN achieved the best image-quality values among the compared methods, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) = 22.51 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) = 0.7574, multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM) = 0.8598, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) = 0.1758. All 12 pairwise comparisons (SRN, IOH, and U-Transformer versus STAA-GAN, designated as the reference group) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction ( α1=0.00417 ), with absolute effect sizes ranging from 0.255 to 3.439. The per-frame inference time was 203 ms. In clinical consistency validation, the mean difference between measurements on generated and original images was ≤0.01 cm with 95% limits of agreement within ±0.13 cm; TOST with Δ=0.2 cm confirmed clinical equivalence for all comparisons ( p<0.001 ). The segmentation Dice coefficient on generated images averaged 0.913±0.045 across five cross-validation folds. External validation on three different ultrasound devices (Philips, GE, Mindray) maintained consistent equivalence (TOST p<0.001 , Cohen's d<0.2 ). These results demonstrate that STAA-GAN produces clinically interchangeable distal ascending aorta images with high fidelity and real-time feasibility. Conclusions STAA-GAN enables extrapolation of the missing distal ascending aorta in standard PLAX views, achieving improved image quality and clinically equivalent diameter measurements on both internal and external validation datasets. These findings support its potential for assisting distal ascending aorta assessment in routine echocardiography.

Purpose

We aim to address the incomplete visualization of the distal AA in standard PLAX views. By aggregating fragmented anatomical features intermittently visible in adjacent frames, we enhance the clarity of vessel wall edges and generate the distal AA structure, thereby completing the missing AA imagery in standard PLAX views.

Materials and methods

We retrospectively collected 1160 TTE videos from Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (August 2022 - December 2024), all showing complete AA anatomy. After de-identification, 1059 cases were randomly split into training/validation/test sets (6:2:2), and 101 cases were reserved for observer agreement experiments. An additional 152 videos from three different device models (EPIQ CVX, GE Voluson E10, Resona A20T) formed an external validation set. Two training data types were constructed: (i) dual-view synchronous data - a standard PLAX sequence and an AO-PLAX sequence acquired after a cranial probe shift, phase-matched at end diastole (ED); and (ii) locally masked data - the distal AA region was masked, forcing the model to infer missing anatomy from left-side context. Input sequences of five frames (ED ± 2) were extracted. The proposed Spatio-Temporal Ascending-Aorta generative adversarial network (STAA-GAN) first aligns adjacent frames using an Edge Boosted Feature Alignment (EBFA) module with multi-stage modulated deformable convolutions. A channel-wise fusion strategy then aggregates temporally aligned features. The fused representation is fed into a Swin-UNet generator enhanced with a Strip based Cross window Prediction (SCP) module to capture long-range structural dependencies. Training employs a composite loss including pixel reconstruction, feature reconstruction, texture consistency, relativistic average least-squares GAN (RaLSGAN), temporal coherence, and structure-aware terms, with data-dependent weighting. Statistical analyzes included Bland-Altman, Passing-Bablok regression, paired t-tests with Cohen's d, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and two one-sided tests (TOST, Δ=0.2cm ).

Results

STAA-GAN achieved the best image-quality values among the compared methods, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) = 22.51 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) = 0.7574, multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM) = 0.8598, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) = 0.1758. All 12 pairwise comparisons (SRN, IOH, and U-Transformer versus STAA-GAN, designated as the reference group) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction ( α1=0.00417 ), with absolute effect sizes ranging from 0.255 to 3.439. The per-frame inference time was 203 ms. In clinical consistency validation, the mean difference between measurements on generated and original images was ≤0.01  cm with 95% limits of agreement within ±0.13  cm; TOST with Δ=0.2  cm confirmed clinical equivalence for all comparisons ( p<0.001 ). The segmentation Dice coefficient on generated images averaged 0.913±0.045 across five cross-validation folds. External validation on three different ultrasound devices (Philips, GE, Mindray) maintained consistent equivalence (TOST p<0.001 , Cohen's d<0.2 ). These results demonstrate that STAA-GAN produces clinically interchangeable distal ascending aorta images with high fidelity and real-time feasibility.

Conclusions

STAA-GAN enables extrapolation of the missing distal ascending aorta in standard PLAX views, achieving improved image quality and clinically equivalent diameter measurements on both internal and external validation datasets. These findings support its potential for assisting distal ascending aorta assessment in routine echocardiography.

title: Characterization of local linearity in deep learning CT denoising networks.
abstract: Background Deep learning algorithms for image processing have been proposed for a wide range of applications. In particular, deep learning CT denoising has demonstrated superior ability to reduce noise compared to conventional methods. However, the nonlinear nature of these algorithms makes it difficult to inspect and visualize how the model accomplishes the denoising task. Purpose We propose a local linearization approach to characterize and analyze the behavior of deep learning algorithms. Example analysis was performed for a classic denoising architecture with convolutional neural network and ReLU activation functions, and was extended to GELU activation and a transformer-based architecture. Methods We defined strictly local linear regions as the input space over which the activation patterns of all ReLU activation functions are the same. The extent of these regions was investigated by perturbing clinically relevant features of a lung lesion. We further defined approximately local linear regions as the input space where Jacobians are similar and linear approximation results in small error. We developed an algorithm to partition input space over a range of lesion and background features into approximately local linear regions, and separately quantified the contribution of the noise realization and anatomical background to this approximation error. The behavior of networks trained with different levels of denoising, as well as alternative architectures, was compared. Results The extent of strictly local linear regions was found to be very small. Perturbations on the scale of 10-8mm-1 were enough to push the network to a neighboring strictly local linear region. However, the Jacobians over a large number of strictly local linear regions were found to be highly similar, which suggests that the network behaves approximately as a piecewise linear system. The partitioning algorithm identified a small number of approximately local linear regions within input spaces characterized by clinically relevant features; this number was similar for the GELU variant but increased for networks trained with more aggressive noise reduction and for a transformer-based architecture, while Jacobians transferred across anatomical backgrounds also increased approximation error. Conclusions The local linearity analysis framework can be a useful tool for elucidating the behavior of neural networks that are traditionally considered as "black-boxes." Preliminary results suggest that the framework can be applied to other differentiable architectures, subject to empirical validation, to characterize these highly nonlinear, data-dependent algorithms over input spaces of interest.

title: Free-breathing fast abdominal simultaneous T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub>, PD and B<sub>1</sub> mapping via deep learning reconstruction.
abstract: Background Multi-parametric quantitative MRI (mqMRI) enables non-invasive tissue characterization and holds significant clinical value in abdominal imaging. Conventional methods are restricted by long acquisition times and motion artifacts induced by physiological processes and irregular breathing, leading to registration errors between sequential acquisitions. Purpose To develop and evaluate a framework for abdominal quantitative imaging under free-breathing conditions with reduced scan time and improved robustness to motion. Methods A novel framework integrating the longitudinal magnetization-controlled multiple overlapping-echo detachment (LMC-MOLED) sequence with synthetic data-driven deep learning reconstruction was proposed. To generate the synthetic dataset for training, a respiratory motion model combining global and local displacement vector fields was developed, ensuring temporal alignment with the inter-phase intervals of LMC-MOLED acquisitions. By applying interpolation to the original template, virtual imaging objects were generated to simulate respiratory-induced deformations while preserving anatomical textures, tissue boundaries, and inter-slice correlations. These objects were subsequently processed with MRI Bloch simulation to generate the final synthetic dataset, which was used to train a BGA-Multi-UNet architecture for motion correction and improved quantitative accuracy. Results The proposed framework enabled simultaneous mapping of T 1 , T 2 , proton density, and B 1 under free-breathing conditions. With a 5-slice interleaved acquisition, the average acquisition time was reduced to approximately one second per slice without the need for respiratory gating. Both numerical and in vivo experiments demonstrated high accuracy and repeatability, with image quality comparable to conventional breath-hold acquisitions while mitigating motion-induced artifacts. Conclusion This framework offers a rapid and reliable solution for multi-parametric abdominal imaging under free-breathing conditions. The combination of synthetic motion modeling with deep learning reconstruction enables accurate quantitative mapping with effective motion correction, offering potential clinical benefits for efficient and robust abdominal magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Rep2Rep-Shuffle: Shuffled Repetition-to-Repetition Learning for Noise-Adaptive Self-Supervised MRI Denoising.
abstract: Purpose MRI applications with low SNR, such as non-proton imaging and low-field imaging, often require multiple signal averages to achieve adequate image quality at the cost of longer scan times. This work proposes Rep2Rep-Shuffle, a self-supervised learning framework that improves MRI denoising performance in repeated-acquisition imaging with limited training datasets. Methods Rep2Rep-Shuffle extends our previously proposed repetition-to-repetition learning (Rep2Rep)-based self-supervised denoising approach with a new shuffled repetition pairing strategy. Instead of using a fixed split between training input and target repetitions, different repetition combinations are randomly generated during training epochs for each dataset, which increases the effective training space when training datasets are limited. In addition, the framework also extends from slice-wise 2D to 3D denoising by exploiting correlations across all spatial dimensions. The proposed method was tested in vivo using sodium MRI and further validated using synthetic noisy MRI datasets. Different training strategies for both 2D and 3D denoising were compared. Results In vivo sodium MRI results demonstrated improved denoising and better preservation of anatomical structures with 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle compared with fixed pairing (Rep2Rep) and 2D denoising. Reader evaluation further confirmed that 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle received higher scores for different assessment categories. In synthetic experiments, 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle achieved the best performance among self-supervised methods and approached the performance of supervised learning. Conclusion Rep2Rep-Shuffle outperforms Rep2Rep for MRI denoising by increasing training diversity through shuffled repetition pairing and by leveraging volumetric spatial correlations. The method is particularly suited for low-SNR MRI applications that acquire multiple repetitions but have limited training datasets.

title: Deep-Reorder: Refined Motion Correction for 3D Brain MRI via Iterative Data Regrouping.
abstract: Purpose Accurate and temporally high-resolution estimation of subject motion is paramount for effective motion-correction in MRI. This work proposes a novel approach for estimating subject motion within a 3D MRI scan with high temporal resolution. Methods Starting from an incoherent sampling scheme, images are reconstructed from temporally ordered k-space fractions via deep learning, enabling motion estimation via registration between each image. Assuming the bulk of the motion is removed using these initial estimates, the remaining misalignment between k-space fractions is expected to be minimally correlated in time. Based on this insight, an iterative strategy is proposed in which shots are arbitrarily regrouped into new k-space fractions, regardless of their original temporal ordering, for subsequent motion estimation and correction. This effectively increases the temporal resolution of the approach, enabling individual correction of all shots. Results When applied to 3D T1w TFE MRI of the brain, the proposed approach "Deep-Reorder" estimated a unique motion state for all shots, producing significantly better estimations of retrospective motion compared to estimation without iterative data regrouping. On prospectively motion-corrupted scans with intentional head movement by volunteers, the proposed approach consistently improved image quality, producing less noisy images with reduced motion artifacts. Conclusion In conclusion, the proposed approach, which is free of external tracking devices or navigators, effectively estimated 3D motion and corrected motion artifacts with increased temporal resolution.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Magnetic Resonance Elastography Versus Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography for Liver Fibrosis Staging in Steatotic Liver Disease.
abstract: Gravitational magnetic resonance elastography (GT-MRE) enables comprehensive biomechanical liver characterization and may overcome limitations of conventional elastography techniques. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) GT-MRE compared with 2D acoustic MRE (AC-MRE) and vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) for liver fibrosis staging. In this prospective study, patients with suspected or known steatotic liver disease underwent GT-MRE (2D and 3D, gradient-echo sequences) and AC-MRE (2D, spin-echo echo-planar imaging) at 1.5 T, plus VCTE with a median interval to MRE of 37 days (IQR, 20-124 days; range, 0-372 days). Statistical analyses included generalized additive models, ordinal logistic regression, and decision tree-based classification. Diagnostic performance was assessed using cumulative receiver operating characteristic analysis and corresponding areas under the curve (AUCs). Ninety-one participants (median age, 55 years [IQR, 45-64]; 41 women) were included, of whom 35 (38%) had histopathological correlation. In the biopsy-confirmed subgroup, 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising exploratory performance for early fibrosis classification. Wave attenuation achieved AUCs of 0.91 for F0 versus ≥ F1 and 0.99 for ≤ F1 versus ≥ F2, while phase angle yielded an AUC of 0.88 for F0 versus ≥ F1, with numerically higher AUCs than conventional stiffness-based metrics. For advanced fibrosis thresholds, all modalities performed well (AUC ≥ 0.84). Obuchowski measures for 3D-derived parameters were 0.95-0.96. Internally cross-validated multiparametric modeling achieved an accuracy of up to 92%. VCTE measurements plateaued beyond F3, whereas AC- and GT-MRE metrics continued to increase with fibrosis severity. 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising performance for liver fibrosis classification and provided biomechanical information complementary to conventional stiffness measurements. Given the limited biopsy-confirmed sample and marked class imbalance at F0, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts before clinical implementation.

title: 2D U-Net Framework for Multiclass Automated Segmentation of Healthy Structures, Ischemic Stroke, and Glioblastoma in the Rat Brain.
abstract: Rodents are essential for preclinical brain disease research, including stroke, tumors, and neurodegenerative disorders. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables longitudinal brain tissue visualization, but accurate segmentation is crucial for meaningful analysis. This study introduces a multitask 2D U-Net, a convolutional neural network designed for automated segmentation and quantification of brain regions, ischemic stroke lesions, and tumors in rats using T 2 -weighted imaging (T 2 -wi) and T 2 -relaxation maps. The model was evaluated on the following three MRI datasets: (i) segmentation of multiple brain regions in healthy rats, (ii) ischemic stroke lesions using T 2 -relaxation maps, and (iii) glioblastoma tumors using T 2 -wi. Performance was assessed using the Dice coefficient (DC), Hausdorff distance (HD), sensitivity (SEN), and volume ratio (VR), comparing network outputs against semiautomatic ground truths and existing models. A total of 1949 images from 111 rats were analyzed, expanded to 5847 through data augmentation. After correcting an animal-level train/test partitioning that prevented data leakage between subjects, the model achieved robust accuracy across all tasks (DC = 0.80-0.96, HD = 0.83-2.16 mm, SEN = 0.75-0.96, VR = 0.89-1.10), showing a strong correlation ( ρ=0.82-0.99 ) with manual annotations. This framework improves segmentation accuracy, robustness, and applicability across different MRI settings and conditions, addressing issues like interrater variability and time inefficiency when analyzing rodent brain MRI data. Datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NOBEL-MRI/Rat-Datasets.

title: The Associations Between Olfactory Bulb Morphology, Volume Change, and Olfactory Recovery.
abstract: Objective To investigate whether olfactory bulb (OB) morphology is associated with olfactory recovery following olfactory training (OT) in individuals with COVID-19-related smell loss. Study design Prospective observational study. Setting University hospital and research center. Methods Twenty women with COVID-19-associated olfactory dysfunction and 19 healthy controls underwent OT for 3 months. OB shape (oval vs non-oval) was classified using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and bilateral OB volumes were manually segmented before and after OT. Olfactory performance was assessed with the Sniffin' Sticks test. Statistical analyses included independent t tests, multimodal analysis of covariance, correlation analyses, and generalized estimating equations. Results At baseline, OB volume correlated significantly with olfactory performance. Changes in left OB volume were positively correlated with changes in odor threshold. Following OT, patients with non-oval OB shapes showed greater improvement in Threshold + Discrimination + Identification (TDI) scores and enlargement of left OB volume compared to those with oval-shaped OB. However, OB morphology did not significantly change over time in both patients and controls. Conclusion OB shape may provide a novel perspective for predicting prognosis after OT. Further studies with larger cohorts and extended training durations are warranted to validate these preliminary observations.

Objective

Prospective observational study.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Supraclavicular Brachiocephalic Vein Cannulation in Pediatric Patients With Hematological Disorders: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation-related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy. Aims This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound-guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure-related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients. Methods This retrospective study included 580 children (303 subclavian vein [SCV], 277 BCV) who underwent ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization between January 2021 and December 2024. We compared first-attempt success rate, overall success rate, procedural duration, intraoperative adverse events, postoperative complications, and catheter malposition. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to improve comparability between the groups with respect to measured baseline covariates. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors. Results After IPTW, the BCV approach was associated with a higher first-attempt success rate (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.05-2.81; risk difference [RD] = 0.119, 95% CI: 0.015-0.222) and a higher overall success rate (RD = 0.091, 95% CI: 0.013-0.168). The mean procedural duration was 6 min shorter in the BCV group (95% CI: -9.5 to -2.5). The BCV approach was independently associated with lower odds of intraoperative malposition (OR = 0.096, 95% CI: 0.037-0.249), postoperative malposition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.16-0.74), and perioperative complications (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.08-0.94). Multivariable regression analysis showed that catheterization approach was independently associated with catheter malposition. Conclusions Compared with SCV, ultrasound-guided BCV cannulation is associated with higher success rates, shorter procedural duration, and fewer malpositions and complications. This technique may offer particular benefits for children with hematological disorders.

title: Thoracic Endometriosis Mimicking a Lung Mass: Management With Single-Stage Biopsy and Microwave Ablation.
abstract: Thoracic endometriosis syndrome is a rare extrapelvic manifestation involving the pleura, diaphragm or lung parenchyma. Presentation as a solitary pulmonary nodule mimicking malignancy is uncommon. We report a 31-year-old asymptomatic woman with an enlarging right lower lobe nodule, measuring 1.8-2.1 cm over 3 months. Following shared decision-making, single-stage image-guided biopsy and microwave ablation (MWA) were performed. Histopathology confirmed pulmonary endometriosis. No clinically significant postoperative complications occurred, and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 1. Follow-up CT at 6 and 12 months demonstrated no obvious local recurrence without additional treatment. This case describes a potential minimally invasive approach for selected pulmonary lesions, although the safety, efficacy and long-term outcomes of MWA for pulmonary endometriosis remain uncertain.

title: Tunable <sup>18</sup>F-Labeling of Erlotinib-Based Small Molecule Nanodrugs for Rapid PET Imaging and Targeted Therapy.
abstract: Small molecule nanodrugs (SMNs) offer unique advantages for cancer therapy, yet accurately tracking their in vivo fate without perturbing their native assembly remains challenging. Here, we report a spacer engineering strategy that enables efficient 1 8 F-labeling while preserving SMNs self-assembly. Erlotinib-based amphiphilic derivatives containing oligoethylene glycol (OEG) spacers of tunable length were designed to simultaneously regulate steric hindrance for aliphatic S N 2 radiofluorination and the amphiphilic balance required for nanoparticle formation. Spacer elongation reduced steric hindrance at the labeling site and thereby improved radiochemical yields, while also enabling precise control over nanoparticle size. The optimized radiolabeled formulation, [ 18 F]E3F NPs , exhibited prolonged blood circulation and rapid tumor accumulation, enabling high-contrast PET imaging of PANC-1 xenografts as early as 15 min after injection. In addition, the corresponding nonradioactive formulation, E3F NPs , showed significantly improved antitumor efficacy compared with nonassembled E3F through reduced EGFR phosphorylation and increased tumor cell apoptosis. This work provides an initial evaluation that spacer engineering can coordinate radiolabeling and self-assembly while enabling PET tracking of SMNs, supporting the development of image-guided cancer theranostics.

title: Classification of brain variants on fetal ultrasound: international Delphi consensus.
abstract: Objective To develop an expert consensus classification and management framework for fetal-brain variants identified on prenatal ultrasound across all trimesters of pregnancy that cannot be categorized confidently as either benign or pathological. Methods A two-round international Delphi survey was conducted among experts in fetal medicine and neurosonography, with survey data collected between September 2025 and March 2026. Forty-eight fetal-brain variants, identified through a scoping literature review of PubMed/MEDLINE from database inception to August 2025, performed between June and August 2025, and illustrated with representative ultrasound images, were evaluated. Brain variants were classified according to clinical significance and recommended management into three predefined categories: 'green' (benign variants requiring no additional investigation or follow-up), 'orange' (requiring neurosonographic follow-up) and 'red' (requiring dedicated neurosonography, fetal-brain magnetic resonance imaging and/or genetic investigations). Consensus was predefined as ≥ 70% agreement. In Round 2, experts confirmed their agreement regarding categorization of variants that had reached consensus in Round 1 and reassessed variants that did not reach initial consensus. Results Forty-eight experts from 14 countries participated in Round 1 and 39 (81.3%) completed both rounds. Of the 48 evaluated variants, 35 (72.9%) reached consensus after two rounds: 12 were classified as 'green', seven as 'orange' and 16 as 'red'. Green variants included isolated choroid plexus cysts < 10 mm across all trimesters, regular asymmetry of the choroid plexuses, isolated cavum septations, cavum vergae, cavum velum interpositum, isolated small cavum septi pellucidi with intact corpus callosum and dolichocephaly with normal head circumference and normal brain morphology. Orange variants included isolated enlargement of intracranial translucency with preserved anatomy, large or bilateral choroid plexus cysts, isolated enlargement of subarachnoid spaces without compression and isolated cyst of the cavum septi pellucidi. Red variants included abnormal posterior fossa markers (loss of normal three-space anatomy, increased brainstem-vermis angle, reduced brainstem-occipital bone distance), periventricular cysts associated with adjacent white-matter abnormalities, thickened corpus callosum and distortion of the interhemispheric fissure, among other findings. Thirteen (27.1%) variants failed to reach consensus, highlighting persistent uncertainty in interpreting subtle isolated asymmetries and selected cystic variants. Conclusions This international Delphi consensus proposes an initial expert-derived classification of commonly encountered feta-brain variants on ultrasound. Because the classification has not been validated against postnatal imaging or neurodevelopmental outcomes and reproducibility has not been assessed, prospective evaluation is required before it can be applied in routine practice. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

title: Early third-trimester maternal cardiac function and morphometry in high-risk pregnancies that subsequently developed fetal growth restriction and/or pre-eclampsia.
abstract: Objective To evaluate maternal cardiovascular function and cardiac morphology in early third-trimester pregnancies at high risk for fetal growth restriction (FGR) and compare findings between pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR and/or pre-eclampsia (PE) and uncomplicated pregnancies. Methods This prospective cohort study included singleton pregnancies at high risk for FGR referred to the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Department at the Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain, between August 2022 and August 2024, for a routine second-trimester fetal anomaly scan. The patients were assessed between 27 + 0 and 28 + 6 weeks' gestation and were only included in the analysis if they did not have a diagnosis of FGR or PE at the time of evaluation; those who subsequently developed FGR and/or PE were identified during follow-up. Maternal echocardiography was performed to assess cardiac output (CO), stroke volume (SV), systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and structural parameters including left ventricular (LV) wall thickness and chamber volumes. Results were compared between pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR (with or without PE), pregnancies that subsequently developed isolated PE and uncomplicated pregnancies. Multivariable analysis was performed using quantile regression of the medians for CO and SVR, adjusted for body mass index (BMI), with FGR and PE assessed independently. Results A total of 948 patients were included in the final analysis, of whom 129 developed FGR and/or PE (including 59 that developed FGR (with or without PE) and 70 that developed isolated PE) and 819 had uncomplicated pregnancies. Median mean arterial pressure (MAP) was higher in the FGR (with or without PE) group (82.0 mmHg) and the isolated-PE group (84.8 mmHg) than in the uncomplicated group (79.7 mmHg; P = 0.027 and P < 0.001, respectively), with the isolated-PE group showing the highest MAP values (isolated PE vs FGR (with or without PE), P = 0.047). Median heart rate was elevated in the isolated-PE group (82.5 bpm) compared with the FGR (with or without PE) group (77.0 bpm; P = 0.03). In the multivariable analysis, FGR and PE were associated independently with lower CO and higher SVR prior to their development. Median SV was reduced in the FGR (with or without PE) group (59.7 mL) and the isolated-PE group (61.1 mL) compared with the uncomplicated group (64.2 mL; P = 0.030 and P = 0.016, respectively). Median BMI-indexed CO was also lower in the FGR (with or without PE) group (0.18 (L/min)/(kg/m 2 )) and the isolated-PE group (0.17 (L/min)/(kg/m 2 )) compared with the uncomplicated group (0.19 (L/min)/(kg/m 2 ); P = 0.005 and P = 0.001, respectively). Median SVR was elevated in the FGR (with or without PE) group (1393 dynes × s/cm 5 ) and the isolated-PE group (1339 dynes × s/cm 5 ) compared with the uncomplicated group (1252 dynes × s/cm 5 ; P < 0.001 and P = 0.01, respectively). Compared with the uncomplicated group, the isolated-PE group showed greater median LV myocardial thickness at end diastole (0.50 vs 0.47 cm; P = 0.003), interventricular septal thickness at end diastole (0.92 vs 0.89 cm; P = 0.031), posterior wall thickness at end diastole (0.98 vs 0.94 cm; P = 0.013) and relative wall thickness (0.45 vs 0.42; P = 0.001). Moreover, the FGR (with or without PE) group had a smaller median LV end-diastolic diameter (4.27 cm) compared with the uncomplicated group (4.48 cm; P = 0.003), indicating that preload may be reduced in patients who developed FGR (with or without PE). LV mass indexed for BMI was similar across groups. Conclusions Maternal cardiovascular alterations may precede the development of FGR and PE and differ by phenotype. Pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR and/or PE showed reduced CO, but those that developed FGR reflected lower preload without tachycardia, while those that developed isolated PE showed hypertensive features with a compensatory rise in heart rate. Maternal echocardiography may aid early risk stratification and guide tailored surveillance and therapy in pregnancies at high risk for FGR. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

title: Advanced Diffusion MRI in the Human Brain: Microstructure Imaging and Structural Connectivity.
abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) is one of the most powerful MRI techniques for exploring the brain's microstructure in vivo. By measuring how water molecules move within tissue, it provides unique insight into the cellular and fiber architecture of the brain-information that conventional MRI cannot reveal. In clinical settings, diffusion imaging is now a valuable tool for early stroke diagnosis, tumour characterization, and surgical planning. In research, it enables the study of brain development, ageing, and disease progression, linking imaging findings to cellular and molecular processes. Over the past three decades, diffusion MRI has evolved from simple diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps to advanced models that capture the complexity of tissue organization. Techniques such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), diffusional kurtosis imaging (DKI), and multi-compartment biophysical models now allow estimation of parameters related to axonal density, myelination, and water exchange between cellular compartments. Combined with tractography, these methods enable noninvasive reconstruction of white-matter pathways and network-level connectivity, transforming dMRI into a central tool for both neuroscience and clinical use. This chapter introduces the principles and applications of diffusion MRI in a progressive manner. We begin with the fundamental physics of diffusion contrast and its clinical relevance, then move to advanced microstructural models that provide richer biological specificity. Subsequent sections describe tractography methods used to map brain connectivity and analyze structural networks. Together, these sections aim to provide readers, especially those with limited imaging background, with an accessible understanding of how diffusion MRI reveals the brain's hidden microstructure and connects it to biological function.

title: [Trauma-From diagnosis to intervention].
abstract: Abdominal trauma represents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge because the large number of potentially involved organs and the complexity of the underlying injuries are difficult to capture within a standardized diagnostic approach. Both blunt and penetrating abdominal injuries can be involved as well as falls from a great height, traffic accidents or violent encounters. In addition, patients may be polytraumatized and the abdomen represents only one component of the injuries sustained but is often clinically prioritized due to the potentially immediate life-threatening nature of injuries to abdominal organs. Such injuries represent an interdisciplinary challenge and their treatment is increasingly carried out using minimally invasive procedures, often within the involvement of interventional radiology. This article aims to present both appropriate diagnostic approaches and minimally invasive treatment options.

title: [Image-guided minimally invasive treatment options for endometriosis].
abstract: Background Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of women of reproductive age with a mean diagnostic delay of 7-10 years. Image-guided procedures show increasingly promising results as minimally invasive alternatives to excision. Objective Structured overview of image-guided minimally invasive treatment options for endometriosis with focus on percutaneous cryoablation. Results Percutaneous cryoablation demonstrates the strongest evidence for extraperitoneal and intramuscular lesions and represents a valid minimally invasive alternative to excision. Three institutional cases illustrate technique and outcomes. Ethanol sclerotherapy is established for ovarian endometriomas. High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) shows promising results for abdominal wall disease; radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and microwave ablation are investigational. Conclusion Interventional radiology offers a growing therapeutic spectrum. Prospective randomized trials are needed for guideline integration.

title: Hybrid CNN-transformer model with gated feature fusion and GAN-based augmentation for MRI image classification.
abstract: Objective Brain tumor classification based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis, yet it remains challenging due to high intra-class variability, inter-class similarity, and limited annotated data. To address these challenges, this study proposes a gated hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN)-transformer architecture (GHCT-Net) that effectively integrates local and global feature representations for robust brain tumor classification in data-limited medical imaging scenarios. Methods The proposed framework combines a ConvNeXt-based convolutional branch for fine-grained spatial feature extraction with a Swin Transformer branch for modeling long-range contextual dependencies. A gate-based fusion mechanism is introduced to adaptively balance the contribution of each feature stream. Additionally, a conditional deep convolutional generative adversarial network (cDCGAN) is employed to generate class-consistent synthetic MRI samples to mitigate data scarcity. The model was evaluated on a public dataset of 7023 MRI images across four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor) under three training scenarios: original, traditionally augmented, and GAN-augmented datasets. Results The results demonstrate that the GHCT-Net achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer architectures, reaching a classification accuracy of 98.39% on the GAN-augmented dataset. Quantitative analysis, along with confusion matrices, t‑distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) visualizations, and gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) interpretability studies, confirms that the model successfully learns discriminative and clinically relevant features. Conclusion Combining a gated hybrid CNN-transformer architecture with GAN-based data augmentation provides a highly effective and robust solution for brain tumor classification, particularly in scenarios constrained by limited medical imaging data.

title: Interpreting liver volume changes after rifampicin in healthy volunteers.
abstract: Rifampicin-associated liver volume changes in healthy volunteers provide an opportunity to examine the human relevance of xenobiotic-induced liver growth. This Comment considers three aspects of the clinical analysis relevant to interpreting the observed response. Clarification of whether the volumetric outcomes and choice of normalisation were prespecified, alongside paired treatment effects and confidence intervals, would help establish the basis for inference and assess the response's magnitude and precision. For a small volumetric response, blinded repeat segmentation of existing magnetic resonance images and details of scan timing and pre-scan intake would help assess reproducibility under comparable physiological conditions. Associations between 4β-hydroxycholesterol and liver volume could also be examined using within-participant rifampicin-minus-placebo differences, with appropriate attention to the crossover design and an exploratory interpretation. Most of these suggestions could be addressed through protocol information and existing imaging and crossover data, strengthening interpretation of the human findings and guiding further investigation of pregnane X receptor-mediated liver growth.

title: CT-based bone mineral density estimation using HU, radiomics, and deep learning.
abstract: Purpose To develop and test models that estimate bone mineral density (BMD) from thoracolumbar junction CT images using Hounsfield unit (HU) assessment, radiomics, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Methods We retrospectively identified patients who underwent lumbar dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and CT covering T12 and L1 within 6 months at four hospitals between 2014 and 2025. In total, 465 patients were eligible for T12 analysis, and 448 for L1. Data from two institutions were used for training/validation and data from the other two for external testing. We developed five models: region-of-interest-based HU regression; volume-of-interest (VOI)-based HU regression; radiomics; CNN; and an ensemble combining VOI, radiomics, and CNN. Performance was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R 2 ), and Bland-Altman limits of agreement (LoA). Results For T12, the CNN model performed best among the single models (MAE: 0.122, RMSE: 0.157, R 2 : 0.603), whereas the ensemble model showed a slightly higher MAE (0.128) but lower RMSE (0.154) and higher R 2 (0.620). For L1, the radiomics model was the best single model (MAE: 0.124, RMSE: 0.155, R 2 : 0.582), while the ensemble showed numerically improved performance (MAE: 0.116, RMSE: 0.145, R 2 : 0.633). Pairwise comparisons showed no significant difference in absolute prediction errors between the ensemble and the best single model at either T12 or L1. Conclusion We developed an ensemble framework integrating volumetric HU assessment, radiomics, and CNNs to estimate BMD from thoracolumbar junction CT images. External testing across two independent institutions demonstrated promising performance for BMD estimation.

To develop and test models that estimate bone mineral density (BMD) from thoracolumbar junction CT images using Hounsfield unit (HU) assessment, radiomics, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

We retrospectively identified patients who underwent lumbar dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and CT covering T12 and L1 within 6 months at four hospitals between 2014 and 2025. In total, 465 patients were eligible for T12 analysis, and 448 for L1. Data from two institutions were used for training/validation and data from the other two for external testing. We developed five models: region-of-interest-based HU regression; volume-of-interest (VOI)-based HU regression; radiomics; CNN; and an ensemble combining VOI, radiomics, and CNN. Performance was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R2), and Bland-Altman limits of agreement (LoA).

Results

For T12, the CNN model performed best among the single models (MAE: 0.122, RMSE: 0.157, R2: 0.603), whereas the ensemble model showed a slightly higher MAE (0.128) but lower RMSE (0.154) and higher R2 (0.620). For L1, the radiomics model was the best single model (MAE: 0.124, RMSE: 0.155, R2: 0.582), while the ensemble showed numerically improved performance (MAE: 0.116, RMSE: 0.145, R2: 0.633). Pairwise comparisons showed no significant difference in absolute prediction errors between the ensemble and the best single model at either T12 or L1.

Conclusion

We developed an ensemble framework integrating volumetric HU assessment, radiomics, and CNNs to estimate BMD from thoracolumbar junction CT images. External testing across two independent institutions demonstrated promising performance for BMD estimation.

title: Prognostic value of dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI and plasma angiogenic markers for survival outcomes in HPV-negative oropharyngeal carcinoma treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) enables non-invasive assessment of tumour vascularity, while circulating angiogenic factors may reflect tumour-associated angiogenic activity. We investigated whether DCE-MRI perfusion parameters and plasma angiogenic factors measured before and early during concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cCRT) are associated with survival in human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). Methods In this prospective single-centre study, 24 patients with locally advanced HPV-negative OPSCC treated with cCRT were analysed. DCE-MRI perfusion parameters (Ktrans, Kep, Ve, iAUC) were analysed at baseline and early intra-treatment (20 Gy), while plasma angiogenic factors (vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF], connective tissue growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor-AB, angiogenin, endostatin, and thrombospondin-1) were analysed at baseline, early intra-treatment and post-treatment (10-12 weeks). Disease-specific survival (DSS) was assessed using univariable Cox regression (hazard ratios [HRs] per 1-SD) and Kaplan-Meier analysis with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Seven patients died of the index cancer. Higher baseline Ktrans (HR per 1-SD 0.30, p = 0.031) and higher early intra-treatment plasma VEGF (HR 0.37, p = 0.043) were nominally associated with better DSS; VEGF also showed separation in Kaplan-Meier analysis (3-year DSS 92% vs. 36%, log-rank p = 0.016). Effect estimates were similar after exploratory adjustment for tumour volume but attenuated after adjustment for stage. No association remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction, and the early VEGF association partly overlapped with local treatment response. Conclusion In this exploratory analysis, baseline DCE-MRI perfusion (Ktrans) and plasma VEGF showed hypothesis-generating associations with DSS in HPV-negative OPSCC. As no association survived multiplicity correction, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts.

title: Pediatric Bow Hunter syndrome: clinical, vascular, and longitudinal findings from a single center and systematic review of the literature.
abstract: Purpose Bow Hunter syndrome (BHS) is a rare cause of pediatric vertebral artery dissection (VAD) and posterior circulation arterial ischemic stroke (AIS) due to dynamic compression during head rotation. Imaging features, vascular evolution, and outcomes remain poorly defined. Methods We reviewed children with definite or probable BHS diagnosed at a tertiary pediatric center between 2010 and 2026. A systematic review identified published pediatric cases (0-18 years) of definite/probable BHS. Results Twelve boys were included (mean age, 7.3 years; mean follow-up, 54.4 months). Posterior circulation AIS occurred in 10/12 (83.3%), with multifocal infarcts of different ages in eight and additional anterior circulation embolic infarcts in three. VAD was bilateral in 6/12 (50%), consistently involving V3. Distal posterior cerebral and/or superior cerebellar artery stenosis or occlusion with collateral networks occurred in 7/12 (58.3%); basilar artery involvement in 4/12. Dynamic vascular imaging demonstrated position-dependent vertebral artery compromise in 9/12 patients (eight by rotational DSA and one by Doppler ultrasound). Craniocervical junction variants were present in 10/12 (83.3%), without flexion-extension instability. Early recurrent AIS occurred in 5/10 despite antithrombotic therapy. Serial imaging showed early vascular evolution followed by stabilization. Two patients underwent surgery; the others were treated conservatively. Conclusions A rotational mechanical mechanism should be considered in children with posterior circulation AIS and V3 abnormalities, particularly when preceded by overlooked prodromal symptoms or minor trauma- and sport-related triggers. Multimodal neurovascular imaging, especially dynamic angiography, is essential for diagnosis, surveillance, and individualized treatment planning aimed at preventing further vascular injury.

title: A machine learning approach to MRI screening for brain arteriovenous malformations in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.
abstract: Background Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an inherited vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in multiple organs. Although brain MRI screening is recommended in all patients with HHT, in many centers, this may be difficult to implement due to organizational constraints. The aim of this study was to develop a machine learning model to predict the presence of bAVMs and other cerebrovascular malformations in patients with HHT, with the goal of supporting risk stratification in centers where genotype information is already available and identifying patients who may benefit from closer and more conservative surveillance. Methods All patients with confirmed diagnosis of HHT, complete genetic work-up, and radiological screening (2018-2026) were included for the analysis. Two end points were defined: probability of detecting bAVMs, and probability of detecting any cerebrovascular findings. Analysis was performed using Python and R. Results A total of 142 patients with confirmed HHT (meeting ≥ 3 Curaçao criteria) were included. For bAVM prediction, both models showed good discrimination, with an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.73-0.94) for Logistic Regression (LR) and 0.85 (95% CI: 0.74-0.96) for Random Forest (RF). Despite the slightly higher AUC, RF showed lower specificity, PPV, and F1 score, higher sensitivity (0.73 vs. 0.69) and same NPV. LR also showed better calibration, with an intercept of -0.30 (95% CI: -1.38-0.78) and slope of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.34-1.40), compared with 1.39 (95% CI: -0.46-3.23) and 2.39 (95% CI: 0.64-4.15), respectively, for RF. In contrast, models predicting overall cerebrovascular malformations showed limited discrimination and poor calibration with both LR and RF. For bAVM prediction, LR identified deletion mutations, ENG, family history, ACVRL1, and truncated variants as the most influential features, while RF SHAP analysis highlighted ACVRL1, ENG, age, pulmonary AVMs, and family history. Conclusion Effective risk stratification was achieved by the phenotype-specific bAVM model, supporting its potential applicability. Upon external validation this tool may enable an efficient allocation of screening strategies.

title: The Lymphatic System in the Fontan Circulation: Pathophysiology, Imaging and Therapeutic Interventions.
abstract: The Fontan circulation, the definitive palliation for patients with univentricular hearts, produces a unique haemodynamic state characterised by chronically elevated systemic venous pressure, reduced cardiac output and the absence of a subpulmonary ventricular impulse. Because lymphatic drainage depends critically on the pressure gradient between the thoracic duct and the systemic veins, this physiology has profound consequences for the lymphatic system. Over the past decade, the lymphatic circulation has moved from being regarded as a passive bystander to being recognised as a central determinant of Fontan failure. Chronic systemic venous hypertension drives lymphatic overproduction and impaired central drainage, leading to progressive lymphatic congestion that manifests as chylothorax, protein-losing enteropathy (PLE), plastic bronchitis, lymphoedema and Fontan-associated liver disease. Advances in magnetic resonance (MR) lymphangiography, in particular dynamic contrast-enhanced MR lymphangiography and T2-weighted MR lymphangiography, now permit direct visualisation of abnormal lymphatic flow and precise planning of image-guided interventions. Percutaneous lymphatic embolisation and thoracic-duct decompression, together with surgical decompression procedures and, ultimately, heart transplantation, have shown clinically relevant efficacy in selected patients with complications refractory to medical therapy. This narrative review synthesises current knowledge on the pathophysiology, imaging and treatment of lymphatic complications in the Fontan circulation. Lymphatic involvement is frequent, under-diagnosed, and prognostically important; the integration of advanced lymphatic imaging and the consolidation of expertise in specialised percutaneous lymphatic intervention represent the most relevant advances of the last decade.

title: Evaluating the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence for pediatric appendicular fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Pediatric fracture detection on plain radiographs can be challenging, and missed fractures can have important clinical consequences. Artificial intelligence has been increasingly investigated as a tool to support fracture detection in children. Objectives This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence models for detecting appendicular fractures on pediatric radiographs. Materials and methods A comprehensive literature search was conducted from inception through February 1, 2026. Studies evaluating AI models for detecting appendicular fractures in pediatric populations using plain radiographs were included. Pooled sensitivities and specificities were calculated using bivariate random-effects meta-analysis, and subgroup analyses were performed based on anatomical site, unit of analysis, and comparator type. Results Sixteen studies were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity for standalone AI models were 92.0% (95% CI, 90.4-93.4%) and 87.9% (95% CI, 84.5-90.6%), respectively, with an hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) area under the curve of 0.96. Considerable heterogeneity was observed (I 2 , 49-78%). No significant differences were found between per-image and per-patient analyses (P=0.78). Differences in diagnostic performance among physicians using AI models, standalone AI models, and physicians without AI models were not significant (P=0.20). Fagan nomogram analysis demonstrated that at 50% pre-test probability, a positive AI result increased post-test probability to 90%, while a negative result reduced it to 7%. Conclusion AI models demonstrate considerable diagnostic accuracy for detecting pediatric appendicular fractures on radiography. Considerable heterogeneity and concerns regarding real-life implementation highlight the need for prospective studies with standardized methodologies.

title: Evaluation of the relationship between the anatomical and morphometric characteristics of the sphenoid sinus in the paediatric population.
abstract: Objectives The aim was to analyse the morphological characteristics of the sphenoid sinus in the paediatric population and the possible effects of sex and age on the prevalence of pneumatization. Methods Patients in the 0-16 age group were determined as the paediatric group, and patients 16+ years of age were determined as the control group. Sphenoid sinus measurements and pneumatization classification were performed by two maxillofacial radiologists. Sphenoid sinus pneumatizations are divided into three groups: sellar, clival, and lateral. Results Types of right lateral pneumatization show significant differences between age groups (P=0.023). Lat-D type was significantly more prevalent in control group, while Lat-B type was observed only in the paediatric group. Like the right side, left lateral pneumatization types also showed statistically significant differences between age groups (P=0.013). Lat-D type is significantly more common in control group, while Lat-C is more frequently observed in the paediatric group. In terms of symmetry, there is a borderline significant difference between age groups (P≈0.05). While the height of the sphenoid sinus exhibited a weak positive correlation with the length of the optic chiasm (R=0.273, P<0.001), the anteroposterior length and width of the sphenoid sinus both demonstrated moderate positive correlations with the intercarotid distance (R=0.333 and R=0.435, P<0.001). Conclusion Lateral pneumatization type showed significant age-related changes. Optic chiasm length correlated with sphenoid sinus height, while intercarotid distance correlated with both sphenoid sinus anteroposterior length and width.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of 3D MRI rendering techniques for evaluation of hourglass-like constrictions in Parsonage-Turner syndrome.
abstract: Objective To evaluate inter-reader agreement and diagnostic accuracy of curved multiplanar reformatting (cMPR) and maximum intensity projection (MIP) techniques for detecting hourglass-like constrictions (HGCs). Materials and methods Thirty brachial plexus 3-Tesla, 3D, 1-mm isotropic MR neurography (MRN) datasets (10 patients without and 20 patients with Parsonage-Turner syndrome (PTS) affecting the suprascapular nerve (SSN)) were retrospectively analyzed by four musculoskeletal radiology fellows for the number and severity of HGCs using both post-processing views in a randomized, blinded fashion. An experienced, attending radiologist served as the reference standard. Inter-reader agreement was assessed using Gwet's AC1 and intraclass correlation (ICC). Image interpretation time was compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results Inter-reader agreement for HGC presence was substantial to almost perfect among fellows (cMPR AC1 = 0.7, MIP AC1 = 0.67) and when compared to the attending (cMPR AC1 = 0.67-0.83, MIP AC1 = 0.63-0.83). Agreement for severe HGC count was substantial to almost perfect (fellows: cMPR ICC = 0.65, MIP ICC = 0.79; vs. attending: ICC = 0.62-0.83, MIP ICC = 0.69-0.88), but poor to fair for mild HGCs (fellows: cMPR ICC = 0.23, MIP ICC = 0.26; vs. attending: ICC = 0-0.21, MIP ICC = 0-0.09). Sensitivity to HGC presence was excellent (cMPR, 85-100%; MIP, 90-100%), though specificity (cMPR, 50-100%; MIP, 40-90%) and diagnostic accuracy (cMPR, 80-90%; MIP, 76-90%) varied. The MIP method required significantly less interpretation time than cMPR (median: 33 vs. 104 s, p < 0.001). Conclusion High inter-reader agreement and sensitivity but variable specificity for HGC detection suggest both techniques are viable tools for MRN, with cMPR better suited for detailed HGC evaluation and MIP for initial screening.

title: Sports-related peripheral neuropathies in athletes: mechanisms, imaging evaluation, and sport-specific patterns.
abstract: Peripheral neuropathy in athletes is increasingly recognized as a significant source of morbidity, with injury patterns varying according to the biomechanical demands of specific sports. Although peripheral nerve disorders in athletes may result from acute trauma, they more commonly arise from chronic, repetitive mechanical stress inherent to athletic activity. Despite their frequency, they frequently remain underdiagnosed, as clinical manifestations often overlap with other musculoskeletal disorders. Mechanisms of injury include compression, traction, laceration, ischemia, and repetitive microtrauma. Distinct athletic modalities are associated with characteristic neuropathies reflecting sport-specific kinematics and loading patterns. Awareness of these biomechanical factors and recognition of typical clinical presentations are essential for accurate assessment of athletes with suspected nerve injury. Diagnostic evaluation frequently requires advanced imaging modalities, particularly magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) and high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS), which enable detailed structural assessment of peripheral nerves and detection of secondary imaging findings. Electrodiagnostic studies may provide complementary functional information in selected cases. Early and precise diagnosis is critical to guide management, facilitate safe return to sport, and prevent long-term functional deficits. While most nerve disorders respond to conservative treatment, severe, progressive, or refractory cases may warrant surgical intervention to restore function and enable return to play (RTP). This review examines mechanisms of injury, clinical evaluation, classification systems, imaging findings, and sport-specific patterns of peripheral nerve injury across diverse athletic disciplines.
