title: Systemic immune-inflammation index predicts neurological recovery in degenerative cervical myelopathy: a comparative analysis of OPLL and non-OPLL patients.
abstract: Purpose To compare systemic inflammatory characteristics between patients with ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) and non-OPLL degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) and to evaluate the prognostic value of the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), alone and in combination with radiological parameters, for postoperative neurological recovery. Methods This retrospective prognostic cohort study included 317 surgically treated patients with DCM (98 with OPLL and 219 without OPLL) with complete 2-year follow-up data. Neurological and clinical outcomes were assessed using the visual analog scale (VAS), Neck Disability Index (NDI), modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score, and mJOA recovery rate; patients were categorized as having favorable recovery (mJOA recovery rate ≥ 50%; n = 231) or unfavorable recovery (< 50%; n = 86). Preoperative hematologic inflammatory indices, including the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and SII, serum biochemical profiles, surgical characteristics, and cervical radiological parameters were collected. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was used to assess maximum spinal cord compression (MSCC), maximum canal compromise (MCC), transverse area (TA), and compression ratio (CR). Full multivariable logistic regression models identified factors independently associated with favorable recovery. Sensitivity analyses separately adjusted for surgical approach, surgical procedure, and the numbers of decompressed and fused levels. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed discriminative performance and optimal cutoffs. Predictors that remained independently associated with favorable recovery in the full multivariable models were retained, and parsimonious logistic regression models were refitted for ROC analysis, nomogram construction, and internal validation. The combined scores represented weighted linear predictors from the corresponding refitted SII-TA models and were not predicted probabilities. Internal validation was performed using 1,000 bootstrap resamples; calibration was assessed using calibration curves and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, and clinical net benefit was evaluated using decision curve analysis. Results Patients with OPLL had significantly higher white blood cell (WBC) counts and SII values than those without OPLL. In the overall cohort, lower SII and larger TA were independently associated with favorable neurological recovery. A combined predictive score was derived from the refitted parsimonious model as follows: Score = - 0.202 + 5.697 × TA - 0.294 × (SII/100). Score ≥ 0.50 was identified as the optimal cutoff for predicting favorable neurological recovery. ROC analysis further identified cutoff values of SII ≤ 556.5 and TA ≥ 0.405 cm² as predictors of favorable outcomes. Subgroup analyses suggested differing predictor patterns between the OPLL and non-OPLL groups. In the OPLL subgroup, lower SII remained independently associated with favorable neurological recovery, with an optimal cutoff value of SII ≤ 558.4. In contrast, in patients with non-OPLL DCM, a distinct combined predictive score was derived from the refitted parsimonious model: Score = - 0.453 + 5.522 × TA - 0.210 × (SII/100). Score ≥ 0.99 was identified as the optimal cutoff for predicting favorable neurological recovery. Corresponding ROC-derived thresholds of SII ≤ 390.6 and TA ≥ 0.445 cm² were identified for predicting favorable neurological recovery in this subgroup. The association between lower SII and favorable recovery remained significant after separate adjustment for each surgical characteristic. The optimism-corrected areas under the ROC curve were 0.749, 0.711, and 0.722 for the overall DCM, OPLL, and non-OPLL DCM models, respectively; goodness-of-fit tests did not indicate lack of fit, and decision curve analysis suggested potential clinical net benefit. Conclusion Systemic inflammatory burden, quantified by SII, was independently associated with long-term neurological recovery in patients with DCM. Subgroup analyses yielded different predictor patterns and SII cutoff estimates in the OPLL and non-OPLL groups; however, these findings should be considered exploratory and require external confirmation. Models integrating systemic inflammatory and radiological parameters may assist risk stratification, but their clinical utility should be established in independent prospective cohorts before implementation.

title: Cage rotation and effective rim support are associated with subsidence after TLIF using a single expandable banana-shaped cage design.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether postoperative cage obliquity and vertebral rim support are associated with 12-month subsidence after TLIF using a single articulating expandable banana-shaped cage design. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 101 patients (109 levels) treated with an articulating expandable banana-shaped cage. Postoperative CT was used to measure cage obliquity angle and cage-rim contact ratio. Subsidence was defined as ≥ 2 mm at 12 months. Spearman correlations were used to examine relationships between cage obliquity and rim-support metrics. Associations of cage obliquity and cage-rim contact with subsidence were evaluated using separate multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for Hounsfield units. Spatial heatmaps visualized the distribution of anterior rim support, which was further quantified using mediolateral contact metrics. Results Subsidence occurred in 16 levels (14.7%). Greater cage obliquity angle was associated with subsidence (OR 1.40 per 5°, 95% CI 1.10-1.84, p = 0.004), whereas greater cage-rim contact ratio was inversely associated with subsidence (OR 0.68 per 10%, 95% CI 0.51-0.90, p = 0.008). Cage obliquity was inversely correlated with cage-rim contact ratio (ρ = -0.370; p < 0.001) and mediolateral contact spread (ρ = -0.457; p < 0.001), but not with contact centroid. Fusion, radiographic correction loss, and patient-reported outcomes did not differ significantly by subsidence status. Conclusions In this single-design cohort, greater residual cage obliquity and reduced cage-rim contact ratio were associated with subsidence, identifying insufficient rotation and reduced effective anterior rim support as potentially modifiable technical factors. These findings provide a rationale for developing and prospectively evaluating intraoperative methods to assess cage rotation and optimize rim support, although the optimal rotational target and its preventive effect require further validation.

title: Atypical-laterality curve patterns in adult idiopathic scoliosis: refining the AdIS classification.
abstract: Purpose The objective of this study was to analyze the distribution of curve patterns in adult idiopathic scoliosis (AdIS) patients according to the AdIS classification by Lin et al. We also aim to identify the prevalence of atypical curve patterns that are not represented within the existing framework and propose a laterality modifier as an extension of the AdIS classification. Methods Adult idiopathic scoliosis patients aged above 18 years who underwent posterior spinal fusion (PSF) between 2023 and 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Radiographic parameters were measured using pre-operative whole spine radiographs. Curves were classified according to AdIS classification by Lin et. al. Reversed curve patterns not represented by the current AdIS classification were recorded as atypical-laterality variants with an added laterality modifier, denoted "R" (reversed). Descriptive statistical analysis was performed. Results A total of 215 patients were included. The existing AdIS classification successfully classified 92.6% of patients, whereas 7.4% exhibited atypical-laterality curve patterns. AdIS type 1 curves were the most prevalent (34.7%), followed by type 2 (17.6%) and type 6 (15.1%). The majority of curves demonstrated non-structural lumbosacral modifiers (89.4%) and preserved global alignment (98.0%). Among the atypical-laterality cases, AdIS 6-R and 5-R curves were the most numerically frequent subtypes, accounting for five (31.3%) and four (25.0%) cases respectively. Conclusion The AdIS classification demonstrated excellent applicability, successfully classifying 92.6% of patients in our study cohort. Atypical-laterality patterns were identified in 16 patients (7.4%), with AdIS 6-R being the commonest pattern encountered.

title: Probe-mediated subcellular organelles translocation enabled ratiometric quantification of nitroreductase activity and microviscosity for hypoxia imaging and precise tumor delineation.
abstract: Quantitative assessment of hypoxia-induced nitroreductase (NTR) upregulation and pathological viscosity elevation offers a critical diagnostic parameter for precise cancer diagnostics.​ We propose a subcellular organelle translocation strategy for ultrasensitive quantification of NTR/microviscosity and subsequent precise evaluation of tumor hypoxia levels. The constructed NTR-sensitive probe Cy826 releases the fluorophore Cy468 upon NTR catalysis, accompanied by a significant fluorescence turn-on response (21.9-fold enhancement) and subcellular organelle translocation from endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to lysosomes, which effectively reduced local probe accumulation and significantly alleviated the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) effect and spectral crosstalk in quantification process. The cyclen-based hemicyanine Cy468 is a fluorophore distinct from our previously reported Cy496, with near-infrared (NIR) emission (~ 720 nm), lower logP, and lysosomal rather than mitochondrial targeting. Cy826 displays high sensitivity (LOD = 8.2 ng/mL) and excellent selectivity toward NTR, along with a strong fluorescence enhancement under high viscosity and molecular crowding conditions. The probe also facilitates real-time monitoring of viscosity changes in ER and lysosomes, and dynamically responds to endogenous NTR activity under varying hypoxia levels. Moreover, after administration of Cy826, the considerable tumor-to-background ratio (TBR > 12) enables high-contrast imaging of hypoxic tumors from early to advanced stages with favorable biocompatibility and metabolic characteristics. Our subcellular organelle translocation strategy proposed in this study offers a novel approach to mitigating ACQ effect in quantification assignment, and the high-performance NIR fluorescent probe drafted in this work provides a prospective tool for precise tumor diagnosis and intraoperative navigation via multi-parameter imaging of hypoxic tumor microenvironment.

title: Endoscopic NIRAF-LSCI multimodal system with pseudo-color visualization for parathyroid autofluorescence localization and tissue perfusion assessment: preclinical validation.
abstract: Postoperative hypoparathyroidism remains a prevalent complication of thyroid surgery, primarily caused by unrecognized parathyroid gland (PG) injury or devascularization. While near-infrared autofluorescence (NIRAF) enables accurate PG localization, it provides no functional perfusion information; conversely, laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI) offers label-free real-time perfusion assessment. Herein, we validated a multimodal endoscopic system integrating NIRAF and LSCI for simultaneous PG identification and vascular evaluation, focusing on LSCI perfusion performance and the clinical practicability of its pseudo-color semi-quantitative visualization. The system was tested in 8 Sprague-Dawley rats, where rat thyroids with homologous blood supply served as perfusion surrogates due to the minute volume of rat PGs. Imaging was performed under three strictly controlled in situ conditions: intact native vascularization, partial vascular occlusion, and complete vascular occlusion. LSCI pseudo-color visualization was generated via a standardized pipeline including temporal laser speckle contrast analysis (tLASCA)-based blood flow index (BFI) calculation, baseline-anchored joint 5th-95th percentile normalization, and Jet colormap mapping. Intraoperative probe-based quantitative NIRAF was used to validate NIRAF-visual signal foci. NIRAF clearly identified PGs with a fluorescence intensity of 149.8 ± 8.7 mV, significantly higher than thyroid (93.8 ± 8.0 mV), trachea (84.6 ± 9.1 mV), and muscle (66.3 ± 10.4 mV) (all P < 0.001), achieving 100% positive predictive value (PPV) and 100% negative predictive value (NPV), with zero false-positive findings among all NIRAF-visual foci. PPV was determined using both probe-based NIRAF and histopathology as dual validation references, whereas NPV was determined using postoperative histopathology alone as the reference standard. LSCI speckle contrast increased progressively with decreasing perfusion, with speckle contrast values mapped to a continuous blue-to-red real-time pseudo-color perfusion visualization. Histopathology confirmed all fluorescent tissues as PGs. This multimodal system targets two core clinical needs for intraoperative PG protection, and its standardized pseudo-color semi-quantitative workflow provides real-time label-free perfusion visualization. It shows potential to serve as an intraoperative adjunct to guide parathyroid preservation decisions and reduce reliance on delayed hormonal test results.

Herein, we validated a multimodal endoscopic system integrating NIRAF and LSCI for simultaneous PG identification and vascular evaluation, focusing on LSCI perfusion performance and the clinical practicability of its pseudo-color semi-quantitative visualization. The system was tested in 8 Sprague-Dawley rats, where rat thyroids with homologous blood supply served as perfusion surrogates due to the minute volume of rat PGs. Imaging was performed under three strictly controlled in situ conditions: intact native vascularization, partial vascular occlusion, and complete vascular occlusion. LSCI pseudo-color visualization was generated via a standardized pipeline including temporal laser speckle contrast analysis (tLASCA)-based blood flow index (BFI) calculation, baseline-anchored joint 5th-95th percentile normalization, and Jet colormap mapping. Intraoperative probe-based quantitative NIRAF was used to validate NIRAF-visual signal foci. NIRAF clearly identified PGs with a fluorescence intensity of 149.8 ± 8.7 mV, significantly higher than thyroid (93.8 ± 8.0 mV), trachea (84.6 ± 9.1 mV), and muscle (66.3 ± 10.4 mV) (all P < 0.001), achieving 100% positive predictive value (PPV) and 100% negative predictive value (NPV), with zero false-positive findings among all NIRAF-visual foci. PPV was determined using both probe-based NIRAF and histopathology as dual validation references, whereas NPV was determined using postoperative histopathology alone as the reference standard. LSCI speckle contrast increased progressively with decreasing perfusion, with speckle contrast values mapped to a continuous blue-to-red real-time pseudo-color perfusion visualization. Histopathology confirmed all fluorescent tissues as PGs. This multimodal system targets two core clinical needs for intraoperative PG protection, and its standardized pseudo-color semi-quantitative workflow provides real-time label-free perfusion visualization. It shows potential to serve as an intraoperative adjunct to guide parathyroid preservation decisions and reduce reliance on delayed hormonal test results.

title: Standard anterior temporal lobectomy using a retractorless technique in patients with drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: long-term seizure outcomes and predictors of postoperative seizure freedom.
abstract: Background Fixed brain retractors risk focal ischemia and cortical injury. Although retractorless dynamic retraction is established in skull base surgery, its role in epilepsy surgery remains poorly characterized. Objective To evaluate long-term seizure outcomes, safety, and reliability of retractorless standard anterior temporal lobectomy (ATL) in drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), and identify predictors of seizure freedom. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 42 patients who underwent retractorless standard ATL for drug-resistant MTLE. Dynamic retraction used bipolar forceps and pressure-controlled suction. The primary outcome was seizure freedom (Engel Class Ia) at minimum 24-month follow-up; secondary outcomes were complications and resection adequacy on postoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models. Results At a mean follow-up of 66.3 months, 69% of patients achieved complete seizure freedom (Engel Class Ia), and 83.3% achieved freedom from disabling seizures (Engel Class I). Postoperative MRI confirmed adequate resection in 95.2% of cases. Complications were uncommon and unrelated to retraction injury. Low preoperative seizure frequency (< 3 seizures/week) was the sole independent predictor of seizure freedom (odds ratio, 24.21; P = 0.026), while higher frequency (≥ 3 seizures/week) was associated with increased recurrence risk (hazard ratio, 7.34; P = 0.042). Conclusion Retractorless standard ATL is safe and effective for drug-resistant MTLE, achieving long-term seizure control while minimizing retraction-associated risks. Preoperative seizure burden was the dominant prognostic marker, supporting early surgical intervention.

title: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to posterior third ventricle pathology: One or two burr hole approaches for ETV and biopsy.
abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) and tumor biopsy is a frequent procedure for third ventricular tumors. While some authors favor one approach to achieve both goals, others support the selection of two approaches to avoid fornical damage and venous hemorrhage. Here the authors present their experience with both techniques. A retrospective analysis was conducted on cases which underwent an ETV and a tumor procedure in lesions of the posterior third ventricle from 2011 to 2025. Patient records, pre- and postoperative imaging and intraoperative video recordings were retrospectively analyzed. Twenty-six patients met the inclusion criteria: 13 were treated with one, the other 13 with two approaches. The surgical goal of ETV and tumor biopsy/resection was achieved in all cases. No procedure was abandoned. No postoperative complication was observed. Intraoperative forniceal injury was observed in 8/26 patients (31%). Intraoperative bleeding was found in 81% (21/26 cases). In 19% of cases (5/26 cases), intraoperative bleeding required a longer irrigation time but no switch to dry field technique or open surgery was needed. On follow up, three patients required ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. Thus, ETV success scored 88.5% (23/26 cases). On 2D MRI, the mean intertrajectory angle was smaller in the one-burr-hole group than in the two-burr-hole group (41.8° ± 3.5° vs. 48.7° ± 5.4°; p = 0.001). Lesions of the posterior third ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus are ideal candidates for an endoscopic approach. The overall success rate is very high with acceptable surgical risks. In this cohort, larger intertrajectory angles were associated with selection of a two-burr-hole approach. The approximate 45° value was derived post hoc and requires external validation.

title: Automated Severity Grading of Lumbar Spinal Stenosis on Sagittal MRI Using a Two-Stage Deep Learning Framework with External Clinical Validation.
abstract: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is a prevalent degenerative condition and a major cause of disability in aging populations. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred modality for assessment; however, severity grading remains inconsistent across readers and institutions, limiting reproducibility and complicating clinical decision-making. This study presents LSS-Net, a two-stage deep learning framework for automated grading of central canal stenosis using sagittal T2-weighted MRI. The first stage performs vertebral localization using a single-stage object detector, enabling standardized extraction of intervertebral regions of interest. The second stage applies a Swin Transformer-based classifier to predict stenosis severity (Normal/Mild, Moderate, Severe). The framework was developed using a multi-center dataset of 1,975 studies and evaluated on a held-out subset. Vertebral localization achieved 97.9% F1-score, while severity classification reached a weighted F1-score of 77.1%. Performance was highest for Normal/Mild and Severe classes, with reduced accuracy observed in Moderate cases, reflecting known diagnostic ambiguity. External clinical validation was conducted on an independent dataset using two expert readers. The model demonstrated substantial agreement with a neurosurgeon (accuracy 75.1%, κ=0.73 ) and moderate agreement with a neuroradiologist (accuracy 51.0%, κ=0.56 ), with inter-expert agreement in a comparable range. These findings suggest that LSS-Net may support more consistent and reproducible LSS grading. However, performance limitations in borderline cases and the restricted use of single-slice sagittal input highlight the need for further validation and extension to multi-sequence and multi-compartment analysis before clinical deployment.

title: Active Learning and Cascaded nnU-Net v2 for Multi-structure Segmentation of Thoracic CT: A Single-Center Pilot Study.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of thoracic structures on chest computed tomography (CT) is important for lung cancer surgery, but manual annotation is labor intensive and particularly challenging for small structures such as pulmonary vessels and nodules. We compared four nnU-Net v2-based segmentation configurations: single-stage full-data training, active learning alone, cascaded segmentation alone, and active learning combined with cascaded segmentation in a retrospective single-center cohort. This retrospective study included chest CT scans from 85 patients. In the cascaded configurations, pulmonary lobes were segmented in the first stage to provide global anatomical context, followed by refinement of the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and nodules within the constrained region. All four configurations were evaluated using the same fixed patient-level internal test set of 30 patients, with segmentation performance assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). The full-data baseline achieved DSCs of 0.92-0.93 for the five pulmonary lobes, with lower performance for the bronchus (0.82), pulmonary vessels (0.67), and pulmonary nodules (0.78). The combined active learning and cascaded configuration improved lobar DSCs to 0.94-0.96. Compared with the baseline, DSC increased to 0.90, 0.77, and 0.86 for the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and pulmonary nodules, respectively (all p < 0.05), while HD95 decreased from 5.4 to 2.5 mm for pulmonary vessels and from 4.8 to 2.1 mm for pulmonary nodules. In this single-center cohort, cascaded segmentation strategies showed improved internal test performance for small thoracic structures, supporting further evaluation in larger multicenter cohorts.

title: DINOv3-SAM: Fusing Semantic and Anatomical Foundation Models for Robust Medical Image Classification.
abstract: Robust medical image classification remains a persistent challenge due to heterogeneous acquisition protocols, label noise, and subtle inter-class variability. In chest radiography, these difficulties are compounded by shortcut learning from non-anatomical artifacts and projection variability, which severely undermine generalization. To address these limitations, we propose DINOv3-SAM, a dual-encoder framework that synergistically integrates complementary visual representations. The architecture combines a self-supervised DINOv3 vision transformer, which captures global semantic context, with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) image encoder, which provides anatomy-aware spatial features. The two feature streams are spatially aligned and adaptively refined through a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), which emphasizes informative channels and diagnostically relevant regions prior to classification. Notably, only the final DINOv3 layers are fine-tuned while SAM remains frozen, yielding a computationally efficient framework with only 5.3 million trainable parameters. We evaluate DINOv3-SAM across five public datasets spanning diverse modalities and diagnostic tasks: pediatric pneumonia classification, cardiomegaly detection, large-scale RSNA pneumonia detection, COVID-19 radiography, and dermatological lesion classification. A unified stratified train/validation/test protocol ensures consistent and fair evaluation across both binary and multi-class settings. Each configuration was trained three times with different random seeds, and comprehensive comparisons against reproduced CNN baselines and published state-of-the-art methods, supported by statistical significance testing, demonstrate improvements across most datasets and metrics. The proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 94.94% (±3.06) on pediatric pneumonia, 97.24% (±0.77) accuracy (AUC 0.998 ±0.001) on COVID-19 radiography, and a mean AUC of 0.8705 (±0.0445) on the challenging RSNA benchmark. These results underscore the efficacy of fusing self-supervised semantic representations with segmentation-informed anatomical cues to enhance robustness against dataset bias, acquisition variability, and cross-domain shifts. The proposed approach offers a reliable foundation for multi-dataset and multi-modality medical image classification in research-oriented decision-support systems.

title: MDF-Net: A Decoupled Multimodal Fusion Network with Contrastive Learning for Reliable Brain Tumor Segmentation on Multi-sequence MRI.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of brain tumors from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is critical for clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal disease monitoring. Multimodal MRI provides complementary information across sequences, yet this complementarity is entangled with substantial cross-modal redundancy. Prevailing coupled fusion schemes merge modalities into a single shared space, where discriminative tumor-specific cues and redundant shared content are blended indiscriminately, an effect further aggravated by cross-scale feature inconsistency and by the difficulty of delineating small enhancing lesions. To address these issues, we recast multimodal segmentation as a decoupled representation learning problem and propose a Multimodal Decoupled Fusion Network (MDF-Net) that explicitly disentangles the fused representation into complementary and non-redundant components. At its core, a Tri-Branch Decoupling (TBD) module separates the fused features into spatial, channel, and instance components, and a Feature Contrastive Learning (FCL) objective enforces their complementarity while suppressing inter-branch redundancy. To provide scale-aware and locally coherent features for decoupling, an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module and a Local Window Self-Attention (LWSA) module jointly model multi-scale context and local dependencies, while a dedicated Small Lesion Refinement (SLR) module improves the delineation of small and ambiguous enhancing tumors through multi-scale detection and boundary-aware refinement. Extensive experiments on two publicly available benchmarks, BraTS 2023 and FeTS 2022, demonstrate that MDF-Net achieves competitive and well-balanced performance relative to recent state-of-the-art methods across tumor sub-regions and multiple evaluation metrics, with particularly accurate whole-tumor boundary delineation. Ablation studies and feature-space visualizations further confirm that explicit decoupling yields a more structured embedding space and that each component makes a complementary contribution to segmentation performance.

title: Predictive Nomogram for High Ki-67 Expression using Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound of Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Identifying reliable prognostic factors for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is challenging, thereby complicating treatment and follow-up decisions. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS)-based nomogram to predict high Ki-67 expression in ccRCC. This retrospective study analysed 312 patients from two centres (training, n = 212; validation, n = 100) who underwent preoperative CEUS. Postoperative pathology confirmed ccRCC. Immunohistochemistry assessed Ki-67 expression and CD34-positive microvascular density (CD34 + MVD). A nomogram was developed using multivariate logistic regression and validated based on the area under the curve (AUC). Predictive performance was compared with tumour-node-metastasis (TNM) staging and World Health Organisation/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grading using the DeLong test. Spearman's correlation coefficients were compared among CD34 + MVD, WHO/ISUP grade, and Ki-67 expression. Significant predictors of high Ki-67 expression included tumour diameter ≥ 3.85 cm (odds ratio [OR]: 1.525, 95% confidence interval: 1.054-2.205), washout time ≤ 34.7 s (OR: 0.942, 95% Cl: 0.911-0.975), and necrosis ≥ 9.158% (OR: 1.105, 95% Cl: 1.021-1.195). The nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.858 (training set) and 0.810 (validation set), outperforming TNM staging (AUC: 0.733) and WHO/ISUP grading (AUC: 0.761). Ki-67 expression correlated negatively with CD34+MVD (r = -0.632) and positively with WHO/ISUP grading (r=0.620), whereas CD34+MVD expression was negatively correlated with WHO/ISUP grading (r = -0.607). The CEUS-based nomogram demonstrated superior predictive accuracy for high Ki-67 expression compared with TNM staging and WHO/ISUP grading, supporting its potential for personalised treatment and more precise follow-up surveillance programmes.

title: Skull-Base Synthetic CT from Brain MRI: Development, Independent-Center Validation, and Radiologist Evaluation.
abstract: We developed and evaluated a deep learning pipeline for skull-base synthetic computed tomography (sCT) generation from routine non-contrast T1-weighted and T2-weighted brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), focusing on clinically relevant bony anatomy for neurosurgical and radiotherapy workflows. We retrospectively collected 184 manually registered T1/T2/CT triplets for training and internal validation (166/18 split) and 43 cases from a second center for independent-center validation. A three-dimensional Swin-UNETR generator was trained with bone-weighted multiscale reconstruction, perceptual, and adversarial losses. Two board-certified radiologists independently scored 16 skull-base structures, artifacts, and diagnostic acceptability on raw sCT in Hounsfield units (HU), without histogram matching; this blinded review was the primary endpoint. Acceptability was 76.7% for Rater 1 and 67.4% for Rater 2 (pooled 72.1%, cluster-robust 95% CI 58.5-82.6%), with mean structure scores from 2.67 to 4.85 out of 5. Raw sCT showed limited absolute HU calibration (global MAE 364±50 HU, bone Dice 0.38±0.09 ), with a compressed dynamic range in which air and soft tissue were overestimated and dense bone underestimated; histogram-matched outputs, reported as a secondary analysis, reached bone Dice 0.88±0.03 and bone MAE 26.31±5.03 HU. Halo artifacts were near-universal, and false-canal artifacts occurred in 21-30% of cases. The method shows promise as a radiation-free adjunct for skull-base visualization, but the present results do not support replacing dedicated CT for diagnostic, dosimetric, or physics-based applications.

title: Multi-task Model with​ Peritumoral MRI Radiomics Learning for Breast Cancer Segmentation-Guided Subtype Classification.
abstract: Accurate breast cancer molecular subtype classification is important for treatment planning, but immunohistochemical assessment may be affected by intratumoral heterogeneity and requires invasive tissue sampling. We hypothesize that segmentation-guided learning of tumor-core and peritumoral microenvironment (PTM) MRI features would improve molecular subtype discrimination over tumor-core-only analysis. A transformer-based segmentation network integrates cross-modal and multi-scale features to delineate tumors, after which the predicted masks are used to construct tumor-core and peritumoral inputs for an energy-regularized classification network. On the test cohort, the retrospective single-center study includes 381 patients with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer and corresponding DCE, DWI, T1WI, and T2WI images. The proposed method achieves a Dice coefficient of 88.29%, a Jaccard index of 79.80%, a precision of 91.98%, and a 95HD of 4.03 pixels for tumor segmentation. For molecular subtype classification, it achieves an accuracy of 84.0%, a macro-averaged sensitivity of 85.7%, a macro-averaged specificity of 94.8%, and a macro-averaged F1 score of 83.9%, providing the best overall performance among the evaluated methods. These findings support further evaluation of segmentation-guided multimodal MRI analysis for preoperative molecular subtype assessment.

title: Performance of Deep Learning Algorithms for Segmentation of Shoulder Anatomy on MRI: A Systematic Review.
abstract: To synthesize the performance and methodological characteristics of fully automated deep learning algorithms for shoulder magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) segmentation. This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. CENTRAL, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched from inception through July 17, 2026. The protocol specified fully automated deep learning-based pixel-wise segmentation of shoulder MRI, an expert-derived MRI-space reference standard, and quantitative segmentation metrics. Two reviewers independently screened records; unresolved disagreements were adjudicated by a senior reviewer. Overlapping datasets were linked during synthesis. Of 354 identified records, 169 duplicates were removed, 185 records were screened, and 53 full-text reports were assessed. Thirty-five reports were included (31 journal articles and 4 full conference papers; 2018-2026). U-Net-based encoder-decoder architectures predominated, with additional region-based, transformer, adversarial, and autoencoder approaches. Dice similarity coefficients ranged from approximately 0.81-0.99 for osseous targets, 0.71-0.99 for shoulder muscles, and 0.58-0.94 for tendon or tear regions; intersection-over-union values for tear or surgical-planning regions ranged from 0.45-0.83. MRI protocols and validation designs were heterogeneous, and most reports described retrospective single-center investigations. Five reports used independent external test sets; several others included multicenter images. Overlapping cohorts precluded a valid pooled participant count. Deep learning achieved high accuracy for shoulder bones and rotator-cuff muscles in selected datasets, whereas tear-region performance was more variable. Multicenter patient-level validation and standardized annotation and reporting are needed before routine clinical deployment.

title: ParetoRx: A Multiobjective Radiogenomic Framework Integrating Pareto Optimization and Q-Learning for Exploratory Compound Prioritization in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Imaging-defined high-risk phenotypes may capture biologically aggressive disease states, but translating them into therapeutic hypotheses remains challenging. We developed ParetoRx, a radiogenomic imaging-informatics framework integrating computed tomography radiomics, pathway-level transcriptomic analysis, multiobjective Pareto optimization, and model-free Q-learning for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Pretreatment CT data from 402 patients were used for model development and internal validation, with 110 patients forming a held-out external cohort. The final radiomics model achieved an external C-index of 0.707 (95% CI 0.627-0.783); high-risk patients had worse overall survival (HR 3.461, 95% CI 1.674-7.153), with minimal change after adjustment for histology (HR 3.444, 95% CI 1.662-7.137). Gene set enrichment and single-sample pathway analyses identified exploratory associations involving E2F targets, MYC targets V1, inflammatory response, and hypoxia, although no pathway met FDR < 0.05. LINCS L1000 perturbational profiles were evaluated using transcriptomic reversal, pathway specificity, and a feasibility-related proxy, with 4188 compounds retained in the common complete-case analysis. Multiobjective Pareto optimization was combined with three-split consensus ranking and sequential policy evaluation. TWS-119 showed consistent prioritization across all three splits (ranks 1, 3, and 4) and was Pareto-optimal in each split. In simulation-based evaluation, model-free Q-learning achieved higher terminal-goal attainment than myopic and static policies across all three splits, with improvements of approximately 6.2-13.3 percentage points over the myopic comparator. These findings support ParetoRx as an exploratory framework for biologically informed compound prioritization and computational sequential decision-making, while independent drug response and clinical validation remain necessary.

title: Diffusion Prior-Driven Vision-Language Adaptation for Few-Shot Medical Anomaly Detection.
abstract: Unsupervised medical anomaly detection faces dual challenges of pathological data scarcity and domain gaps when transferring general-purpose vision-language models to fine-grained tasks. This study aims to address the misalignment between global semantic representations and local pathological nuances by proposing a novel hybrid supervision framework. We propose a flexible vision-language adaptation framework in which diffusion-based pseudo-anomaly synthesis serves as an optional training enhancement. For CheXpert and BUSI, region-guided diffusion generates localized pseudo-anomalies to provide additional discriminative supervision. For BrainMRI, the framework is trained exclusively on normal reference images without any synthetic anomaly augmentation, allowing us to assess its effectiveness independently of the diffusion synthesis component. The architecture incorporates a local-enhanced feature rectifier to enhance local textural representation, a zero-initialized hypersphere-aligned residual adapter for stable cross-modal manifold alignment, and a temperature-scaled mapmaker for multi-scale dense anomaly localization. Performance was evaluated across three medical imaging modalities under multiple few-shot configurations. Our method remains highly competitive compared to state-of-the-art approaches in terms of image-level detection and pixel-level localization. On the ultrasound dataset under a 32-shot setting, the framework achieved an image-level area under the curve of 94.2% and a pixel-level area under the curve of 96.6%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework across the evaluated medical imaging modalities under different training configurations. In particular, its competitive performance on BrainMRI without synthetic anomaly augmentation suggests that the vision-language adaptation framework can remain effective when offline pseudo-anomaly generation is unavailable. The code involved in this study is publicly available on website https://github.com/SWLee777/DiffVLA .

title: Propagation of Low-Dose-Induced Noise Characteristics Across Deep Learning Layers in CT Imaging.
abstract: Dose reduction in computed tomography (CT) imaging impacts diagnostic accuracy for human observers and potentially artificial intelligence (AI) systems. As noise propagates through an AI model, its characteristics change, possibly influencing model performance. This study aims to develop a configurable low-dose CT simulation tool in image-space and analyze noise behavior in deep learning (DL) layers. The noise characteristics were quantified using the noise power spectrum (NPS) within homogeneous phantom regions. NPS area under the curve (intensity) and median frequency (texture) were reported. Low-dose CT images were simulated using a custom program that was calibrated for configurable noise intensity and texture. Noise was generated at texture levels. Pre-trained U-Net features were extracted from reference and simulated low-dose images, enabling NPS-based analysis of noise propagation across deep learning layers. NPS from simulated low-dose CT images matched reference NPS for various intensity and texture values. Feature analysis revealed progressive convergence of noise characteristics across deep learning layers, with batch normalization mitigating amplification observed after convolution and ReLU activation. Differences in noise texture between low-dose simulations converge along the U-Net contracting path. The image-space simulation tool offers a viable alternative for researchers lacking access to raw data, supporting future AI-focused dose optimization studies. However, whether these outcomes translate to segmentation performance remains unclear and warrants further investigation.

title: Diagnostic Performance and Calibration of AI Models for Thyroid Ultrasound Malignancy Classification: From TN5000 to ThyroidXL.
abstract: We evaluated cross-dataset transportability of three frozen encoders for binary benign-versus-malignant thyroid ultrasound classification using expert-defined nodule regions and one external cohort. Logistic regression classifiers using DINOv2, TinyUSFM, and ResNet18 features were developed on 3500 TN5000 images, calibrated on 477 duplicate-clean validation images and tested on 958 images. External evaluation used maximum image scores from 2083 ThyroidXL images in 739 patients with cytological or histopathological outcomes. No external retraining, recalibration or threshold adjustment was performed. Additional analyses evaluated four classifiers, encoder-recommended preprocessing and calibration intercepts and slopes. Internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were 0.9081 for TinyUSFM, 0.8946 for DINOv2, and 0.8896 for ResNet18. Primary external AUROCs were 0.8464 (95% confidence interval, 0.8164-0.8731), 0.7954, and 0.7833, respectively. Sensitivities at frozen high-sensitivity thresholds were 0.9972, 0.9717, and 0.9887, but specificities were 0.1736, 0.1891, and 0.1373. External calibration intercepts were negative; slopes were 0.891, 0.645, and 0.697. DINOv2 ranked first externally with four of five classifiers. With recommended preprocessing, ResNet18 ranked first numerically (0.8329 versus 0.8214 for DINOv2); their paired difference was inconclusive. Encoder rankings depended on the classifier and preprocessing. These results apply to the three evaluated implementations, not pretraining strategies generally. Transported patient scores overestimated malignancy and had low specificity. Prospective assessment is needed before clinical use.

title: Critical Validation of Deep Learning-Based Cervical Vertebral Fracture Detection on Computed Tomography Localizer Radiographs.
abstract: Localizer radiographs are low-resolution two-dimensional overview images acquired prior to computed tomography (CT) scans. Their automated analysis could support the early detection of cervical vertebral fractures in trauma patients and thus enable immediate adjustment of imaging protocols. This study investigated to what extent deep learning-based methods can reliably detect such fractures on localizer radiographs, with a focus on critically validating model behavior beyond standard performance metrics. On a custom-annotated dataset of 346 trauma patients, two approaches were compared: a full-image binary classification and a two-step pipeline that first localizes the cervical spine and then classifies the cropped region. Model validity was assessed through a permutation test, occlusion testing, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, an analysis of potential confounders, and a subgroup analysis by anatomical fracture location. The full-image classifier formally achieved the highest test-set performance with a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.477, compared with 0.349 for the cervical-spine-level classifier. Our validity analysis indicates that the full-image classifier does not primarily rely on the fracture region itself, rendering it unsuitable for clinical use. This work therefore presents a case study of shortcut learning and illustrates validation methods that may be of value for comparable studies on small datasets with visually subtle targets.

title: The Deep Learning-Based Prediction Method for Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis of Thyroid Cancer Based on Multimodal Data.
abstract: Thyroid cancer is a common malignant tumor worldwide, and there is a risk of misdiagnosis or over-treatment for small-sized thyroid cancer. The key to eliminating this risk lies in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis. The traditional manual prediction methods are not ideal, so this paper proposes an intelligent prediction method based on deep learning. This method is based on common clinical examination data, including ultrasound images, ultrasound image text descriptions, and blood test data. A deep convolutional neural network model is proposed using data from these three modalities as inputs. The model integrates multimodal data features through mean cross-attention and extracts fine-grained classification information from the fused feature map through a bilinear CNN network, demonstrating strong feature discrimination ability. Through collecting data and conducting various experiments, the experimental results show that the model proposed in this paper has good performance in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis, is better than the manual prediction, and has broad application prospects. Future research will continue to strive for data collection, increasing the amount of collected data and improving multi-center representativeness, and enhancing the diagnostic and predictive capabilities of the network model through technological improvements.

title: Nondisease Sources of Radiomic Texture Variation on Plain Radiographs: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Anatomical Region, Projection, and Resolution in a Public Fracture Archive.
abstract: Radiomic texture features from plain radiographs feed machine learning models on the assumption that they reflect tissue rather than anatomy or acquisition. In a public multihospital fracture archive, we quantified how anatomical region and radiographic projection, each adjusted for the other and for image resolution, shift 17 radiomic features, how much feature variance resolution explains, and a bony superimposition contrast defined within region. This retrospective cross-sectional secondary analysis used FracAtlas (4083 musculoskeletal radiographs from three hospitals); 4024 images were analyzed. For each z-scored feature (10 first-order, 7 Gy-level co-occurrence matrix [GLCM]), linear models estimated adjusted differences (β, SD units), and resolution by variance explained (R 2 ), with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction within each factor. Superimposition (hip and shoulder vs hand and leg; n = 3630), a grouping of regions, was analyzed as a pooled regional contrast rather than an independent factor. Region shifted 16 of 17 features (radiomic uniformity, hand vs leg - 0.66 SD [95% CI - 0.72 to - 0.59]). Resolution explained up to 16.8% of single-feature variance and changed the fracture log-odds coefficient by more than 15% for 7 of 10 interpretable features. Projection had the smallest effects (radiomic 10th percentile, lateral vs frontal - 0.32 SD). The superimposition contrast produced the largest shifts (GLCM energy - 2.26 SD [95% CI - 2.36 to - 2.16]). Radiomic texture on plain radiographs varies substantially with anatomy and acquisition, independently of fracture status. Radiograph radiomics studies should record and adjust for region, projection, and resolution, report region-specific estimates, and validate across sites.

title: Panognostics-Plus: An Integrated Multi-Task AI Framework for Automated Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation with Dental Charting and Structured Reporting-Development and Technical Validation Study.
abstract: Dental charting from panoramic radiographs is essential for clinical assessment, yet remains time-consuming. This study presents Panognostics-Plus, an automated cloud-based AI framework for panoramic radiograph analysis integrating dental charting and structured radiological reporting. Panognostics-Plus was developed using a retrospective dataset of 1,595 panoramic radiographs and a YOLO-based architecture comprising modules for dental anatomy, dental treatment, and periapical diagnostics. Anatomical structures and dental treatments were analyzed using a two-stage pipeline, whereas periapical lesions were analyzed by detection-and-classification. YOLOv8m, YOLOv9m, YOLO11m, and YOLO26m were benchmarked. Detection was evaluated by precision, sensitivity, F1-score, AP, and mAP; segmentation by IoU and Dice; and processing time. Model differences were assessed using Friedman tests with Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons. YOLO26m achieved the highest overall performance. The largest mAP0@50:0.95 gains were observed for crowns (+ 21.3%), radicular cysts (+ 20.5%), root canal treatments (+ 17.3%), bridges (+ 14.3%), periodontal bone level (+ 14.3%), and periapical granulomas (+ 13.5%). Dental implants achieved precision, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.99, 0.98, and 0.98, respectively. Radicular cysts achieved precision, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.95, 0.93, and 0.94 versus 0.92, 0.90, and 0.91 for periapical granulomas. Significant differences were observed in 8 of 10 detection tasks and all segmentation tasks (all p < 0.001); periodontal bone level (p = 0.193) and dental fillings (p = 0.073) were nonsignificant. Dice coefficients reached 0.97 for dental anatomy and 0.96 for dental treatments. The workflow generated a segmentation overlay, dental chart, and structured radiological report in 15 ± 1.4 s per radiograph. Panognostics-Plus may improve panoramic radiograph analysis and clinical efficiency, although further validation is required.

title: Data Leakage and Unverified Provenance in Public Brain Tumor MRI Datasets: A Systematic Audit.
abstract: Brain tumor MRI classification studies routinely report accuracies above 99%, yet many public datasets in this domain trace to a few original sources and are often combined or cross-validated without accounting for shared origin. We audited seven brain tumor MRI datasets (34,525 images) for leakage within datasets and overlap between datasets typically treated as independent. Internal leakage was detected with perceptual hashing and rotation-aware structural similarity. Cross-dataset overlap was detected with ResNet-50 embedding similarity, checked against a random-pair baseline, a DenseNet-121 sensitivity analysis, and blinded two-rater review (all 75 sampled above-threshold pairs were true duplicates; 95% CI 95.1-100). A further blinded review just below the threshold found roughly half of the sampled pairs were also duplicates, so reported overlap is a lower bound. True-duplicate leakage between training and evaluation splits occurred in three of four datasets with predefined splits, including a peer-reviewed dataset and one documented as overlap-free. For 14 of 16 dataset pairs, 15.6-99.1% of the smaller dataset's images were automatically matched to the other, including datasets described as collected from named hospitals. In a controlled experiment on the one dataset with patient identifiers, image-level splitting yielded higher accuracy than patient-level splitting (97.10 ± 0.69% vs. 91.82 ± 2.77%; Welch's t-test, p = 0.017), with a 10.1-point drop in meningioma F1. This addresses within-dataset correlation only, so it is a conservative estimate of total inflation. Reported performance warrants cautious interpretation, and tooling for verifying dataset independence is lacking. We propose a checklist for dataset creators and researchers.

title: Clinical Context-Dependent Value of bpMRI-Derived Imaging Representations for Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification.
abstract: The objective was to evaluate the clinical context-dependent value of biparametric MRI (bpMRI)-derived imaging representations for prostate cancer (PCa) risk stratification, with emphasis on whether imaging features provide complementary information in patients within the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) gray zone. This dual-campus retrospective study included 536 patients with pathologically confirmed PCa who underwent pretreatment bpMRI. Patients were classified as low/intermediate and high-risk according to NCCN criteria. Patients from Campus 1 were randomly divided into training and internal test cohorts, and Campus 2 served as an independent test cohort. Radiomics, vision transformer, and contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) features were extracted from T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging, and apparent diffusion coefficient maps. Clinical and combined clinical-imaging models were developed. Performance was assessed using ROC analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, and SHAP interpretation, with predefined evaluation in the PSA gray zone. In the independent test cohort, the combined model achieved the highest overall discrimination, with an AUC of 0.921, followed closely by the clinical baseline model (AUC, 0.907). Among imaging-only models, the radiomics model showed the highest overall AUC (0.844). SHAP identified PSA as the dominant predictor, indicating clinically driven overall performance. In the PSA gray zone, clinical and combined model performance declined (AUCs, 0.381 and 0.600), whereas CLIP achieved the highest AUC (0.785) and favorable net benefit. The value of bpMRI-derived imaging representations for PCa risk stratification is context-dependent. CLIP-derived representations may provide complementary discrimination when PSA-based information is less informative, supporting context-aware evaluation of imaging AI models.

title: CrossBoneNet: An Ultralightweight Hybrid CNN-ViT Architecture via Asymmetric Reversed Cross-Attention for Radiographic Fracture Detection.
abstract: Misdiagnoses in emergency departments are often associated with the difficulty in interpreting radiological findings on bone fractures due to millimetric fractures, overlapping bones, or superimpositions. Despite the high efficiency of state-of-the-art models in diagnosing such cases, their massive computational requirements severely hinder their implementation on resource-constrained devices in real-world clinical settings. In this study, we propose an ultralightweight CNN-ViT model, CrossBoneNet, which is designed for edge AI compatibility with minimal memory requirements. CrossBoneNet combines local microfracture detection using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and global anatomical recognition using vision transformers (ViTs). The model merges features from both architectures using the proposed asymmetric reversed cross-attention, where CNN features act as queries and ViT features act as keys and values-to efficiently map fine-grained local anomalies into a broader global anatomical context. Operating with a minimal parameter count (0.593 M) and low computational cost (1.527 GFLOPs), CrossBoneNet achieved a PR-AUC of 0.8498 ± 0.0086 and a ROC-AUC of 0.8427 ± 0.0072 on the MURA dataset in a patient-wise isolated evaluation. It achieves highly competitive performance-remaining within a 4% margin of the 88.59 million parameter ConvNeXt-Base model-while delivering over 99% memory savings. After fine-tuning on the FracAtlas dataset, CrossBoneNet achieved a specificity of 0.9760 ± 0.0080 and PR-AUC of 0.7568 ± 0.0414, demonstrating effective cross-domain transfer learning. With a compact footprint (< 3 MB) and high specificity at the default 0.50 operating threshold, CrossBoneNet demonstrates potential as a point-of-care decision support and worklist prioritization tool on resource-constrained devices, while calibrating the decision threshold (e.g., τ=0.3837 and τ=0.3449 ) enables high-sensitivity screening modes (achieving 85.03% and 89.96% sensitivity on MURA, respectively), pending prospective validation. This retrospective study establishes proof of concept; future work will focus on prospective clinical trials and expansion to multiclass fracture classification.

title: Unleashing the potential of saturation-transfer MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) in neuro-oncology: quantitative molecular CEST and MTC mapping.
abstract: Neuro-oncology biomarkers allow probing tissues beyond anatomical or relaxation contrast. However, new techniques are needed to achieve mechanistic elucidation and effective therapeutic interventions. Quantitative MRI techniques, such as T 1 , T 2 , diffusion, and perfusion imaging, provide insights into tumor biology, infiltration, microstructure, and hemodynamics, and have been implemented clinically, but are limited in probing cellular and molecular changes. Saturation transfer (ST) MRI methods, including magnetization transfer contrast (MTC) and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), exhibit enhanced sensitivity to semisolid macromolecular content, mobile proteins, tissue metabolites, and acidosis. Despite these advantages, ST-MRI techniques typically have been qualitative or semi-quantitative, time-consuming, and impractical for clinical implementation. However, emerging ST-MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) represents a significant analytical advancement by integrating RF saturation preparation into a pseudo-randomized MRF acquisition framework with a deep learning-based reconstruction. This approach enables simultaneous, clinically realistic, quantitative mapping of bulk water relaxation properties (e.g., T 1 and T 2 ), semisolid macromolecular parameters, and exchangeable solute dynamics (e.g., pool size ratios and exchange rates). We provide a comprehensive background, methodological principles, and evolving clinical applications of ST-MRF in neuro-oncology. We explore current advancements, strengths, limitations, and future possibilities for clinical translation into neuro-oncology workflows, including tumor characterization, treatment response monitoring, infiltration mapping, and biomarker development.

originalAbstract: Neuro-oncology biomarkers allow probing tissues beyond anatomical or relaxation contrast. However, new techniques are needed to achieve mechanistic elucidation and effective therapeutic interventions. Quantitative MRI techniques, such as T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub>, diffusion, and perfusion imaging, provide insights into tumor biology, infiltration, microstructure, and hemodynamics, and have been implemented clinically, but are limited in probing cellular and molecular changes. Saturation transfer (ST) MRI methods, including magnetization transfer contrast (MTC) and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), exhibit enhanced sensitivity to semisolid macromolecular content, mobile proteins, tissue metabolites, and acidosis. Despite these advantages, ST-MRI techniques typically have been qualitative or semi-quantitative, time-consuming, and impractical for clinical implementation. However, emerging ST-MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) represents a significant analytical advancement by integrating RF saturation preparation into a pseudo-randomized MRF acquisition framework with a deep learning-based reconstruction. This approach enables simultaneous, clinically realistic, quantitative mapping of bulk water relaxation properties (e.g., T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>), semisolid macromolecular parameters, and exchangeable solute dynamics (e.g., pool size ratios and exchange rates). We provide a comprehensive background, methodological principles, and evolving clinical applications of ST-MRF in neuro-oncology. We explore current advancements, strengths, limitations, and future possibilities for clinical translation into neuro-oncology workflows, including tumor characterization, treatment response monitoring, infiltration mapping, and biomarker development.

title: MORSE-PI: flexible and artefact-free image reconstruction for structural and functional QSM and other phase-critical imaging applications.
abstract: Purpose Phase imaging applications such as QSM are highly sensitive to noise amplifications, phase singularities, and other artefacts, particularly in challenging scenarios such as ultra-high field (7 T), under-sampled or single-echo acquisitions. We present a novel image reconstruction method, MORSE-PI, designed to produce high-SNR, artefact-free, and singularity-free phase images for both structural (SWI, QSM) and functional (fQSM) phase-based brain imaging. Methods MORSE-PI extends our previous approach, MORSE, by introducing a Virtual Reference Coil (VRC). The VRC is constructed as a linear combination of coil sensitivity maps, with correlations enhanced between coil elements using the noise covariance matrix. Such a VRC ensures robust signal support across the entire brain and is used to correct phase offsets in the MORSE-derived coil sensitivity estimates, resulting in artefact-free, high-SNR phase. Results Compared to GRAPPA with ASPIRE phase correction, MORSE-PI demonstrates greater robustness to artefacts such as noise amplification and aliasing, and shows improved reproducibility in structural imaging at both 3 T and 7 T. Unlike ESPIRiT and GRAPPA combined with adaptive coil combination methods, MORSE-PI yields singularity-free phase maps. MORSE-PI enables high-SNR reconstructions even for the most challenging scenarios, such as single-echo EPI at 7 T. Its efficient, containerised implementation using the Gadgetron framework supports deployment on the MRI scanner console during measurements. Conclusion MORSE-PI offers a flexible and computationally efficient solution for generating high-SNR, artefact- and singularity-free phase images in both single- and multi-echo GRE and EPI acquisitions. This makes it particularly well-suited for structural and functional QSM, as well as other phase-based MRI applications. Its robustness and rapid computational time facilitate efficient deployment on scanners across field strengths.

title: Observer agreement in sonographic glandular tissue component classification and sonographic breast density assessment: a multi-institutional study.
abstract: Purpose The sonographic glandular tissue component (GTC) is a potential imaging biomarker for stratifying breast cancer risk in women with dense breasts. This study evaluated the reproducibility, reliability, and clinical applicability of GTC classification and GTC-based sonographic breast density assessment in a multicenter observer study. Methods Fifteen readers (nine physicians and six sonographers) from 12 institutions independently assessed 100 paired ultrasound images twice, 1 month apart, with the dataset rearranged for the second reading. GTC was qualitatively classified into four categories according to its estimated proportion within the fibroglandular tissue (FGT): minimal, mild, moderate, and marked; minimal/mild were grouped as low GTC and moderate/marked as high GTC. Sonographic breast density was categorized as sonographic dense breast (high GTC), sonographic non-dense breast (visible fat lobules), or intermediate, with intermediate cases further divided into high or low categories using an FGT-to-FAT (subcutaneous and retromammary fat) ratio cutoff of 1. Interobserver and intraobserver agreement was evaluated using κ statistics. Results Substantial interobserver agreement was observed for the four-class GTC classification, the two-class GTC classification, and sonographic breast density assessment. Intraobserver agreement was moderate for the four-class GTC classification and substantial for the two-class GTC classification and sonographic breast density assessment. The majority-vote sonographic breast density assessment showed substantial agreement with the mammographic ground truth, whereas individual-reader assessments showed moderate concordance with mammographic breast density both overall and in intermediate-density breasts. No significant differences in agreement were observed between physicians and sonographers. Conclusion Substantial interobserver agreement and moderate-to-substantial intraobserver agreement support the reproducibility and reliability of GTC classification and GTC-based sonographic breast density assessment.

title: Agreement between fully automated artificial intelligence and cardiac radiologists for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment in an asymptomatic screening cohort.
abstract: This retrospective single-center study evaluated segment-level agreement between experienced cardiac radiologists and a research AI platform for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Asymptomatic individuals undergoing CCTA at a health screening center were studied, excluding those with prior revascularization, coronary anomaly, or total occlusion. Stenosis grade and plaque composition were independently assessed by the AI platform and two cardiac radiologists at the segment level, with disagreements between the two radiologists resolved by consensus. Agreement was evaluated using Cohen's κ, quadratic weighted κ for ordinal grading, observed agreement, and positive and negative agreement for dichotomized significant stenosis. The cohort comprised 172 participants and 2,582 segments. Significant stenosis was uncommon (18/2,582, 0.7%), with moderate agreement (κ = 0.412; observed agreement 98.5%; positive agreement 0.418; negative agreement 0.992). Agreement was fair for ordinal stenosis grade (κ = 0.397; quadratic weighted κ = 0.573; observed agreement 84.0%) and plaque composition (κ = 0.330; observed agreement 81.8%). Stenosis-grade agreement was lower in plaque-containing than plaque-free segments, an exploratory finding given marked differences in subgroup size and prevalence. Myocardial bridging and image quality were not major descriptive determinants of discordance. In this low-prevalence cohort, AI-based CCTA analysis showed high negative agreement for radiologist-defined significant stenosis but limited concordance for grading and plaque characterization. Reflecting low prevalence and few positive cases, the findings do not establish independent rule-out performance but support prospective evaluation of AI as an expert-supervised pre-reading or triage adjunct, with positive, ambiguous, or plaque-containing findings requiring expert review.

title: Accelerated aortic stenosis progression is associated with greater CT-derived extracellular volume.
abstract: Rapid progression of aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with adverse outcomes, yet the myocardial changes accompanying faster progression remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated the association between the rate of AS progression and myocardial fibrosis assessed by computed tomography (CT)-derived extracellular volume fraction (ECV), and the impact on clinical outcomes. We studied 134 patients with classical high-gradient severe AS who underwent pre-transcatheter aortic valve implantation cardiac CT with a delayed dual-energy acquisition for ECV quantification and had at least two echocardiograms ≥ 6 months apart. Progression was defined as the annualized change in peak aortic jet velocity. Rapid progression was defined as an increase > 0.30 m/s/year. Patients were followed for a composite of cardiovascular hospitalization, urgent aortic valve replacement, or death. ECV correlated with progression rate (Spearman ρ = 0.33, p < 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, faster progression remained independently associated with ECV (β = 2.52, p = 0.001). Rapid progressors had higher ECV than slow progressors (31.5% vs. 28.3%, p < 0.001). Over a median follow-up of 16.2 months, 36 patients (26.9%) reached the composite outcome. Patients with both rapid progression and high ECV had an event rate of 69 versus 11 per 100 patient-years in those without (adjusted HR 6.22, 95% CI 3.13-12.32). Faster AS progression is independently associated with greater diffuse myocardial fibrosis, irrespective of stenosis severity, and their combination identified patients at higher risk of adverse events. These findings suggest that AS progression rate and myocardial tissue characterization carry complementary prognostic information in severe AS.

title: Preoperative classification of histopathological growth patterns in colorectal liver metastases using prospective 18 F-FDG PET/CT.
abstract: Colorectal liver metastases (CLM) exhibit distinct histopathological growth patterns (HGPs) at the metastasis-liver interface, clinically relevant for prognosis and potential predictive value. This study investigates the feasibility of using Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) to preoperatively classify HGPs in CLM and secondly investigate PET parameters as prognostic markers for overall survival (OS). In a prospective study at Umeå University Hospital (June 2013-December 2017), 78 patients with resectable CLM underwent contrast-enhanced liver MRI and 18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging. HGP classification was performed on tissue sections according to 2017 international guidelines. PET features (SUV mean [standardised uptake value], SUV max , metabolic tumour volume [MTV] and first-order texture metrics) were analysed to distinguish encapsulating (eHGP) from replacement (rHGP) patterns. In pretreated patients, multivariate logistic regression including both metabolic and texture parameters identified significant associations for parameters from the fixed level threshold algorithm (VuePoint Sharp IR) with small odds ratios. Overall, PET parameters showed limited ability to discriminate between eHGP and rHGP. OS was superior with eHGP versus rHGP (log-rank p = 0.045). In chemonaïve patients, SUV-based metrics showed unadjusted exploratory associations with OS after liver surgery, varying by reconstruction/delineation and were not significant after correction for multiple testing. FDG-PET-derived parameters were not reliably associated with HGP and did not support non-invasive HGP prediction in this cohort. eHGP was associated with superior survival, underscoring the value of HGP assessment for prognostication while alternative non-invasive biomarkers remain to be identified.

title: Hypoxia-powered MRI guides supramaximal biosurgical sampling of glioblastoma infiltration: the GLIOXY initiative.
abstract: Purpose To assess the feasibility of using hypoxia-powered magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to guide prospective sampling of high-response habitats beyond contrast enhancement in glioblastoma. Methods Nine treatment-naive patients with histologically confirmed isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wildtype glioblastoma underwent blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) MRI during a controlled transient hypoxic stimulus on the evening before surgery. Anatomical segmentation and voxel-wise temporal decomposition generated normalized hypoxia response maps. Otsu thresholding defined a high-response habitat outside contrast enhancement. Targets were confirmed with the surgeon according to anatomical accessibility and eloquence, transferred to neuronavigation, and sampled before major debulking. We divided the specimen for formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded neuropathology and frozen-tissue storage. Results Neuronavigation transfer succeeded in all nine cases. Eight targets were accessible and sampled. Seven sampled targets contained tumor. One yielded reactive cortex and white matter without definite tumor. title: Mask-aware knowledge distillation for low-latency pneumothorax classification in chest radiographs.
abstract: Accurate pneumothorax classification requires strong discrimination with low deployment cost. We developed a mask-aware knowledge distillation framework in which a mask-guided ResNet-50 teacher transferred dynamically annealed logits and lesion-weighted multilevel attention to a MobileNetV3-Small student, while masks and teacher-side components were removed at inference. A fixed stratified 20% SIIM-ACR hold-out set was reserved for testing; the remainder underwent five-fold cross-validation, with PTX-498 positives used only for training augmentation. The Mask-aware KD student achieved a mean validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of [Formula: see text], and the five-model student ensemble achieved a fixed-test AUC of 0.946 (95% confidence interval, 0.935-0.956) versus 0.950 for the teacher ensemble. Validation-selected 90% and 95% sensitivity targets yielded test sensitivities of 0.929 and 0.973. Uniform-attention KD achieved a lower AUC of 0.936. The student ensemble required 5.00 million parameters, 1.49 billion multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), and 51.00-ms single-threaded CPU latency at [Formula: see text]. Training-time lesion guidance enabled numerically similar discrimination with substantially lower inference cost. No independent external validation was performed, and generalizability across institutions, acquisition protocols, portable radiography settings, and patient populations remains uncertain; verified patient-level evaluation remains necessary before clinical translation.

title: Decoding tumor heterogeneity using MRI for predicting response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in hepatocellular carcinoma: a multicenter study.
abstract: Purpose Tumor heterogeneity hinders accurate prediction of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We developed a habitat model using routine in-phase (IP) and opposed-phase (OP) MRI sequences, which provide complementary structure- and lipid-related information, to predict response to ICI therapy in HCC. Methods This study included 883 HCC patients from six institutions and public databases. We developed habitat, radiomics, peritumoral, clinical, and combined models to predict partial response (PR) in five institutions. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to evaluate survival differences based on prediction scores. Habitat model interpretability was assessed using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) along with multi-omics and pathological analyses in the public databases and one external institution. Results The habitat model showed numerically higher AUCs among the independent models, with AUCs of 0.923, 0.918, and 0.897 in the training set and two external validation sets, respectively. The combined model also showed favorable performance with AUCs of 0.959, 0.965, and 0.955, respectively. Calibration curves showed generally close agreement, while decision curve analyses suggested potential clinical net benefit of the habitat and combined models. Patients with higher habitat scores had significantly longer progression‑free and overall survival (all P < 0.05). Exploratory biological analyses showed that the higher habitat score group was associated with enhanced immune activity, downregulated fatty acid-related pathways, and shorter tumor-inflammatory spatial distances. Conclusion The IP and OP MRI-based habitat model showed potential for treatment-response prediction and prognostic stratification in patients with HCC receiving ICI therapy.

title: CT attenuation changes across freeze-thaw preservation states in donated bodies: a preliminary multi-organ anatomical analysis.
abstract: Purpose To establish the thermal preservation state as a critical pre-analytical variable in quantitative post-mortem CT of donated bodies, with the aim of enabling reliable multi-donor comparisons, improving the performance of automated segmentation tools, and providing a translational experimental model applicable to CT-guided thermal interventions. Material and methods Eight body donors underwent whole-body CT in up to three preservation states: fresh, frozen (- 20 °C), and thawed. CT datasets were automatically segmented using TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer. Mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values were extracted for major organs and tissue groups. The primary analysis was within-donor: Friedman tests with Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons in donors with complete data (n = 7), complemented by linear mixed-effects models using all available scans. Results Freezing produced a consistent reduction in CT attenuation across all soft tissues and muscle, with near-complete recovery after thawing. In the primary repeated-measures analysis, preservation state had a significant effect after FDR correction in six of the nine tissue groups (liver, spleen, brain, aorta, pancreas and muscle; q = 0.023-0.042), but not in kidney, heart or bone. Brain and pancreas showed the strongest effects (Kendall's W = 0.80 and 0.76). In the liver, the median within-donor change was - 59.7 HU at freezing and + 60.3 HU at thawing. Mixed-effects models confirmed a significant reduction at freezing in liver, spleen, brain, kidney, pancreas and muscle (β = -35.1 to -52.7 HU) and no residual difference after thawing in any tissue group. Bone attenuation remained stable across all preservation states. Conclusion Freeze-thaw preservation systematically alters CT attenuation in soft tissues while minimally affecting bone. Preservation state should therefore be considered a critical pre-analytical variable in quantitative post-mortem CT, particularly for studies relying on automated segmentation, radiomics, and translational applications involving thermal tissue imaging.
