Humeral component loosening, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were supported as components of the diagnostic criteria, whereas cloudy fluid, postoperative stiffness, serum WBC count, and D-dimer were not supported as independent criteria. Arthroscopic tissue biopsy, frozen section, and selective ultrasound-guided aspiration or synovial biopsy were supported as adjuncts to diagnosis. Five intraoperative tissue specimens, prolonged aerobic and anaerobic culture incubation, and routine perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis were supported. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) and synovial neutrophil testing were supported as adjuncts; alpha-defensin was considered potentially useful but insufficiently validated for formal inclusion; and leukocyte esterase inclusion was not recommended. Routine use of bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), or positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) was not supported. Evidence remained insufficient to determine the clinical significance of polymicrobial molecular results or routine negative control samples.

Conclusion

The 2025 ICM provides a consensus framework for the diagnosis of shoulder PJI, identifying several measures that can be incorporated into current clinical practice. However, substantial uncertainty remains because most recommendations are supported by limited evidence and several diagnostic tests lack sufficient sensitivity. Prospective, shoulder-specific studies are needed to define diagnostic thresholds and determine the role of emerging molecular, biomarker, and imaging modalities.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Resisted Anterior Drawer (RAD) Test for Lateral Elbow Instability in Lateral Epicondylitis.
abstract: Background Lateral epicondylitis (LE) is increasingly recognized as a multifactorial condition in which subtle lateral elbow instability may contribute to persistent pain. However, reliable clinical tests to detect such instability are lacking. Purpose To determine the diagnostic accuracy of the resisted anterior drawer (RAD) test for detecting lateral elbow instability in patients with LE. Methods Consecutive adult patients diagnosed with LE underwent standardized clinical examination followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The RAD test was considered positive when pain during resisted wrist extension, with the elbow in extension, decreased by at least 1 point on a visual analogue scale (VAS) with anteromedial stabilization of the radial head. MRI-defined instability was defined as the presence of lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injury, posterior sagging, or ulnohumeral joint-line opening of grade ≥1. Diagnostic indices were calculated with 95% confidence intervals and likelihood ratios, and the continuous reduction in pain was evaluated with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results A total of 500 elbows were analyzed (mean age: 51 years). MRI evidence of instability was present in 57.4% of elbows. The RAD test demonstrated a sensitivity of 95.8% (95% CI 92.8-97.6%), specificity of 82.2% (95% CI 76.5-86.7%), and overall accuracy of 90.0% (95% CI 87.1-92.3%), with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 5.4 and 0.05. The area under the ROC curve for the reduction in pain was 0.92 (95% CI 0.90-0.95). The magnitude of pain reduction during the RAD maneuver correlated with the severity of MRI-defined instability (Spearman ρ = -0.71). Increasing MRI severity was associated with a higher number of corticosteroid infiltrations, whereas symptom duration showed only a weak association with structural instability. Conclusion In this Level III diagnostic study, the RAD test showed high sensitivity and good specificity for MRI-defined lateral elbow instability in patients with LE, and the magnitude of pain reduction was correlated with MRI-defined severity. These findings suggest that the RAD test may be a useful screening maneuver for instability-related pain in patients with LE. A prospective, blinded cohort study with an independent reference standard is required to confirm its clinical utility. Level of evidence Level III, Diagnostic Study.

title: Association of Respiratory-Related Sarcopenia Classification With Postoperative Complications and Overall Survival in Older Patients With Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Introduction Respiratory function and muscle measures have previously been studied together. We evaluated a classification combining peak expiratory flow and a computed tomography-derived pectoralis muscle index in older patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Methods This retrospective cohort included 742 patients aged ≥65 y undergoing minimally invasive McKeown esophagectomy during 2020-2021. Pectoralis muscle index was the bilateral pectoralis major area at T4 divided by height squared, a surrogate of chest-wall muscle reserve. Two isolated-abnormality phenotypes were combined exploratorily into mild, alongside normal and severe categories. Logistic and Cox regression evaluated associations. Survival discrimination was assessed in the development cohort; stratified Cox sensitivity analyses addressed nonproportional hazards. Results Normal, mild, and severe comprised 340, 310, and 92 patients. Adjusted pneumonia odds ratios versus normal were 1.548 (95% confidence interval, 1.039-2.306) for mild and 2.973 (1.746-5.064) for severe. The leakage model retained no other covariates. In the T/N-stratified survival model, hazard ratios were 2.445 (1.948-3.067) and 3.585 (2.618-4.908), respectively. Adding the classification increased the apparent C-index from 0.837 to 0.861. Pneumonia areas under the curve were 0.616 for the four-group framework and 0.613 for the simplified classification. Conclusions The classification was associated with postoperative outcomes and overall survival. Its simpler grouping had observed discrimination close to the four-group framework. However, its clinical utility in preoperative optimization still requires further validation in prospective studies.

title: Acoustic Correlates of Endoscopically Identified Vocal Fold Lesions in a Large Clinical Cohort: Perceptual Associations and Screening Performance.
abstract: Benign vocal fold lesions are among the most common causes of dysphonia, yet large cohort studies integrating endoscopic, perceptual, and acoustic domains remain scarce. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and distribution of vocal fold lesions in a large clinical cohort and to determine acoustic characteristics linked to endoscopically detected vocal fold lesions and able to differentiate them from structurally normal vocal folds, corroborated by perceptual severity ratings. Methods In this cross-sectional cohort study, 782 patients with dysphonia underwent videolaryngostroboscopy, standardized acoustic recording, and auditory-perceptual evaluation using the Consensus Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice (CAPE-V) and GRBAS scales. Acoustic parameters (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio [HNR], and smoothed cepstral peak prominence [CPPS]) were compared across lesion categories and entered into multivariable logistic regression models. Results Vocal fold polyps were the most prevalent lesion (32.1%), followed by nodules (24.0%), Reinke's edema (16.0%), cysts (13.9%), and granuloma (7.9%). All acoustic parameters differed significantly across categories (P < .001), with polyps showing the greatest deviation from normal values. CPPS was the strongest independent predictor of lesion presence (adjusted OR 1.62 per 1-dB decrease, P < .001) and correlated most strongly with CAPE-V overall severity (r = -.71, P < .001). The combined acoustic model discriminated lesion from non-lesion voices with excellent accuracy (AUC = 0.91). Conclusions Acoustic changes, such as decreased CPPS and HNR and increased jitter and shimmer, were related to vocal fold lesions identified by endoscopy. CPPS had the greatest separation between patients with a lesion, identified endoscopically, and structurally normal patients. These acoustic measures should be viewed as a screening/triage marker of vocal fold abnormality and not as a marker of benignity or lesion-specific etiology, however, because the study excluded malignant, neurological, and other major voice pathologies. Acoustic assessment is thus a useful non-invasive complement to laryngeal endoscopic assessment, but should not replace it.

title: MONKEY Challenge: Machine-learning for Optimal detection of iNflammatory cells in KidnEY transplant biopsies.
abstract: Purpose Accurate quantification of inflammatory cells in Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)-stained kidney transplant biopsies is essential for Banff classification but remains subjective and labor-intensive. To address this, the MONKEY challenge benchmarked deep learning (DL) methods for automated detection of mononuclear leukocytes and their subtypes. Materials and methods A multicenter dataset of 118 biopsies with co-registered PAS and immunohistochemically restained slides, comprising over 131,000 annotated cells, was used. The algorithms were evaluated on hold-out validation and test set using Free-response Receiver Operating Characteristic (FROC) analysis, alongside precision, recall, and F1-scores. Results Across diverse architectures, performance converged, with the top models achieving F1-scores up to 0.75 for overall detection. Lymphocyte detection performed well (F1 up to 0.78), whereas monocyte detection remained more challenging (F1 up to 0.47). To explore the potential clinical applicability of automated inflammatory cell detection, the winning model was integrated with renal tissue segmentation models, enabling compartment-specific evaluation and quantitative assessment of Banff-related lesions. In an independent multicenter cohort of 180 kidney transplant biopsies, DL-derived quantitative measurements demonstrated strong correlations with consensus pathologist scoring for several inflammation-related Banff lesions, particularly total inflammation and interstitial inflammation. Conclusions This study establishes the first multicenter, PAS-based, IHC-validated benchmark for inflammatory cell detection and provides a clinically grounded resource to support the development of robust, generalizable AI systems for transplant pathology. Beyond benchmark performance, our extended tissue-specific analyses demonstrate that inflammatory cell detection on routine PAS slides can be anatomically contextualized and translated into quantitative measurements that align with conventional Banff lesion assessment, providing a foundation for future AI-assisted evaluation of kidney transplant biopsies.

title: Performance of artificial intelligence versus clinician left-ventricular segmentation of cardiac MRI for mortality prediction: a retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study.
abstract: Background Ejection fraction, a key measure of cardiac function, is used in health care for clinical decision making and risk stratification. We hypothesised that a deep-learning artificial intelligence (AI) segmentation of ejection fraction obtained from cardiac MRI (CMR) outperforms expert clinician segmentation for the prediction of all-cause mortality. Methods In this retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study, we studied a cohort of 27 382 consecutive patients who underwent cardiac MRI (CMR) in the UK and the USA. Patients were referred for CMR from nine hospitals to Barts Heart Centre (BHC), London. Patients were identified from the reporting archive at BHC as having undergone a CMR between Oct 1, 2014 and Dec 31, 2019. A further cohort of patients was also identified from University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre (UPMC), Pittsburgh, PA, USA, as having undergone a CMR between June 1, 2010 and March 31, 2016. Mortality data were obtained from national and local databases. AI segmentation was done on all CMR studies, and Cox proportional hazards models were fitted to compare the prognostic value of AI-measured versus clinician-measured left-ventricular volume metrics. Model fit was compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), discrimination using C indices and the incremental value of AI over clinician segmentation using likelihood-ratio tests of nested models. Findings 27 382 patients received a baseline CMR (26 106 patients from BHC and 1276 from UPMC). The median follow-up was 5·6 years (IQR 4·4-6·9), during which 3458 (13%) of 27 382 patients died. AI ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 57 936 vs 58 097, ΔAIC 161 favouring AI) and marginally better discrimination (C index 0·669 vs 0·637; ΔC 0·033 [95% CI 0·026-0·041]). AI ejection fraction significantly improved model fit when added to clinician ejection fraction (χ 2 =168, p<0·0001), with only slight improvement when clinician ejection fraction was added to AI (χ 2 =7·5, p=0·023). After adjustment for age and sex, AI-derived ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 55 684 vs 55 742; ΔAIC 59) and had marginally better discrimination (C index of 0·781 vs 0·777; ΔC=0·004 [95% CI 0·002-0·006]). Interpretation AI-derived ejection fraction shows marginally superior prediction for mortality than clinician-derived ejection fraction in patients who had CMR. Findings support the potential utility of AI for first-line ejection-fraction measurement with clinician oversight, although this should be investigated in prospective studies. Funding National Institute for Health and Care Research Clinical Lectureship and the British Heart Foundation Accelerator Award.

title: Point-of-care ultrasound in older adults: a scoping review.
abstract: Multimorbidity, non-specific symptoms, and atypical disease manifestations are common in adults aged 65 years or older, complicating diagnostic and prognostic assessment. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) provides real-time bedside imaging that can support clinical decision making in this population; however, evidence on its use in older adults has not been systematically mapped. This scoping Review, endorsed by the European Geriatric Medicine Society, mapped POCUS utilisation across health-care settings, application domains, clinical indications, and outcomes. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed original research articles investigating the use of POCUS in older adults (defined as studies that exclusively enrolled older adults ≥65 years or reported a mixed-age study population with a mean age of 65 years or older) and published in English or another language represented within the review team (Italian, French, German, Spanish, Danish, or Turkish) with no restrictions on publication date. Of the 3897 records, 240 (6%) studies were included; 87 (36%) focused on older adult or geriatric-targeted populations and 153 (64%) on mixed-age populations with a mean age of 65 years or older. Evidence came predominantly from acute care, with few studies in geriatric settings. Thoracic POCUS was the most frequently investigated single-organ domain; multiorgan POCUS was also prominent. Diagnostic support and prognostic stratification predominated, whereas longitudinal monitoring and patient-centred outcomes were infrequent. Evidence on POCUS applications in older adults remains uneven, highlighting the need for further research in under-represented geriatric care settings and on patient-centred outcomes.

title: Radiologic phenotype and the size dependence of adverse histologic features and recurrence in resected lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Objectives The eighth edition TNM classification measures part-solid lung adenocarcinoma by the solid component alone. We examined whether CT-measured size carries the same pathologic and prognostic meaning in part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed 3857 consecutive patients with resected non-mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (2011-2022), using phenotype and size from preoperative CT reports. Shape-constrained additive models estimated the size-dependent prevalence of seven adverse features, including high-grade (HG) patterns, micropapillary component and spread through air spaces (STAS). Five-year cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) was estimated with death as a competing risk. Results Tumors were part-solid in 2100 and solid in 1757 patients. In part-solid tumors, HG patterns, micropapillary component and STAS rose most steeply at 1.25-1.36 cm of total size (0.85-0.93 cm of solid component); in solid tumors, HG patterns and STAS were already frequent at the smallest measured sizes. Lymphovascular, pleural and nodal involvement became prevalent at larger sizes in both phenotypes. Among 3580 patients analyzed for recurrence (467 recurrences; median follow-up, 56.6 months), solid tumors had higher CIR than part-solid tumors within each matched solid-component size stratum (feature-present tumors > 2.5 cm: 42.7% vs 19.6%). In part-solid tumors, 5-year CIR was 1.4% when HG morphology was the most advanced feature, 11.0% with local invasion and 50.0% with nodal involvement. Conclusions Measuring the solid component narrows but does not close the difference in pathologic risk between part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma of the same size. These associations warrant external validation and evaluation in preoperative risk models.

Objectives

The eighth edition TNM classification measures part-solid lung adenocarcinoma by the solid component alone. We examined whether CT-measured size carries the same pathologic and prognostic meaning in part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma.

Materials and methods

We retrospectively analyzed 3857 consecutive patients with resected non-mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (2011-2022), using phenotype and size from preoperative CT reports. Shape-constrained additive models estimated the size-dependent prevalence of seven adverse features, including high-grade (HG) patterns, micropapillary component and spread through air spaces (STAS). Five-year cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) was estimated with death as a competing risk.

Results

Tumors were part-solid in 2100 and solid in 1757 patients. In part-solid tumors, HG patterns, micropapillary component and STAS rose most steeply at 1.25-1.36 cm of total size (0.85-0.93 cm of solid component); in solid tumors, HG patterns and STAS were already frequent at the smallest measured sizes. Lymphovascular, pleural and nodal involvement became prevalent at larger sizes in both phenotypes. Among 3580 patients analyzed for recurrence (467 recurrences; median follow-up, 56.6 months), solid tumors had higher CIR than part-solid tumors within each matched solid-component size stratum (feature-present tumors > 2.5 cm: 42.7% vs 19.6%). In part-solid tumors, 5-year CIR was 1.4% when HG morphology was the most advanced feature, 11.0% with local invasion and 50.0% with nodal involvement.

Conclusions

Measuring the solid component narrows but does not close the difference in pathologic risk between part-solid and solid adenocarcinoma of the same size. These associations warrant external validation and evaluation in preoperative risk models.

title: ISLES'24: Final stroke infarct prediction with multimodal imaging and clinical data. Where do we stand?
abstract: Accurate estimation of brain infarction (i.e., irreversibly damaged tissue) is critical for guiding treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke. Reliable infarct prediction informs key clinical interventions, including the need for patient transfer to comprehensive stroke centers, the potential benefit of additional reperfusion attempts during mechanical thrombectomy, decisions regarding secondary neuroprotective treatments, and, ultimately, prognosis of clinical outcomes. This work introduces the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation (ISLES) 2024 challenge, which focuses on the prediction of final infarct volumes from pre-interventional acute stroke imaging and clinical data. ISLES'24 provides a comprehensive, multimodal setting where participants can leverage all clinically and practically available data - including full acute CT imaging, sub-acute follow-up MRI, and structured clinical information - across a train set of N=150 cases. On the hidden test set (N=98), the top-performing model, a multimodal nnU-Net-based architecture, achieved a Dice score of 0.285 ± 0.213 and an absolute volume difference of 21.2 ± 37.2 mL, underlining the significant challenges posed by this task and the need for further advances in multimodal learning. This overview of the ISLES'24 challenge offers two primary contributions: first, it provides a standardized, clinically realistic benchmark for post-treatment infarct prediction, built on a comprehensive, open, and multimodal longitudinal stroke imaging dataset; second, it provides insights into the strengths and limitations of current algorithms and delineates key research directions to guide the development of next-generation infarct prediction models.

title: Retraining-free multi-task MR image restoration using a pretrained diffusion model with Bayesian optimization.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often requires long scan times, and efforts to shorten scans can lead to image degradation, such as undersampling artifacts, increased noise, and reduced spatial resolution. A restoration framework that can address multiple types of degradation without task-specific retraining would therefore be valuable. In this study, we evaluated whether a pretrained score-based diffusion model combined with Bayesian optimization, termed task guidance design with Bayesian optimization (TGD-BO), could provide retraining-free, multi-task MR image restoration for compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction, super-resolution (SR), and denoising (DN). TGD-BO incorporates data-consistency guidance and gradient guidance into the reverse diffusion process and parameterizes their time-varying strengths using compact low-dimensional B-spline-based guidance schedules. For each task, the schedule was optimized by Bayesian optimization using four paired degraded/reference slices from a single adaptation case, and the resulting task-specific schedule was then applied unchanged to an independent test set. In single-task experiments, TGD-BO improved upon the fixed-guidance diffusion baseline in denoising, compressed-sensing reconstruction, and super-resolution, although the improvement in super-resolution was modest. Compared with task-specific supervised baselines, TGD-BO did not uniformly achieve higher peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) or structural similarity (SSIM); in super-resolution, it showed lower PSNR and SSIM but better perceptual similarity as assessed by learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). In joint-task experiments, schedules optimized directly for DN + CS and DN + SR yielded numerically better image-quality metrics than applying the corresponding single-task schedules. Sensitivity analyses showed that the selected schedule and test performance were unchanged when 1, 4, or 8 slices from the same adaptation case were used, whereas changing the adaptation case substantially affected test performance. These results suggest the feasibility of adapting a single pretrained diffusion prior across multiple MR image restoration tasks through guidance calibration without task-specific weight retraining, while indicating that robustness to adaptation-case selection and computational cost require further investigation.

title: Measurement-derived residual-risk verification through four-way k-space partitioning in self-supervised accelerated brain MRI.
abstract: Self-supervised accelerated MRI reconstruction reduces dependence on fully sampled training targets, but it does not inherently provide a separate basis for verifying whether reconstructed image content remains locally consistent with acquired measurements. We developed a measurement-derived verification framework that partitions acquired k-space into four roles: reconstruction input, self-supervised reconstruction-loss evaluation, residual-risk learning, and reserved verification. Residuals from the reserved measurements were transformed into spatial residual-risk targets using density-compensated adjoint projection, probe-based gain normalization, anatomical support weighting, percentile scaling, and logarithmic compression. Using fastMRI brain multicoil data, we evaluated 201 training, 40 calibration, and 40 AXT2 test volumes, comprising 636 test slices and 999,792 sampled pixels. The primary Full-CNN achieved AUPRC 0.8348, mean absolute error 0.0834, Spearman correlation 0.9389, and AUROC 0.9818. The secondary A4-CNN achieved AUPRC 0.8452 with similar scale and rank agreement. MRI-volume intervals achieved at least 90% sampled-location coverage in 39 of 40 test volumes for both predictors. AUPRC declined and MAE increased with fewer reserved measurements and under AXFLAIR sequence shift. Residual-risk maps showed moderate correspondence with fully sampled reference error and differed from the tested predictive-variance measures. The framework provides a measurement-derived verification layer for assessing local residual inconsistency in self-supervised accelerated MRI without requiring fully sampled development targets.

title: Diffusion tensor imaging and structural MRI reveal early microstructural injury and progressive atrophy of the olfactory bulb in type 1 diabetic rats.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can detect early olfactory bulb microstructural abnormalities in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) rats and to investigate their relationship with structural and histopathological changes. Methods Control and STZ-induced T1DM rats underwent DTI, high-resolution structural MRI and histological examination at 2 and 12 weeks after model induction. Fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (Da), and radial diffusivity (Dr) were measured in the olfactory nerve layer/glomerular layer/external plexiform layer (ONL/GL/EPL), granule cell layer (GCL), and subependymal zone (SEZ). Results Compared to the controls, T1DM rats showed decreased FA and increased MD, Da, and Dr in the ONL/GL/EPL at 2 and 12 weeks after model induction. In the GCL, FA was decreased, whereas Dr was increased. No significant diffusion abnormalities were detected in the SEZ. Ultrastructural examination revealed axolemmal disruption, demyelination, reduced axoplasmic content, and axonal vacuolization in the ONL. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) demonstrated olfactory bulb atrophy as early as 2 weeks, initially involving the GCL and SEZ, with more extensive and regionally heterogeneous atrophy at 12 weeks. Nissl staining confirmed structural atrophy, and increased caspase-3 immunoreactivity supported apoptosis-related tissue injury. STZ-induced T1DM causes early, layer-specific olfactory bulb microstructural abnormalities and progressive structural atrophy. Conclusion The differing spatial and temporal distributions of diffusion abnormalities and atrophy suggest that DTI and volumetric MRI capture partially distinct aspects of diabetes-associated olfactory bulb injury. DTI may provide a sensitive, noninvasive approach for detecting early microstructural abnormalities before widespread structural loss develops.

title: HSMD: A Hilbert-scanning mamba dense network for 3D MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Long MRI acquisition times motivate the use of k-space undersampling for accelerated imaging, but undersampling often introduces aliasing artifacts and structural detail loss. Existing 2D slice-wise reconstruction methods fail to fully exploit inter-slice anatomical correlations. This study develops a Hilbert-Scanning Mamba Dense Network (HSMD) for high-quality 3D MRI reconstruction, which leverages inter-slice contextual information to improve reconstruction fidelity. The proposed HSMD consists of a Shallow Feature Extraction Module (SFEM) and five cascaded Multi-Directional Spatial Attention (MDSA) modules. The SFEM is responsible for extracting local detailed features and coarse-scale structural context from undersampled MRI inputs. The MDSA modules extract and fuse multi-directional spatial information along the depth, height, and width dimensions to enhance the representation of 3D structural features. Furthermore, a multi-directional Hilbert selective state-space scanning strategy is introduced into MDSA to capture long-range spatial dependencies within 3D volumetric data, thereby improving structural representation while preserving spatial locality. Experimental results on the BraTS and UCSF-PDGM datasets under diverse acceleration factors validate that the proposed HSMD achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. The HSMD exhibits excellent capability in 3D undersampled MRI reconstruction, holding promising prospects for efficient and reliable clinical MRI applications.

title: Deep learning-derived functional MRI connectivity maps of cervical spinal cord segments during hand grasping.
abstract: Task-based fMRI of the cervical spinal cord is limited by physiological noise and small sample sizes. The primary objective of this study was to examine whether a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based denoising framework can improve the detection of task-dependent functional connectivity between cervical spinal segments using generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis. An open dataset of 26 healthy adults performing a hand-grasp task with alternating right- and left-hand blocks during 3 T fMRI was analyzed. A CNN with Inception V3 transfer learning (91.0% slice-level and 89.2% block-level accuracy) was trained to classify grasp versus rest, and the trained model was then utilized to derive denoised time series from masks of the spinal segments C5-C8. A gPPI model with a C6 ventral horn seed was evaluated using FDR correction and permutation testing (n = 1000). C6 showed positive task-dependent connectivity with C7 (β = 0.72, p = 0.003) and C8 (β = 0.58, p = 0.018), and negative connectivity with C5 (β = -0.31, p = 0.041), which is broadly consistent with the organization of the cervical myotomes. The C6-C5 effect was marginal and was not detected when conventional time series were used (p = 0.21), and therefore it requires replication. Grad-CAM maps aligned with ventral horn motor pools (Dice = 0.89 at C7). These results suggest that deep learning-based denoising may increase the sensitivity of spinal cord fMRI to segmental connectivity, although validation in larger cohorts is needed.

title: Integrated deep learning reconstruction combining phase correction, denoising, and super-resolution for prostate diffusion-weighted imaging.
abstract: Objective To evaluate integrated deep learning reconstruction (Integrated DLR), which combines phase correction, denoising, and super-resolution, for prostate diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) by comparing it with compressed sensing (CS) and deep learning-based denoising reconstruction (Denoising DLR). Methods This single-center, retrospective study included 47 patients scanned on a single-vendor 3-T system. Three DWI datasets were reconstructed from identical raw data using CS, Denoising DLR, and Integrated DLR. Two radiologists rated overall image quality, noise, artifact, and prostate delineation. Apparent signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was assessed in all patients. In 21 patients with pathologically confirmed prostate cancer, we assessed lesion conspicuity, lesion localization/anatomical relationship, Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) version 2.1 DWI scores, apparent lesion contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Comparisons were performed using Friedman tests followed by Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results Scores for overall image quality, noise, and prostate delineation were highest with Integrated DLR, followed by Denoising DLR and CS, for both readers (all p < 0.001); apparent SNR showed the same pattern (p < 0.001). Artifact scores did not differ among methods. Lesion conspicuity differed among methods for Reader 2 (p = 0.044) but not for Reader 1 (p = 0.199), whereas Integrated DLR yielded the highest lesion localization/anatomical relationship scores for both readers (both p < 0.001). Integrated DLR also yielded the highest apparent CNR and lesion ADC (both p < 0.001), while PI-RADS DWI scores were unchanged. Conclusion Integrated DLR improved prostate DWI image quality and lesion visibility compared with CS and Denoising DLR, potentially facilitating visual assessment of prostate DWI.

title: NA-DIP: A Noise-Aware Deep Image Prior for Generating Dedicated Brain PET-Quality Images from Whole-Body PET Acquisitions.
abstract: Purpose To generate dedicated brain PET-quality images from routine whole-body PET acquisitions by robustly enhancing the brain region using a noise-aware deep image prior (NA-DIP) approach. Methods NA-DIP integrates anatomy-guided priors derived from patient-specific μ-maps or MR images, a regularization strategy for enhanced denoising, and a variance-based early stopping criterion that adaptively monitors noise without requiring prior noise assumptions. Using noisy PET images as self-supervised targets, the method was first evaluated using simulation data spanning three noise levels to investigate the trade-off between noise suppression and bias. It was then applied to brain images extracted from 90-s-per-bed-position whole-body acquisitions from 15 pediatric FDG-PET studies spanning a broad range of patient demographics, physiological variability, and image noise levels. Using the corresponding 360-s-per-bed-position dedicated brain scans as the reference, NA-DIP-enhanced images were evaluated for noise reduction, standardized uptake value (SUV) accuracy, and image quality in a blinded reader study. Results NA-DIP demonstrated a superior noise-bias trade-off compared with Gaussian filtering and conventional DIP stopping strategies, particularly under high-noise conditions. The inclusion of MR or μ-map guidance further improved performance. Across pediatric patients, NA-DIP-enhanced 90-s images exhibited lower noise than the corresponding 360-s dedicated brain images while showing modest variability in SUV measurements. Blinded readers rated the NA-DIP-enhanced images as comparable to or better than dedicated brain images in most cases. Conclusion NA-DIP enhanced brain PET images from whole-body acquisitions demonstrated good quantitative agreement and image quality comparable to or exceeding the reference, supporting the feasibility of eliminating separate dedicated brain scans.

title: An approximation of MRI R<sub>2</sub>* as a rapid surrogate of nigral iron in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Nigral iron accumulation is a robust imaging marker of Parkinson's disease and is commonly assessed using R 2 * mapping. However, its clinical implementation is limited by long acquisition times. An alternative metric, effective R 2 , derived from dual-contrast proton density- and T2-weighted MRI, has recently been proposed as a fast surrogate of tissue iron content. Using data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), we evaluated the diagnostic and longitudinal performance of effective R 2 in the substantia nigra (SN) across multiple scanner platforms. Cross-sectional analysis demonstrated significantly higher effective R 2 values in de novo Parkinson's disease patients (n=187) compared with prodromal subjects (n=26), with consistent effects across acquisition protocols. In Siemens data (177 patients and 25 prodromal subjects), effective R 2 achieved good discriminative performance for Parkinson's disease classification (AUC = 0.85). Longitudinal analysis for 14 patients over 36 months showed no significant change in effective R 2 values despite clinical progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. These findings indicate that effective R 2 provides robust cross-sectional discrimination of early Parkinson's disease but with limited sensitivity to disease progression.

In Siemens data (177 patients and 25 prodromal subjects), effective R<sub>2</sub> achieved good discriminative performance for Parkinson's disease classification (AUC = 0.85). Longitudinal analysis for 14 patients over 36 months showed no significant change in effective R<sub>2</sub> values despite clinical progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. These findings indicate that effective R<sub>2</sub> provides robust cross-sectional discrimination of early Parkinson's disease but with limited sensitivity to disease progression.

title: Multimodal MRI reveals brain structural and functional abnormalities associated with wearing-off phenomenon in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Objectives The pathogenesis of the wearing-off (WO) phenomenon in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. This study aims to explore the abnormalities in brain structure and function among PD patients with WO. Methods A total of 39 PD patients with wearing-off (PD-WO) and 43 PD patients without wearing-off (PD-nWO) were prospectively enrolled. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was employed in this study to evaluate structural differences, and functional connectivity (FC) was used to assess functional differences between the two groups. Results Compared with PD-nWO patients, PD-WO patients showed significantly reduced gray matter volume (GMV) within the left middle occipital gyrus (MOG.L), bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG.L/R), as well as the left triangular division of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFGtriang.L). Regarding functional connectivity, PD-WO patients exhibited widespread abnormalities, including weakened connectivity in the cerebellar-basal ganglia-sensorimotor cortex circuits, hippocampus-postcentral gyrus, and cerebellar-occipital (cuneal cortex) pathways, as well as enhanced connectivity between cerebellar subregions and between the cerebellum and occipital cortex (lingual gyrus) and parahippocampal gyrus. Conclusions This preliminary single-center cross-sectional study revealed significant differences in brain structure and function between PD-WO and PD-nWO patients. These findings provide a better understanding of the neural mechanisms behind the WO phenomenon in PD and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

title: Methylphenidate-associated brain structural changes and neuroimaging predictors of treatment response in youth with ADHD: a systematic review.
abstract: Background Methylphenidate (MPH) is a psychostimulant widely prescribed to children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Although its clinical efficacy is well established, its lasting effects on the developing brain remain unclear. Objective This systematic review aimed to examine associations between long-term MPH treatment and brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD using structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), distinguishing longitudinal treatment-effect studies from cross-sectional medication-history comparisons and baseline neuroimaging predictors of treatment response. Methods A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE and Embase databases. Studies were included if they investigated structural brain changes (gray matter volume, white matter integrity and cortical thickness) after at least four weeks of MPH treatment in children with ADHD. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed using the NIH quality assessment tool. Results Eight studies met the inclusion criteria: three longitudinal studies using repeated MRI to assess within-subject treatment effects, two cross-sectional comparisons based on medication history, and three studies using baseline neuroimaging to predict subsequent treatment response. Greater putamen volume was associated with medication status ad volume with better treatment response in the cross-sectional and predictive analyses, while cortical effects were less consistent and mainly age-dependent in frontal areas. White matter findings were subtle and inconsistent across studies, and cortical thickness evidence-limited to one study-suggests short-term, possibly transient effects in children. Conclusion MPH treatment is associated l with age-dependent differences in brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD; however, the limited number of included studies varied substantially in design, (cross-sectional and predictive studies alongside longitudinal treatment-effect studies), methodology, and reported outcomes, making firm causal conclusions difficult. Future research should prioritize larger, standardized, long-term longitudinal studies that account for developmental factors.

title: A Teleglaucoma Screening System for Individuals at Risk of Open-Angle Glaucoma: Long-Term Clinical Outcomes and Comparative Cost Analysis.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the clinical effectiveness and economic impact of a teleglaucoma screening program for individuals at increased risk of developing open-angle glaucoma (OAG). Design Prospective cohort study with retrospective evaluation of long-term clinical outcomes and comparative cost analysis. Participants Consecutive individuals with risk factors for OAG enrolled in a teleglaucoma screening program between 2020 and 2022. Methods A targeted teleglaucoma screening program was implemented within the Donostialdea Integrated Healthcare Organization (Gipuzkoa, Spain). Consecutive individuals with risk factors for OAG were included. The teleglaucoma assessment included best-corrected visual acuity, non-contact tonometry, pachymetry, and peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer optical coherence tomography (pRNFL-OCT), performed by an optometrist and reviewed asynchronously by glaucoma specialists. Findings consistent with glaucoma or suspicious for glaucoma were considered positive screening results, whereas ocular hypertension (OHT) or the absence of abnormalities were considered negative screening results. Clinical effectiveness was evaluated through analysis of glaucoma-related diagnoses recorded using ICD-10 codes during a five-year follow-up period. A comparative cost analysis was conducted from a societal perspective. Patient satisfaction was assessed using the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8). Main outcomes measures Agreement between teleglaucoma classifications and glaucoma-related ICD-10 diagnoses recorded during follow-up, diagnostic performance indicators, patient satisfaction, and costs. Results A total of 1,112 patients were included (mean age 60.2 years), of whom 63.1% were women. Positive screening results were identified in 8.2% of participants. Overall agreement between the teleglaucoma assessment and follow-up ICD-10 diagnoses was 92.6%, with a mean follow-up of 3.7 ± 0.8 years. Sensitivity was 64.5%, specificity 93.4%, and negative predictive value 98.9%. Patient satisfaction was high, with a mean score of 8.5/10. The economic analysis demonstrated a 50% reduction in total costs compared with conventional care, with a cost per patient of €40.7 versus €81.2. Conclusions The teleglaucoma system demonstrated a high ability to rule out disease among individuals at risk of glaucoma, reduced costs and achieved high patient satisfaction. However, moderate sensitivity and the use of coded clinical records as the reference standard should be considered.

title: External validation of a deep-learning algorithm for perimetric glaucoma detection on color fundus photographs in the Rotterdam Study.
abstract: Purpose To externally validate a deep-learning (DL) algorithm detecting perimetric glaucoma on color fundus photographs (CFPs) in a population-based cohort. Design External validation in a prospective population-based cohort. Participants Participants aged 50-80 years from three Rotterdam Study cohorts. Methods We applied the winning Artificial Intelligence for Robust Glaucoma Screening (AIROGS) challenge algorithm, trained on 101,442 macula-centered CFPs to detect referable presumed perimetric glaucoma. Performance was assessed at eye and participant level, with participant-level cluster bootstrap confidence intervals. Misclassified cases underwent qualitative review. Longitudinal detection was evaluated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Additionally, paired analyses compared macula- with disc-centered CFPs. A post-hoc analysis examined the effect of image quality on positive predictive value (PPV). Main outcome measures Sensitivity at 95% specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), partial AUC (pAUC) for 90-100% specificity, PPV, and precision-recall AUC (PR-AUC). Results Among 19,088 eyes (9,837 participants), 201 eyes (1.1%) had perimetric glaucoma. At eye level, sensitivity at 95% specificity was 70.6% (95% CI: 63.8-76.8), with an ROC-AUC of 0.911 (95% CI: 0.887-0.934) and a PR-AUC of 0.343 (95% CI: 0.274-0.427). At participant level, sensitivity was 68.8% (95% CI: 61.8-75.9) and ROC-AUC 0.909 (95% CI: 0.882-0.934). Overall, this resulted in 5.1 referrals per detected glaucoma case. True positives showed more advanced visual field damage than false negatives (median mean deviation -10.8 vs -5.8 dB; P < 0.001). Among true positives with prior imaging, 33 of 61 (54%) were flagged before conversion, typically 4-7 years before diagnosis. Discrimination in the 90-100% specificity range was higher for disc- than macula-centered CFPs (pAUC 0.860 vs 0.802; P = 0.003). PPV improved substantially after excluding CFPs with incomplete optic nerve head (ONH) visibility. Conclusions The DL-algorithm achieved meaningful discrimination for perimetric glaucoma in an external population-based dataset. Correctly identified cases were frequently flagged at an earlier examination, years before the perimetric diagnosis. Despite having been trained exclusively on macula-centered CFPs, the DL-algorithm showed no loss of discriminative performance on disc-centered CFPs. Incomplete ONH visibility was an important source of false positives. These findings support CFP-based deep learning as a scalable triage tool for glaucoma screening and highlight image acquisition standards for implementation.

title: Hyperspectral Histopathology with Spectral-Spatial Multiple-Instance Learning for Acute Leukemia Classification.
abstract: Background Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) may show overlapping morphology on bone-marrow trephine sections, while definitive ancillary testing is not always immediately available. We evaluated whether microscopic hyperspectral imaging (HSI) combined with patient-level spectral-spatial deep learning could support differentiation of AML, ALL, and normal marrow. Methods This retrospective single-center study included 78 patients (26 AML, 26 ALL, and 26 normal marrow). H&E-stained bone-marrow trephine sections were imaged across 400-1000 nm. Patient-level nested stratified five-fold cross-validation was defined before region-of-interest (ROI) sampling to prevent information leakage. We developed HemaSpec-MIL, a new hierarchical spectral-spatial multiple-instance learning algorithm and a major methodological output of this study. The framework combines multi-scale spectral encoding, morphology encoding, bidirectional cross-attention, and gated multiple-instance aggregation to generate patient-level probabilities. The primary endpoint was pooled out-of-fold macro-AUC. Results HemaSpec-MIL achieved a pooled out-of-fold accuracy of 0.897, macro-F1 of 0.897, and macro-AUC of 0.957. One-vs-rest AUCs were 0.964 for AML, 0.945 for ALL, and 0.962 for normal marrow. Performance exceeded spectral-only, morphology-only, 3D-CNN, Vision Transformer, and spectral Transformer baselines. Ablation analysis supported complementary contributions from the spectral branch, morphology branch, cross-attention fusion, gated patient-level aggregation, and spectral augmentation. Conclusions Microscopic HSI combined with the newly developed HemaSpec-MIL framework enabled accurate internal differentiation of AML, ALL, and normal marrow while preserving wavelength- and tissue-level interpretability. Independent multicenter validation and acquisition harmonization are required before clinical translation.

title: Association of Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscopy-Derived Fundus Metrics with Corneal Remodeling after Transepithelial Photorefractive Keratectomy: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the associations between preoperative fundus metrics and postoperative corneal remodeling following transepithelial photorefractive keratectomy (TransPRK). Methods This retrospective observational study included 103 patients (200 eyes) who underwent TransPRK. Corneal parameters were measured preoperatively and at 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively. A screening strategy using two standardized metrics, A = SD(Δ)/SD(T₀) and B = median(|Δ|)/SD(T₀), was implemented to identify high-variability corneal parameters, where Δ denotes the change from preoperative baseline, SD(Δ) the standard deviation of the change, and SD(T₀) the preoperative standard deviation of the same parameter. Patient-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE) models adjusted for age, sex, preoperative spherical equivalent (SE), and preoperative corneal epithelial thickness (CET) were used to examine the associations between retained corneal parameters and preoperative fundus metrics, including fundus tessellation density (FTD), parapapillary atrophy (PPA) area, vertical cup-to-disc ratio (VCDR), and rim-to-disc area ratio (RDAR). The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate. Results Twenty-seven corneal parameters were identified as high-variability parameters, most showing their greatest change at 1 month postoperatively. VCDR was positively associated with changes in TNP K1 and TCRP K1 (standardized β = 0.065 to 0.076), and these associations remained significant after BH correction at both 1 and 3 months (all q < 0.05). RDAR was negatively associated with the same parameters in these generalized estimating equation (GEE) models (standardized β = -0.071 to -0.060) and remained significant at 3 months postoperatively (q < 0.05); PPA area and FTD were not significantly associated with any corneal parameter. Conclusions Preoperative VCDR was significantly associated with corneal changes after TransPRK, independent of surgical parameters, whereas the association for RDAR was partly attenuated after adjustment. These findings suggest that posterior segment structure may influence anterior corneal remodeling through biomechanical pathways, though further prospective validation is warranted.

title: Predicting early EGFR-TKI treatment response in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma from H&E histopathology with weakly supervised multiple-instance learning.
abstract: Background This study sought to construct a deep-learning pipeline using an attention mechanism and multiple-instance learning (MIL) to predict early treatment response to epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) directly from routinely available hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) of pretreatment tissue in patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Methods We retrospectively obtained clinicopathological data from 100 patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma. The model employed ResNet-50 for feature representation and integrated a gated-attention pooling mechanism for feature aggregation at the patient level. This weakly supervised approach did not require pixel-level manual annotations and enabled direct slide-level prediction of early treatment response. Results The proposed gated-attention model attained an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.891 in 5-fold cross-validation, which was numerically higher than those of mean pooling (0.837), max pooling (0.821), ABMIL (0.869), CLAM (0.874), and TransMIL (0.863); however, the difference relative to CLAM did not reach statistical significance (unadjusted P = 0.062). In ablation analyses, replacing gated attention with mean pooling resulted in the largest reduction in AUC (0.054). Patient-level nuclear morphometric profiling revealed that the early adverse response group exhibited larger nuclear areas (78.3 ± 22.1 μm² vs. 62.7 ± 18.4 μm² in the favorable response group), along with elevated nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, nuclear eccentricity, and chromatin texture entropy. Chromatin texture entropy was positively correlated with the model-predicted probability of adverse response (r = 0.58, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the adverse response group displayed a higher frequency of TP53-associated alterations (62.5% vs. 38.3%), which encompassed next-generation sequencing findings and p53 immunohistochemical surrogates. In exploratory analyses, a four-variable clinical model yielded an AUC of 0.792, whereas an integrated model incorporating the multiple instance learning (MIL) risk score demonstrated an apparent AUC of 0.918 in this cohort, warranting further out-of-sample validation. Conclusion This study demonstrates that a lightweight and weakly supervised computational-pathology model can support the early estimation of EGFR-TKI treatment response. This pipeline uses routinely acquired H&E slides without requiring additional tissue sampling, provides biologically interpretable outputs, and may support clinical decision-making in precision oncology.

title: Effectiveness of Upfront Radiotherapy in Central Nervous System Germ Cell Tumors.
abstract: Background and purpose Radiotherapy (RT) is essential for curing central nervous system germ cell tumors (CNS-GCTs) except for pure mature teratoma (MT), but the optimal target volume, dose, and timing remain controversial. This study evaluated the benefit of upfront RT in CNS-GCTs. Materials and methods We reviewed CNS-GCT patients under 30-year-old treated from 2015 to 2023. Patients with pure germinomas (PG) received whole-ventricular irradiation (WVI) with tumor bed (TB) boost. Patients with malignant non-germinomatous germ cell tumor (MNGGCT) received WVI or whole-brain irradiation (WBI) with TB boost, with or without craniospinal irradiation (CSI), before or after platinum-etoposide-based chemotherapy (CTX). Serum alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin levels guided diagnosis when histopathology was unavailable. Patients with MT were treated surgically. The primary endpoint was 5-year event-free survival (EFS); secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), neurocognitive outcomes, and endocrinopathy rates. Results Twenty-nine patients were analyzed: 13 PGs, 7 MNGGCTs with upfront RT, 7 MNGGCTs with upfront CTX, and 2 MTs. The median follow-up of these tumors was 6.0, 6.6, 3.7, and 10.3 years, respectively. PGs receiving upfront RT achieved 5-year EFS and OS of 100% and 100%, respectively. For MNGGCTs receiving upfront RT, 5-year EFS and OS was 85.7% and 85.7%, respectively; 1 patient died from post-treatment disease progression. MNGGCTs treated with upfront CTX had 5-year EFS and OS of 41.7% and 60.0%, respectively; 2 patients relapsed (1 died), and 1 died from treatment-related complications. Both MTs remained event-free over 6 years following surgery alone or with Gamma Knife radiosurgery. Conclusions Upfront RT provided excellent outcomes in PGs and may eliminate the need for CTX in those achieving complete response.

title: Evaluation of image-matching and prostate movement angle using anatomical characteristics obtained from planning computed tomography.
abstract: Introduction Setup errors and prostate movement may be associated with individual patient anatomy and internal physiological conditions. We evaluated image-matching and angle of prostate movement during prostate radiotherapy using anatomical characteristics. Methods We included 103 patients who underwent prostate volumetric-modulated arc therapy. Body mass index (BMI) and the volumes of the lesser pelvic cavity, bladder, rectum, and prostate were measured using planning computed tomography. Patients were divided into small- and large-value groups according to the median value of each anatomical characteristic. The medians and standard deviations of bone setup errors and inter- and intra-fraction prostate movements were calculated in the anterior-posterior (AP), left-right (LR), and superior-inferior (SI) directions using pelvic bone and fiducial markers with the ExacTrac X-ray system. Prostate movement angles were calculated from the approximation equation of correlation between the AP and SI direction for both groups (rectum volume, bladder capacity). Results The average setup errors in the LR direction exhibited a moderate positively correlation (r = 0.43) with lesser pelvic cavity volume in the small-value group, and a moderate negative correlation (r = -0.45) in the large-value group, as determined by BMI and lesser pelvic cavity volume. Intra-fraction prostate movement angles were tilted 6.7° in the AP direction in the large rectal volume group and 3.1° in the SI direction in the large bladder volume group. Conclusions Image-matching and prostate movement angles differed between groups stratified according to patient anatomical characteristics, suggesting the potential utility of anisotropic margins and careful patient setup. Implications for practice Evaluating patient-specific anatomical characteristics before radiotherapy planning may help estimate susceptibility to setup errors and facilitate the definition of anisotropic margins based on individual prostate movement angle information.

title: Evaluation of the experience of imposter phenomenon in advanced practice and consultant therapeutic radiographers.
abstract: Introduction Research suggests a high prevalence of imposter phenomenon among healthcare professionals, which is associated with negative impacts on professional identity, performance, well-being, careers, and service development. This local NHS service evaluation explored the imposter phenomenon among advanced and consultant therapeutic radiographers in a single radiotherapy department. This research aimed to understand determinants and the impact of imposter phenomenon, and to investigate management strategies, generating recommendations for future practice. Methods This qualitative research adopted an interpretivist approach, utilising purposive homogeneous sampling in recruitment. Data collection was via semi-structured focus groups; data analysis was inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Researcher reflexivity and independent observer review enhanced the credibility and trustworthiness of findings. Results Four key themes were identified from the data. Imposter phenomenon was context-dependent, influenced by a complex blend of individual, interpersonal, and systemic factors. Most participants identified with feelings of imposter phenomenon and experienced surges throughout their careers. Organisational factors such as strong hierarchy, isolation, and lack of role clarity compounded imposter phenomenon. Peer comparison and perceived judgment were strong individual determinants. Management strategies included role planning, mentorship, peer support, clear development pathways, and reflective practice. Conclusion Clear role definition and career pathways, alongside interprofessional education, could reduce feelings of imposter phenomenon among advanced practice and consultant therapeutic radiographers. Individualised transition plans, mentorship, peer support, shared workspaces, and structured feedback can enhance confidence, collaboration, and performance. Implications for practice Organisational and professional guidance on career development, funding, workforce strategies, and strategic planning would support role efficacy, staff wellbeing, and retention, ultimately improving service delivery and patient care.

originalAbstract:
Introduction

Research suggests a high prevalence of imposter phenomenon among healthcare professionals, which is associated with negative impacts on professional identity, performance, well-being, careers, and service development. This local NHS service evaluation explored the imposter phenomenon among advanced and consultant therapeutic radiographers in a single radiotherapy department. This research aimed to understand determinants and the impact of imposter phenomenon, and to investigate management strategies, generating recommendations for future practice.

Methods

This qualitative research adopted an interpretivist approach, utilising purposive homogeneous sampling in recruitment. Data collection was via semi-structured focus groups; data analysis was inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Researcher reflexivity and independent observer review enhanced the credibility and trustworthiness of findings.

Results

Four key themes were identified from the data. Imposter phenomenon was context-dependent, influenced by a complex blend of individual, interpersonal, and systemic factors. Most participants identified with feelings of imposter phenomenon and experienced surges throughout their careers. Organisational factors such as strong hierarchy, isolation, and lack of role clarity compounded imposter phenomenon. Peer comparison and perceived judgment were strong individual determinants. Management strategies included role planning, mentorship, peer support, clear development pathways, and reflective practice.

Conclusion

Clear role definition and career pathways, alongside interprofessional education, could reduce feelings of imposter phenomenon among advanced practice and consultant therapeutic radiographers. Individualised transition plans, mentorship, peer support, shared workspaces, and structured feedback can enhance confidence, collaboration, and performance.

Implications for practice

Organisational and professional guidance on career development, funding, workforce strategies, and strategic planning would support role efficacy, staff wellbeing, and retention, ultimately improving service delivery and patient care.

title: MRI-guided HDR brachytherapy or integrated VMAT boost for tumour-targeted dose escalation in localised prostate cancer: long-term results of the TARGET study.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate local control of the gross tumour volume in localised prostate cancer following focal dose escalation delivered by integrated boost volumetric modulated arc therapy (IB-VMAT) or high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy. Materials and methods Patients with localised prostate cancer and an intraprostatic lesion identified on multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) were included in a prospective, non-randomised phase II study. Eighty patients received VMAT to the prostate 76 Gy/38 fractions. Boost strategy involved an IB of 95 Gy/38 fractions (IB-VMAT) or a single fraction of 10 Gy (HDR-VMAT). Three patients received 6 months androgen deprivation therapy. The primary endpoint was 3-year local control (LC) assessed by MRI or MRI-guided biopsy. Secondary outcomes included biochemical failure-free survival (bFFS), toxicity and health-related quality of life (HRQoL), assessed using CTCAE v.4.0, the American Urological Association Symptom Score and EPIC. Results Median follow-up was 4.8 years (IQR, 4.0-8.0). Sixty-six patients underwent a 3-year MRI or MRI-guided biopsy; one patient demonstrated recurrence within the boost volume. Four patients demonstrated intraprostatic failure outside the boost volume and three patients developed regional/distant metastases. Eight patients experienced biochemical failure (4 IB-VMAT; 4 HDR-VMAT). Overall, 5-year bFFS was 86.9% (95% CI, 79.1-95.5). No substantial differences in late toxicities and HRQoL were observed between cohorts. Conclusion Intraprostatic tumour-targeted dose escalation using IB-VMAT or HDR-VMAT provided high rates of LC and bFFS with limited adverse impact in late toxicity and HRQoL. Randomised studies are needed to further define the merits and differences between the two techniques.

title: A prospective randomized evaluation of AI assisted GTV contouring in head-and-neck radiotherapy.
abstract: Background AI-assisted contouring has demonstrated efficiency and consistency benefits for organs-at-risk in radiotherapy. However, its impact on gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation remains unexplored. The aim of this study was to evaluate AI-assisted GTV contouring in head and neck cancer radiotherapy in an exploratory randomized controlled clinical trial. Methods In this prospective, single-centre, randomized controlled evaluation, patients referred for curative-intent radiotherapy of head-neck cancer were randomized to manual contouring (control) or AI-assisted contouring (intervention) of gross tumor volumes using an in-house developed segmentation model. The primary endpoint was the extent of editing during a blinded multidisciplinary target conference, using normalized Added Path Length (APL). Secondary endpoints included conference duration, self-reported contouring time, and perceived complexity of the cases. Results Between Sept 11, 2023, and Jan 20, 2025, 85 patients were enrolled; 83 were included in the analysis (41 control, 42 AI-assisted). The median difference in APL (AI-assisted minus control, negative favoring the intervention) was -0.02 [-0.32; 0.07] for GTV-T and 0.06 [-0.01; 0.14] for GTV-N. Conference duration, contouring time, and perceived complexity were similar between groups. No adverse events were reported. Conclusion The median difference in APL between groups was consistent with no relevant effect for GTV-T. For GTV-N, however, AI-assisted contouring tended towards more editing during peer review for APL, but not for supplementary contour metrics. No efficiency benefits were demonstrated. Overall, these findings do not indicate a concern, but warrants further research before widespread adoption.

title: <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET-based radiomics for the prediction of aggressive/high-grade tumor in patients with cartilaginous tumors: A preliminary study.
abstract: Objective To assess the role of texture analysis of pre-treatment 18 F-FDG PET in the prediction of aggressive/high-grade tumor subtypes of cartilaginous tumors. Materials and methods Patients with cartilaginous tumors (benign cartilaginous tumors or CSs) who underwent pre-treatment 18 F-FDG PET for primary staging or restaging of recurrent disease were included in this retrospective study. Demographic and clinicopathologic data were collected. Textural and conventional PET parameters (maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), SUVmean, metabolic tumor volume (MTV), and total lesion glycolysis (TLG)) were obtained from PET/CT images using LIFEx program. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression analysis was performed for feature selection. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to determine predictors of aggressive/high-grade tumor subtypes in cartilaginous tumors. Results A total of 29 18 F-FDG PET scans from 26 patients were included in the present study. Among 29 included 18 F-FDG PET scans, 18 (62.1%) scans were performed in patients with a benign/low-grade tumor(benign cartilaginous tumors and G1-2 CSs), while 11 (37.9%) scans were performed in patients with an aggressive/high-grade tumor(G3, dedifferentiated, mesenchymal, and other aggressive CSs). In the LASSO logistic regression analysis, seven potential predictors were selected for predicting aggressive/high-grade cartilaginous tumors. Whereas SUVmax (p = 0.025), SUVmean (p = 0.028), GLRLM_Run Entropy (p = 0.007), GLSZM_ZSE (p = 0.011), and GLSZM_SZLGLE (p = 0.007) were significantly associated with aggressive/high-grade pathology in univariate analysis, GLRLM_Run Entropy was found as the only independent predictor in multivariate analysis. Conclusion Tumor heterogeneity assessed by texture analysis of pre-treatment 18 F-FDG PET may be a significant predictor of aggressive/high-grade tumor subtypes in cartilaginous tumors.

title: Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Neoplasms: Integrating WHO Classification with CT, MRI, and Molecular Imaging.
abstract: Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (pNENs) are a heterogeneous group of tumors within gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (GEP-NENs), with variable clinical behavior and prognosis. The World Health Organization (WHO) classification distinguishes well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) from poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs), including the recognition of grade 3 NETs (NET G3) as a separate entity with important clinical implications. Multiphasic computed tomography (CT) and multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are central to detection, staging, and follow-up, with MRI offering superior sensitivity for liver metastases, particularly with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and hepatobiliary phase (HBP). Molecular imaging with somatostatin receptor-targeted PET and 18 F-FDG PET provides complementary biologic information by assessing receptor expression, metabolic aggressiveness, and tumor heterogeneity. SSTR-targeted PET supports confirmation of neuroendocrine phenotype, whole-body staging, and selection of candidates for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, whereas 18 F-FDG PET identifies aggressive or dedifferentiated tumor components that may influence prognosis and favor chemotherapy-oriented strategies. Despite advances, noninvasive grading remains limited, requiring integration of imaging with histopathology. An integrated multimodality approach combining CT, MRI, molecular imaging, and pathology is therefore essential for accurate staging, biopsy targeting, treatment stratification, and personalized management.

title: Clinical significance of the COPD assessment test in evaluating treatment response in Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease.
abstract: Background In Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease (MAC-PD), sputum culture conversion is a key endpoint but does not fully reflect symptom burden. We evaluated the COPD Assessment Test (CAT) as a patient-reported measure of disease severity and treatment response. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 179 treatment episodes in 174 patients with MAC-PD who continued therapy for at least 12 months. CAT scores were assessed at baseline and at 6 and 12 months. We examined associations of baseline CAT scores with chest computed tomography (CT) scores and sputum culture status, and of CAT changes (Δ6 and Δ12) with the 12-month culture-positive versus culture-negative/sputum-unobtainable classification and a study-defined composite incorporating 12-month radiographic response and the microbiologic course through 24 months. Results Baseline CAT scores correlated weakly with CT scores and were higher in baseline culture-positive and poorly controlled episodes. Neither Δ6 nor Δ12 differed by 12-month culture classification. Δ12 was more favorable in well-controlled than in poorly controlled episodes (p = 0.010), but discrimination was limited (area under the curve, 0.646 in all classifiable episodes and 0.682 in those with baseline CAT > 2). In the latter subgroup, an exploratory decrease of at least 3 points showed a sensitivity of 52.0% and a specificity of 71.9%. Conclusions CAT may complement microbiologic and radiographic assessments by capturing patient-reported symptom changes. The limited discriminatory performance does not support the use of CAT alone to classify treatment control.

title: [Unfavorable prognosis of pathogenic variants in the telomerase complex in cases of familial pulmonary fibrosis].
abstract: Introduction Pathogenic variants located in genes involved in telomere homeostasis (telomere-related genes [TRGs]) are associated with cases of familial pulmonary fibrosis (FPF). The aim of our study was to characterize the clinical presentation and prognosis of patients with FPF according to the presence or absence of a pathogenic variant involving a TRG. Methods We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-center study including all patients with FPF followed at the Rare Lung Diseases Reference Center of Bichat-Claude-Bernard Hospital (Paris, France) and analyzed between 2021 and 2024, using next-generation sequencing of a single 30-gene panel associated with FPF. Results Fifty-six patients were included. Median age at diagnosis of interstitial lung disease (ILD) was 65 years. Thirty-three patients (59%) exhibited a CT pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), four (7%) had a nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern, and three (5%) displayed a bronchiolocentric interstitial pneumonia pattern. The diagnoses retained after multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) were as follows: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 29 patients (52%), hypersensitivity pneumonitis in four (7%), ILD associated with rheumatoid arthritis in four (7%), and idiopathic NSIP in three (5%). A pathogenic TRG variant was detected in 12 patients (21%): TERT (n=4), PARN (n=4), RTEL1 (n=3), and TERC (n=1). Introduction

Pathogenic variants located in genes involved in telomere homeostasis (telomere-related genes [TRGs]) are associated with cases of familial pulmonary fibrosis (FPF). The aim of our study was to characterize the clinical presentation and prognosis of patients with FPF according to the presence or absence of a pathogenic variant involving a TRG.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-center study including all patients with FPF followed at the Rare Lung Diseases Reference Center of Bichat-Claude-Bernard Hospital (Paris, France) and analyzed between 2021 and 2024, using next-generation sequencing of a single 30-gene panel associated with FPF.

Results

Fifty-six patients were included. Median age at diagnosis of interstitial lung disease (ILD) was 65 years. Thirty-three patients (59%) exhibited a CT pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), four (7%) had a nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern, and three (5%) displayed a bronchiolocentric interstitial pneumonia pattern. The frequency of pulmonary and extrapulmonary manifestations at diagnosis did not differ significantly between patients with or without a pathogenic TRG variant. Patients carrying a pathogenic TRG variant underwent more rapid annual decline in forced vital capacity (-4.54 vs. -1.75 percentage points; P=0.044).

Conclusion

These results confirm the unfavorable prognostic impact of an identified pathogenic variant of a TRG in patients with FPF, which is associated with a particularly rapid decline in respiratory function.

title: Fluid fluctuation and visual outcomes in neovascular age-related macular degeneration: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Fluctuation in retinal thickness and fluid during anti-vascular endothelial growrh factor (VEGF) therapy has emerged as a candidate prognostic biomarker in neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD), but the evidence is heterogeneous and has not been quantitatively synthesized. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to December, 2025, for studies reporting retinal fluid or thickness fluctuation metrics and best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) outcomes in eyes receiving anti-VEGF therapy for nAMD, including both observational studies and post hoc analyses of randomized trials. Between-group mean differences (MDs) in BCVA change were pooled using random-effects models, stratified by study design and OCT parameter, and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Seventeen studies comprising 19 reports and 9,873 eyes were included. Among observational studies at 24 months, eyes in the highest fluctuation category had significantly smaller BCVA gains than those in the lowest for every parameter examined: intraretinal fluid (MD -7.00 letters, 95% CI -10.27 to -3.72), subretinal fluid (-5.02, -8.09 to -1.95), pigment epithelial detachment (-8.41, -14.54 to -2.27), total fluid (-9.42, -12.69 to -6.15), and central subfield thickness (-10.56, -14.40 to -6.73), with low to moderate heterogeneity (I² 0-42.6%). Among post hoc analyses of randomized trials at 24 months, the pooled difference was -6.02 letters (-8.72 to -3.32), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 77.2%) that leave-one-out analysis showed did not alter the direction or significance of the estimate. Greater fluctuation was additionally associated with approximately twice the odds of macular fibrosis and atrophy. Certainty of evidence was low to very low for most fluid compartments, limited principally by the non-randomized nature of the exposure and by the absence of a standardized definition of fluctuation across studies. Temporal anatomical stability, rather than the presence of fluid at any single visit, may therefore carry prognostic information beyond conventional measures of disease activity, though prospective evaluation using a common metric is required before stability can be adopted as a treatment target.

title: Whole-tumor dual-layer spectral detector CT quantification for preoperative identification of poorly differentiated cervical squamous cell carcinoma: An interpretable prediction model.
abstract: Objectives To develop an interpretable dual-layer spectral detector CT (DLCT) model for preoperative identification of poorly differentiated cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and to compare two-dimensional region-of-interest (2D ROI) with whole-tumor three-dimensional volume-of-interest (3D VOI) parameter-extraction strategies. Methods This retrospective study included 205 surgically treated patients with CSCC who underwent contrast-enhanced DLCT before surgery. Patients were assigned to training (n = 113), internal validation (n = 47), and temporal validation (n = 45) cohorts. Parameters were extracted using 2D ROI- and 3D VOI-based analyses. Clinical, 2D DLCT, 3D DLCT, and DLCT-clinical fusion models were developed using multivariable logistic regression and evaluated by discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Results 3D VOI-based analysis showed higher interobserver reproducibility than 2D ROI-based analysis (mean intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.950 vs. 0.875; P < 0.001). The 3D DLCT model included arterial-phase 70-keV virtual monoenergetic attenuation (CT 70keV-AP ), arterial-phase normalized effective atomic number (NZeff AP ), and venous-phase normalized iodine density (NID VP ). Its areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) were 0.897, 0.895, and 0.885 in the training, internal validation, and temporal validation cohorts, respectively. The 2D DLCT and 3D DLCT models did not differ significantly in AUCs after multiple-comparison correction. The fusion model achieved AUCs of 0.900, 0.916, and 0.881, respectively, outperforming the clinical model without significantly improving on the 3D DLCT model. Conclusions 3D DLCT quantification provides an interpretable and noninvasive imaging biomarker for preoperative identification of poorly differentiated CSCC and may support individualized risk stratification. External validation in larger multicenter cohorts is needed to confirm generalizability.
