To address this, we propose a novel motion-guided semi-supervised spatiotemporal framework that propagates sparse supervision from the label of the end-diastolic (ED) frame to the entire sequence. Our framework jointly optimizes motion estimation and segmentation. First, a motion decoder estimates dense displacement fields to warp the ED label, generating high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unannotated frames. Concurrently, the segmentation network employs a Temporal Kernel Segmentation (TKS) module with dynamic convolutions to adaptively capture rapid cardiac deformations, alongside a Multi-Scale Spatial Propagator (MSP) to recover fine anatomical boundaries. The motion-derived pseudo-labels directly supervise the segmentation network, ensuring temporal coherence.

Main results

Extensive experiments on a multi-center cohort from three clinical centers demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the compared methods, achieving superior segmentation accuracy and robust generalization capabilities.

Significance

The proposed framework effectively mitigates the burden of manual data annotation while providing temporally coherent full-cycle cardiac analysis, holding significant potential for efficient and reliable clinical assessment of cardiovascular diseases.

title: Segmentation-perturbation propagation in pretrained foundation-model embeddings versus IBSI-aligned radiomics for radiologist-assessed lung-nodule malignancy classification on the LIDC-IDRI cohort.
abstract: Objective Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort. Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone.&#xD.

title: Quantifying multi-lesion detection and localization in whole-body FDG PET/CT with a multimodal foundation model.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop a 3D AI framework for detecting and localizing multiple lesions in whole-body FDG PET/CT, and to evaluate whether a pretrained PET/CT foundation model can improve lesion detection performance compared with conventional training from scratch.ApproachThe AutoPET cohort comprised 1,014 studies divided into 700 training, 114 validation, and 200 subject-independent test studies. Tumor masks were converted into 3D bounding boxes. We developed a one-stage 3D lesion detector using a PlainConvUNet backbone to extract multi-scale encoder-decoder features for lesion classification and box regression. To leverage foundation-model representations, the PlainConvUNet backbone was initialized with weights from our previously developed multi-center PET/CT foundation model, pretrained using masked autoencoding, and subsequently fine-tuned for lesion detection. Four configurations were compared: PET+CT trained from scratch, PET only, CT only, and PET+CT initialized from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model. Detection performance was evaluated using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) and alternative FROC (AFROC) analyses, qualitative analysis, and lesion-size-stratified operating curves.Main resultsMultimodal PET+CT consistently outperformed either modality alone across task-based detection metrics, demonstrating the complementary contributions of metabolic and anatomical information. Importantly, initialization from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model further enhanced lesion detection performance compared with training the same PET+CT detector from scratch, increasing absolute FROC sensitivity by 0.034-0.041 across the evaluated 1-4 false-positive-per-scan operating range and improving AFROC AUC by 0.028. Detection performance increased with lesion size, with small lesions remaining the most challenging. The separation between the pretrained and randomly initialized PET+CT configurations was more evident in the smaller-lesion strata, whereas their operating curves increasingly overlapped for larger lesions.SignificanceThis study provides a detection-centered, task-based characterization of multi-lesion analysis in whole-body PET/CT. Multimodal PET+CT improves lesion detection compared with either modality alone, lesion size is a major determinant of detection performance, and initialization from a pretrained PET/CT foundation model provides an additional performance improvement.

title: FASA-Net: A Frequency-Domain-Enhanced and Anatomically Constrained Vision-Language Framework for Automated Chest X-ray Report Generation.
abstract: Automated radiology report generation can reduce radiologists' workloads by producing preliminary reports from medical images. However, generating chest X-ray reports remains challenging. Subtle lesions and organ boundaries may be underrepresented, visual regions may be poorly aligned with medical terminology, and long reports require coherent clinical descriptions. To address these challenges, we propose FASA-Net, a vision-language framework that combines frequency-domain enhancement with anatomical semantic constraints. Its Frequency-Domain Pyramid Attention Network (FPAN) integrates frequency-domain analysis and a multiscale feature pyramid to enhance local structures and high-frequency visual details. The Anatomical Semantic Constraint Attention (ASCA) module guides cross-modal interactions between visual regions and anatomy-related terms to reduce the risk of regional misalignment and semantic hallucination. The Context Aggregation Module (CAM) incorporates a summary of the text generated so far into decoding to improve coherence and terminological consistency. Experiments on the public IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR datasets show competitive performance on natural language generation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L, together with improved clinical label consistency measured using CheXbert-based clinical efficacy metrics. Ablation studies, visualizations, and case studies further illustrate the contributions of FPAN, ASCA, and CAM to visual detail enhancement, anatomical semantic alignment, and contextual aggregation. FASA-Net therefore has potential as an auxiliary tool for chest X-ray report generation, although clinical deployment requires further validation using multicenter data, radiologist assessments, and prospective studies.

title: A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography.
abstract: Objectives Full-field digital mammography (FFDM) is the standard for breast cancer screening but has reduced sensitivity in dense breasts. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) improves cancer detection compared to 2D mammography but is limited by cost and longer reading times. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced mammography has demonstrated improved sensitivity compared to 2D mammography. This study compares AI-enhanced 2D mammography (DM+AI) with DBT in recalling interval breast cancers (IBCs). Methods : A multi-reader, multi-case crossover study was conducted using the Emory BrEast Imaging Dataset, which includes paired FFDM and DBT images with biopsy-proven outcomes. Six radiologists reviewed 53 IBC and 53 screen-detected cancer (SDC) cases, with random assignment to DM+AI or DBT, followed by crossover after a washout period. Primary outcomes included recall rate of IBCs. Secondary outcomes included recall rate of SDCs, interpretation time, and subgroup analysis by breast density. Results : For IBCs, DM+AI and DBT demonstrated similar recall rates (41.5% vs 40.9%) and detection rates (14.8% vs 11.9%). DM+AI identified more non-invasive (31.5% vs 13.0%) and mass-forming (61.0% vs 21.8%) cancers. For SDCs, recall and detection rates were comparable across modalities. In fatty breasts, recall was higher with DM+AI (91.7% vs 50.0%), while DBT performed better in extremely dense breasts. DM+AI enabled faster interpretation, averaging 24.1 seconds less per case. Conclusion : AI-enhanced 2D mammography demonstrated comparable performance to DBT with shorter interpretation times, supporting a stratified screening approach. Advances in knowledge This study is the first direct comparison of AI-enhanced mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis for IBC detection.

title: Quantitative Hepatobiliary MRI for Early Prognostic Assessment After Liver Transplantation: Survival Prediction Using the Contrast Enhancement Index.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of the contrast enhancement index (CEI) derived from gadobenate dimeglumine (Gd-BOPTA)-enhanced hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for early assessment of liver graft function after liver transplantation (LT). Methods This retrospective study included LT recipients undergoing Gd-BOPTA-enhanced MRI within 6 months after transplantation. CEI was calculated using liver-to-psoas signal intensity ratios on pre-contrast and HBP images acquired 90-120 minutes after contrast administration. ROC, Kaplan-Meier, and age-adjusted Cox regression analyses evaluated associations with mortality. Results Seventy patients (median age, 62 years; interquartile range [IQR], 48-74) were included. CEI was quantifiable in all cases (median, 1.27; IQR, 1.09-1.37). Non-survivors had significantly lower CEI values than survivors (median, 1.17 vs 1.31; p = 0.03; Cliff's δ = -0.28). ROC analysis showed moderate discrimination for mortality (AUC, 0.667; 95% CI, 0.529-0.793), with an optimal cutoff of 1.301 (sensitivity, 88%; specificity, 51.2%). Patients with CEI <1.301 had significantly lower overall survival (log-rank p = 0.028). After adjustment for recipient age, CEI remained associated with mortality (HR per 0.1-unit increase, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.98; p = 0.035). Conclusion Quantitative CEI measurement on Gd-BOPTA HBP MRI is feasible after LT, and lower CEI values. Advances in knowledge This study links quantitative Gd-BOPTA-enhanced HBP MRI with overall survival after LT, supporting CEI as a potential non-invasive imaging biomarker for postoperative risk stratification.

abstract: Objectives This systematic review aims to evaluate the techniques and reported patterns of heatmap-based visual explanations in deep learning (DL) systems for dental radiographic classification tasks. Methods A literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore Library, Oria.no and Google Scholar to retrieve studies using DL for dental classification tasks. Only articles with a visual explanation (heatmap) were selected. Risk of bias assessment was done with QUADAS-2, PROBAST-AI and CEBM. The heatmap technique, reasons for inclusion, explanations provided and patterns were analysed. Results In the 136 studies reviewed, Grad-CAM was the most commonly used technique. The predominant reason for using visual explanations was to understand the decision-making process of the DL model. Some heatmaps reflect established radiographic criteria, while others exhibit unique, label-dependent patterns that sometimes emphasise irrelevant areas. Cropping to the region of interest influences visual explanations. Conclusions Visual explanations seem clinically plausible to domain experts when aligned with domain knowledge, but clinical plausibility does not equal technical faithfulness. Formal faithfulness testing was rarely performed among the included studies. Therefore, explanations should not be assumed to accurately represent the model's underlying reasoning. Limitations include the evaluation of studies not primarily designed for visual explanation assessment. No funding was received for this review. Authors declare no competing interests. Advances in knowledge Visual explanations, while clinically plausible when aligned with domain knowledge, remain insufficiently validated and should not be assumed to faithfully represent model reasoning. An implausible explanation does not necessarily indicate model failure. Domain/task-specific evaluation metrics for explainable AI in dentomaxillofacial radiology are needed.

title: Lessons learned from a decade of EUS(-FNA) staging in esophageal and GEJ carcinoma: towards a selective staging strategy.
abstract: Endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration (EUS(-FNA)) is recommended by current guidelines as part of the staging for esophageal and gastro-esophageal junction (GEJ) carcinoma, yet its incremental value over modern 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) remains uncertain. This Lessons Learned article reflects on over a decade of EUS(-FNA) and FDG-PET staging in 402 patients with potentially curable esophageal or GEJ carcinoma at a high-volume tertiary referral center. In 91.3% of patients, EUS(-FNA) did not alter the radiation field as would have been defined by FDG-PET. EUS(-FNA) resulted in an expansion of the radiation field in 4.5% and reduction in 4.2% of patients. Squamous cell carcinoma showed more than two-fold greater likelihood of radiation field modification. Among 193 patients classified as FDG-PET non-suspicious for malignant lymph nodes (LNs), EUS-FNA identified malignant LNs in eight patients (4.1%), which influenced the radiation field. In 5 of 402 patients (1.2%) a malignant LN was detected with EUS-FNA in a station that would not have routinely been resected surgically. In patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT), LN staging is of direct therapeutic consequence: underestimation of nodal disease may result in geographic miss, while overestimation leads to unnecessary irradiation. In contrast, in patients treated with perioperative 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin and docetaxel (FLOT) followed by surgical lymphadenectomy, most involved LN stations are routinely addressed surgically, limiting the added value of EUS(-FNA) for treatment planning. Therefore, we view EUS(-FNA) as a selective staging tool in patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive CRT, rather than a procedure applied routinely to all patients.

title: Long-term Prognostic Value of Sequential Coronary CT Angiography and Quantitative PET in Suspected Chronic Coronary Syndromes: A Multicentre study.
abstract: Background and aims The long-term prognostic value of a guideline-recommended selective sequential anatomical-functional imaging strategy using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) followed by quantitative [15O]H2O positron emission tomography (PET) remains uncertain. We evaluated its long-term prognostic value in patients with first symptoms suggestive of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Methods In this multicentre European cohort, symptomatic patients first underwent CCTA and were selectively referred to quantitative [15O]H2O PET in case of suspected obstructive stenosis (≥50%). Patients were stratified according to CCTA findings and PET-derived ischaemia (normal CCTA; non-obstructive CAD on CCTA; obstructive CAD on CCTA without ischaemia; obstructive CAD on CCTA with ischaemia). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and hospitalization for unstable angina (UA). Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were calculated. Results Among 3,918 patients (61.0±9.8 years; 54.3% female) with a median follow-up of 5.1 [3.8-8.0] years, 278 (7.1%) experienced the primary endpoint. aHRs increased stepwise across CCTA-PET categories. Compared to normal CCTA, non-obstructive CAD and obstructive CAD without ischaemia were associated with a higher risk of the combined primary endpoint (aHR 1.89, [95%CI: 1.23-2.91], p=0.004; aHR 3.20, [95%CI: 1.95-5.25], p<0.001). Among patients with obstructive CAD on CCTA, PET-derived ischaemia further increased the risk of the primary endpoint (aHR 1.55, [95%CI: 1.05-2.30]; p=0.029), but not when excluding UA from the composite endpoint (aHR 1.37, [95%CI 0.90-2.07]; p=0.141). PET-derived ischaemia primarily predicted events within the first year, while obstructive CCTA findings remained associated with long-term hard outcomes. Conclusions A sequential strategy combining CCTA and quantitative [15O]H2O PET provides robust and incremental long-term risk stratification. While PET-derived ischaemia refines prediction of short-term and symptom-driven events, CCTA-derived CAD remains the principal determinant of long-term hard outcomes.

title: Serum brain-derived tau in lacunar stroke and cerebral small vessel disease.
abstract: Introduction Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) selectively quantifies tau of central nervous system origin in blood and has demonstrated strong correlations with infarct volume and functional outcome in general ischaemic stroke, but data in lacunar stroke and cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) are lacking. Patients and methods In a prospectively collected cohort of 101 lacunar stroke patients with an MRI-confirmed recent small subcortical infarct (RSSI) and 47 controls, we measured serum BD-tau using the HD-X SIMOA platform at baseline and 3 and 15 months after stroke. We examined associations of BD-tau with infarct size, chronic CSVD neuroimaging features (white matter hyperintensities [WMHs], lacunes, microbleeds, total SVD score), CSVD progression on follow-up MRI and functional outcome. Results Baseline serum BD-tau was higher in RSSI patients than controls (median 9.54 [7.32-12.20] vs 7.75 [6.18-9.44] pg/mL; P = .003) and correlated with infarct diameter (rs = 0.222, P = 0.039). Brain-derived tau did not correlate with time from stroke symptom onset to blood sampling (rs = 0.150, P = .179). Brain-derived tau was not associated with chronic CSVD neuroimaging features (WMHs, lacunes, microbleeds, SVD score; all P > .05) at any timepoint. Longitudinally, BD-tau returned to control levels by 3 months (P = .374) and remained stable at 15 months (P = .985). Brain-derived tau was neither associated with new vascular MRI lesions on follow-up nor functional neurological outcome. Conclusion Serum BD-tau is elevated acutely in CSVD-related RSSI, correlates with infarct size and normalises by 3 months. Brain-derived tau was not associated with chronic CSVD neuroimaging features or disease progression, suggesting sensitivity to acute neuronal injury rather than chronic or progressive CSVD.

title: Association of colonic motility on magnetic resonance enterography with endoscopic disease activity and chronic structural damage in ulcerative colitis.
abstract: Background Colonic motor dysfunction has been described in ulcerative colitis (UC) but has been less systematically assessed using quantitative imaging. We examined whether motility changes are associated with endoscopic disease activity and imaging features of disease chronicity. Methods This prospective cross-sectional study included 49 adults with known UC who underwent magnetic resonance enterography and colonoscopy and 30 control participants. Colonic motility was quantified using GIQuant software. Endoscopic activity was graded by Mayo endoscopic subscore (MES) (0-3). Associations between motility and MES were assessed by ordinal regression and diagnostic performance by area under the curve. Imaging features of chronicity were recorded in segments with low endoscopic activity (MES ≤1). Results GIQuant values were lower in patients with UC than control subjects in every colonic segment (mean difference -205.9 to -110.1 units; all false discovery rate-adjusted P ≤.001). Higher motility was associated with lower MES (odds ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.38; 95% confidence interval, 0.28-0.52). The area under the curve was 0.83 for MES ≥1, 0.70 for MES ≥2, and 0.73 for MES ≥3. In segments with MES ≤1, chronicity features were associated with lower GIQuant values, with the largest differences observed for loss of haustration and increased pericolic fat. Conclusions GIQuant-derived bowel wall motion is lower in UC and inversely associated with endoscopic activity. Correlations with chronic magnetic resonance enterography features remain present in segments with MES ≤1. Prospective validation with standardized colonic cine magnetic resonance imaging and concurrent symptom measures is needed before clinical use.

title: Changes in Breast Cancer Optoacoustic Imaging Features During Neoadjuvant Therapy and Correlation with Pathologic Response: A Feasibility Study.
abstract: Objective To assess whether changes in optoacoustic/ultrasound (OA/US) imaging features during neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) correlate with treatment response, compared to US-derived tumor volumetric changes. Methods In this IRB-approved, HIPAA-compliant prospective study, 20 patients with cT1-T4, cN1-3 breast cancer underwent serial OA/US imaging at baseline, post-cycle 1, mid-therapy, and presurgery. Optoacoustic/US features, including internal vessels (OAint), internal hemoglobin (OAHb), deoxyHb, peripheral zone (OApz), and boundary zone (OAbz) were assessed using a validated scoring system. US tumor volume and OA/US changes were compared to residual cancer burden (RCB) and pathologic complete response (pCR). Responders were defined as RCB 0-II; non-responders were defined as RCB III. Comparisons were made using Wilcoxon Rank-Sum tests and univariate logistic regression. Results Mean age was 50.4 years (SD ± 9.5). Mean tumor size was 26.3 mm (SD ± 9.7). Pathology showed pCR in 6 (30%), partial response in 11 (55%), and no response in 3 (15%), with mean overall residual tumor cellularity of 32.7% (SD ± 33.5). Regression analysis showed no significant correlation between percent volume change and pCR at cycle1 or mid-therapy. Patients achieving pCR had significantly lower residual OAHb after cycle 1 (76.4% vs 108.8%, P = 0.01). At preoperative, all OA/US features decreased significantly more in pCR vs non-pCR cases (all P < 0.05). Higher individual and total OA/US scores at cycle 1 reflecting elevated hemoglobin and lower relative oxygen saturation predicted RCB III status. The RCB III tumors had significantly higher mean residual deoxygenated blush score at cycle 1 (117.8% vs 64.8%, P = 0.03). Conclusion Optoacoustic/US feature changes were more highly correlated with pCR than US volumetric decrease and show promise as a potential tool to non-invasively identify pCR. Early cycle 1 OA/US scores may help identify poor responders.

title: Clinical Implications of Background Parenchymal Enhancement on Breast MRI.
abstract: Breast MRI is an essential tool for breast cancer detection, evaluation, and characterization, offering greater sensitivity than mammography and ultrasound. Normal breast tissue demonstrates variable enhancement on MRI, known as background parenchymal enhancement (BPE), which reflects the physiologic enhancement of fibroglandular tissue after gadolinium administration. Initially considered an incidental finding, BPE is now recognized as a dynamic imaging feature influenced by several factors, including age, menopausal status, exogenous hormone use, and prior breast cancer treatments. Increasing evidence supports its clinical relevance since variations in BPE have been associated with differences in breast cancer risk, lesion detection, and imaging interpretation. Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) is emerging as an important imaging biomarker with potential applications in risk stratification, evaluation of disease extent, and monitoring response to neoadjuvant therapy. Differences in BPE patterns may also correlate with tumor biology and molecular subtypes, further supporting its role in personalized breast imaging assessment. This article provides a comprehensive review of BPE, highlighting its biologic basis, imaging characteristics, and clinical implications in breast cancer care. It also examines the evolving role of artificial intelligence tools in the assessment and quantification of BPE, which may improve standardization and integration into clinical decision-making and research.

title: Opportunistic Osteoporosis Screening Using CT-Derived Volumetric Bone Mineral Density Reference Curves.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) scans are a widely available yet underused resource that can be leveraged for opportunistic osteoporosis screening. This study aimed to develop sex- and site-specific reference curves for volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) to define dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-anchored percentile thresholds for osteoporosis classification, and to evaluate whether these thresholds identified individuals who subsequently sustain a major osteoporotic fracture (MOF). A retrospective cohort of 4,418 clinical CT scans was analyzed, including a subset of 1,088 scans with corresponding DXA imaging within one year. MOF incidence and timing following CT were obtained from linked administrative health data. CT images were segmented with deep learning models to extract the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and femoral neck from which vBMDs were assessed using internal calibration. Sex-specific vBMD centile curves were generated for each region using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape. A receiver operating characteristic analysis with the Youden index defined percentile thresholds that aligned with DXA-defined osteoporosis. Clinical relevance was assessed by determining the proportion of participants classified as osteoporotic by the CT-derived percentile thresholds who subsequently sustained a MOF, and by evaluating the association between CT-defined osteoporosis and time to incident fracture using Cox proportional hazards models. The cohort included 2,368 males and 2,050 females. At the vertebral body, 66.3% (n=67) of female and 41.9% (n=26) of male fracture cases had vBMD values below the CT-defined osteoporosis threshold, consistent with osteoporosis. Among these, 44.8% (n=30) of females and 76.9% (n=20) of males had not undergone DXA screening. Individuals classified as osteoporotic based on CT-derived thresholds had up to 2.86 times higher risk of sustaining an MOF across all vertebral sites in both sexes. These findings indicate that CT-derived vBMD percentile thresholds offer clinically meaningful cut-points for opportunistic screening and support their use as a diagnostic flag for further evaluation.

title: Translating absolute risk of breast cancer into screening frequency: a framework to guide practice.
abstract: Background Current precision mammography screening trials use heterogeneous risk models, risk strata, and screening intervals, with no consensus on how absolute breast cancer risk should translate into screening frequency. A standardized, risk-model-agnostic approach could improve consistency in trial design and facilitate broader clinical implementation. To develop and evaluate a risk-model-agnostic framework that maps guideline-defined absolute breast cancer risk cut points to screening intervals that can guide the design of future personalized screening strategies and translate smoothly to routine clinical practice. Methods Screening interval and frequency derived from the absolute risk of breast cancer in US women is the main outcome. Results The framework yielded a gradient of estimated screening intervals that scaled with absolute risk: annual (2%-3%); annual with supplemental imaging/counseling (≥3%); biennial (1%-2%); and potentially less frequently. When compared with ongoing intervention trials, screening intervals assigned by trials varied widely and were not uniformly aligned with absolute-risk levels, underscoring the lack of standardized mapping between risk and screening intensity. Conclusion A risk-model-agnostic framework based on absolute-risk cut points can provide a transparent and standardized method for specifying screening intervals in personalized mammography screening. This approach may improve consistency in future intervention trials and facilitate equitable implementation of precision screening across population settings.

title: Intraoperative demonstration of a check-valve mechanism in a spinal extradural arachnoid cyst with nerve root incarceration.
abstract: Spinal extradural arachnoid cysts (SEDACs) are rare lesions thought to arise from a dural defect associated with a check-valve mechanism, although direct intraoperative evidence is limited. We report a 17-year-old female presenting with persistent low back pain and bilateral lower extremity numbness. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a cystic lesion at the Th12-L1 level displacing the dural sac, while computed tomography myelography failed to identify a communicating tract. Surgical exploration was performed due to persistent symptoms and a suspected dynamic mechanism. Intraoperatively, a dural defect at the nerve root sleeve with nerve root incarceration was identified. Cerebrospinal fluid leakage ceased after closure of the defect, confirming a check-valve mechanism. The cyst was resected and the defect repaired. The patient's symptoms resolved completely, with no recurrence at 2-year follow-up. This case provides direct intraoperative evidence of the proposed pathophysiology of SEDAC.

title: Navigated robotic-arm-assisted hybrid multi-portal endoscopic fenestration of a thoracic intradural arachnoid cyst: a technical case report.
abstract: Endoscopic treatment of spinal intradural lesions is technically demanding because bimanual manipulation, irrigation control, neural protection, and dural closure are constrained. A 44-year-old woman with myelopathy from a dorsal T4-T10 intradural arachnoid cyst underwent endoscopic fenestration at T4/5. The hybrid multi-portal technique combined unilateral biportal-style exposure, a uniportal working-channel endoscope, intraoperative navigation, and robotic-arm camera stabilization. An accessory portal enabled bimanual intradural manipulation. Irrigation pressure was reduced after durotomy, and the dura was closed with sutures and clips reinforced by sealants. Day 1 magnetic resonance imaging confirmed cord decompression, and lower-limb sensory and bladder symptoms had resolved at 6 weeks. To our knowledge, this is the first reported navigated robotic-arm-assisted hybrid multi-portal endoscopic fenestration of a thoracic intradural arachnoid cyst. This single case demonstrates technical feasibility but not superiority over open or microscopic surgery.

title: Pretherapeutic Tumor Growth Velocity Refines Survival Stratification Beyond Clinical, Molecular, and Surgical Factors in IDH-Mutant Lower-Grade Gliomas.
abstract: Background Contemporary risk stratification of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant lower-grade gliomas relies primarily on molecular characteristics and surgical tumor burden but does not capture dynamic tumor behavior. Our primary objective was to determine whether pretherapeutic tumor growth velocity (TGV) provides independent prognostic information for overall survival (OS) beyond established factors. Methods This multicenter retrospective study included 569 adults with grade 2-3 IDH-mutant gliomas from three French centers, comprising a development cohort (n = 440) and two external validation cohorts (n = 129). TGV was derived from automated, outcome-blinded volumetric analysis of serial preoperative MRI using mean diameter expansion and log-volume growth. Prognostic value was assessed using multivariable Cox regression, external validation, decision curve analysis, and exploratory random survival forests. Results During a median follow-up of 6.8 years, 73 deaths occurred in the development cohort. Higher TGV was independently associated with shorter overall survival after adjustment for age, sex, grade, 1p/19q status, and postoperative residual tumor volume (HR per 1-mm/year increase, 1.046; 95%CI, 1.011-1.083; P=.011), and was independently replicated externally (HR, 1.077; 95% CI, 1.005-1.153; P=.035). Findings were consistent using log-volume growth and after accounting for CDKN2A/B status. Adding TGV improved prognostic model fit (likelihood-ratio χ²=5.70; P=.017), with greatest incremental value in astrocytomas. Decision curve analysis demonstrated additional clinical utility, while survival forests identified TGV among the strongest survival predictors alongside 1p/19q status and postoperative residual tumor volume. Conclusions Pretherapeutic TGV independently predicts survival beyond contemporary molecular and surgical factors in IDH-mutant lower-grade gliomas. This accessible MRI-derived biomarker may refine individualized risk stratification, particularly in astrocytoma.

title: Krebs Von Den Lungen-6 as a biomarker for lung disease activity and diagnosis in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
abstract: Objectives Children with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and lung disease (LD) are at increased risk of serious complications and premature mortality, making early detection and intervention critical. Krebs von den Lungen 6 (KL-6) is a blood-based biomarker for interstitial lung disease in adults; however, its role in pediatric LD is unclear. This study evaluates KL-6 as a discriminatory and disease activity biomarker for sJIA-LD. Methods Thirty-two patients with sJIA-LD were enrolled through the Childhood Arthritis and Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry. Comparators included sJIA patients without LD, children with primary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and healthy control children. Results Median KL-6 levels were significantly higher in sJIA-LD (596.3 U/mL [IQR 273.5-5,896.3]) compared to sJIA without LD (193.0 U/mL [151.0-252.0], p < 0.0001) and healthy controls (171.9 U/mL [89.7-224.3], p = 0.001), with no difference versus PAP (596.3 vs. 1429.9, p = 0.30). A cut-off of 259.5 U/mL yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 80.9% specificity for LD (AUC 0.856, p < 0.0001). At 371.5 U/mL, specificity reached 100% with 68.7% sensitivity and 100% positive predictive value. SJIA-LD features associated with higher median KL-6 levels included oxygen requirement, abnormal pulse oximeter (<90%), and abnormal chest radiographs. KL-6 strongly correlated with physician global assessment of lung disease but not with markers of systemic inflammation or macrophage activation syndrome. Conclusion KL-6 is a useful biomarker for discriminating LD and evaluating disease activity in sJIA-LD. Future efforts should focus on the utility of KL-6 for monitoring disease progression, treatment response, and predicting long-term disease trajectories.

title: Prediction of Pedicle Screw Loosening For Lumbar Fusion Surgery With Preoperative Volume Of Interest-Based Hounsfield Units in Lumbar Vertebral Bodies On Computed Tomography.
abstract: Study design Retrospective cohort study. Objective To assess whether preoperative Hounsfield unit (HU) values measured using the volume of interest (VOI) method on computed tomography (CT) scans predict pedicle screw loosening after single-level lumbar fusion surgery. Summary of background data Pedicle screw loosening is a major complication after spinal fusion surgery, particularly in patients with osteoporosis. While CT-derived HU values using region of interest (ROI) analysis have been associated with bone quality, the 3-dimensional VOI method enables volumetric assessment of the vertebral body. However, the clinical utility of VOI-based HU values for predicting screw loosening remains unclear. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 82 patients who underwent single-level lumbar interbody fusion with bilateral pedicle screw fixation. HU values at L1-L5 were measured using a 3D VOI technique. Screw loosening was assessed using follow-up CT scans taken at least 12 months after surgery. Differences in HU values between the loosening and nonloosening groups were evaluated. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to determine cutoff HU values and predictive performance. Results Pedicle screw loosening was observed in 26 out of 82 patients (31.7%). HU values were significantly lower in the loosening group across all vertebral levels (P<0.05). The mean HU value across L1-L5 was 235.7±35.2 HU in the loosening group and 283.2±65.6 HU in the nonloosening group (P<0.001). The average HU value across L1-L5 showed moderate predictive performance for screw loosening, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.723, a sensitivity of 88.5%, and a specificity of 50.0%. Conclusions Preoperative VOI-based HU values were significantly associated with pedicle screw loosening after single-level lumbar fusion surgery and demonstrated moderate predictive performance. VOI-based HU assessment may serve as a potential adjunctive tool for preoperative risk stratification of pedicle screw loosening.

Preoperative VOI-based HU values were significantly associated with pedicle screw loosening after single-level lumbar fusion surgery and demonstrated moderate predictive performance. title: Malposition Rates of Subaxial Cervical Pedicle Screws Placed Using Intraoperative Computed Tomography (O-arm)-Based Three-dimensional Navigation.
abstract: Study design Cohort retrospective review. Objective To investigate placement accuracy and malposition rates of cervical pedicle screws (CPS) using intraoperative CT (O-arm) based three-dimensional navigation. Background CPS placement is technically demanding due to small pedicle sizes and risk of damage to neurovascular structures in the neck. Computer navigation (CN) has been shown to improve accuracy rates in thoracolumbar pedicle screw placement. However, there are limited studies on CN use for placing CPS. Materials and methods We identified 100 patients who underwent CN CPS placement (C3-C7). Screw position was evaluated on axial, coronal, and sagittal planes and graded as follows: 0-fully in bone; I-minor breach deemed inconsequential (<25% of screw width); II-minor breach considered not ideal, but acceptable (25%-50% of screw width); and III-major breach considered dangerous or that compromised strength of fixation. Results Four hundred thirteen CN CPS screws (C3-C7) were placed in 100 patients (54M:46F). Rates of serious screw malpositions: combined Gr II/III = 42/413 (10.2%). Breaking down the combined Gr II/III screws per level: C3 = 8/33 (24.2%), C4 = 9/63 (14.3%), C5 = 8/72 (11.1%), C6 = 10/85 (11.8%), C7 = 7/160 (4.4%). Conclusion Our study shows a 10.2% nonoptimal rate (combined Gr II and III) using intraoperative three-dimensional imaging and CN. Our results add to a limited number of studies that have reported on this procedure. To our knowledge, this is the biggest study on a uniform technique of navigated pedicle screw placement that included only subaxial levels C3-C7.

title: Expansion of the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score to Outpatients With Spine Metastases: Prospective Assessment on an Ongoing Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objectives For inpatients with spinal metastases, the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score accurately assesses prognosis, with scores of 0 to 3 exhibiting significantly longer survival than scores >3. This study examines the accuracy of this algorithm for outpatients prospectively considered for enrollment in the Spine Patient Optimal Radiosurgery Treatment for Symptomatic MEtastatic Neoplasms (SPORTSMEN) phase II randomized controlled trial. Methods From July 2025 to January 2026, outpatients at an NCI-designated cancer center were evaluated. Prognosis was assessed per an adjusted Metastatic Spine Score adjusted for consisting of: age at presentation (60+ vs. younger), duration of metastatic disease diagnosis (6+ mo vs. sooner), refractory to or on active systemic therapy (yes/no), additional nonspine metastatic focus (yes/no), severe malnutrition of chronic disease (yes/no), brain metastases (yes/no), and presenting symptomatology (asymptomatic or spine/back pain alone=no; additional neurological symptoms=yes) with each category scored a 0 (no) or 1 (yes) and a cumulative score derived. Scores of 0 to 3 were compared with scores >3 and correlated with outcomes. Positive prognosis=time to death/hospice >90 days from presentation. The Fisher test was used for statistical analysis. Results A positive prognosis was exhibited in 8/9 patients with scores of 0 to 3 (8/8 patients without brain metastases) versus 3/9 patients with scores >3 (P=0.0498). The overall accuracy of the Metastatic Spine Score (8/9 positive + 6/9 negative=14/18 patients) was 78%. Conclusion The Metastatic Spine Score provides an accurate prognostic assessment of outpatients with spine metastases, with scores of 0 to 3 yielding significantly better prognosis than scores >3. These findings also support brain MRI evaluation before radiotherapy decisions regarding spinal metastases. This study adds further support for establishing the Metastatic Spine Score as the standard-of-care for accurately evaluating prognosis in this patient population for outpatients as well as inpatients.

title: Racial, Ethnic, and Regional Influences on National Patterns of Mammographic Screening.
abstract: Objectives We sought to evaluate whether there were clinically significant disparities in screening mammography rates according to race, ethnicity, and United States geographic region in patients with access to health care systems. Methods We queried the Cosmos Epic national database to ascertain mammographic screening rates for women aged 50 to 65 who had 1 or more ambulatory encounters with a primary care physician between November 9, 2020, and November 8, 2023. Patients with a previous breast cancer and those with missing race or ethnicity data were excluded. Results The overall mammographic screening rate was 63.8% in the 7,837,164 individuals who met study criteria. There were no clinically meaningful differences in screening according to race. However, screening was less frequent in those with Hispanic ethnicity versus non-Hispanic (58.9% vs. 64.3%, P<0.001). Rates also varied according to region, with the lowest rates in the West (55.5%, P<0.001). Screening rates for Black and White groups were within 5% of one another in all 4 regions. With respect to ethnicity, the South was the only region where the Hispanic population rate had a lower rate over 5% (61.8% vs. 55.7%, P<0.001). Conclusions Many patients receiving health care in the US do not receive recommended mammogram screening, but there were no clinically significant differences by race. Lower rates were noted in Hispanic populations, particularly in the South. Targeted educational and community outreach efforts in this region are warranted.

title: How Much Do Horizontally Referenced and Interteardrop-referenced Acetabular Coverage Indices Differ During Standing in Adults With Hip Pain?
abstract: Background Acetabular coverage is conventionally assessed using the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and acetabular index. However, on standing radiographs, these measurements may be referenced either to the pelvis or to the weightbearing horizontal. Whether selection of these reference lines leads to clinically relevant differences in acetabular coverage interpretation is uncertain. Questions/purposes (1) How do horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements compare in patients with nonarthritic hip pain? (2) How are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity associated with differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced acetabular coverage measurements? (3) What are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity in young adults undergoing assessment for unilateral nonarthritic hip pain? (4) How are hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation associated with the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity? Methods In this retrospective comparative study, 598 patients evaluated at a tertiary-referral young-adult hip clinic between June 2021 and June 2025 were identified; 10% (60 of 598) were excluded for bilateral hip involvement or prior procedures, 5% (28 of 598) for insufficient radiographs, and 3% (17 of 598) for age 50 years or older, leaving 493 patients age 16 to 49 years with unilateral nonarthritic hip conditions and standing AP pelvic radiographs to be included. The mean ± SD age was 35 ± 8 years; 39% (191 of 493) were male. Diagnoses included dysplasia; cam-type, mixed, and pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement; isolated labral tears; and other nonarthritic hip conditions. In each hip, LCEA and acetabular index were measured using horizontal and interteardrop-referenced measurements, and classification disagreement was assessed using LCEA (< 20°, 20° to 25°, 25° to 40°, > 40°) and acetabular index (< 0°, 0° to 10°, > 10°) categories. Associations between pelvic obliquity magnitude and measurement-difference magnitude were assessed using linear regression, with directional relationships assessed graphically. Pelvic obliquity was measured as the angle between the interteardrop and horizontal reference lines, with direction defined relative to the clinically evaluated side. Hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation were compared across pelvic obliquity magnitude and direction groups. After interrater standardization, each patient was randomly allocated to one of two observers, who performed all measurements for that patient; a third observer reviewed a random sample. Interobserver intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.69 to 0.87. Results Mean ± SD absolute differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements were 2° ± 1° for both LCEA and acetabular index. Classification disagreement occurred in 14% (69 of 493) using LCEA-based categories and 10% (51 of 493) using acetabular index-based categories, most notably when interteardrop-referenced LCEA indicated borderline dysplasia and horizontally referenced LCEA indicated normal coverage (29% [28 of 95]). Each 1° increase in pelvic obliquity magnitude was associated with an approximately 1° greater measurement difference for LCEA (β = 0.89 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.86; p < 0.001) and acetabular index (β = 0.90 [95% CI 0.87 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.88; p < 0.001). Mean absolute pelvic obliquity magnitude was 2° ± 1°; 40% (197 of 493) had pelvic obliquity of 2° to < 5° and 3% (14 of 493) had pelvic obliquity ≥ 5°. The clinically evaluated hemipelvis was abducted in 44% (218 of 493), adducted in 39% (192 of 493), and neutral in 17% (83 of 493). Lesser trochanter-based hip-length discrepancy was 2 ± 2 mm with a neutral pelvis, 3 ± 3 mm with abduction, and 4 ± 3 mm with adduction (p < 0.001), and increased from 3 ± 3 mm to 5 ± 3 mm and 7 ± 3 mm across increasing pelvic obliquity magnitude categories (p < 0.001). Hip center of rotation-based values were 2 ± 2 mm in all three direction groups (p = 0.03) and 2 ± 2 mm, 3 ± 2 mm, and 3 ± 3 mm across increasing magnitude categories (p = 0.22). Conclusion These findings indicate that horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements can yield discordant acetabular coverage estimates and radiographic classifications for the same patient. As standing radiographs become more widely incorporated into hip evaluation, comparison of horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements may provide additional information by revealing pelvic-obliquity-associated differences in measured coverage while standing. In patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity, these differences may warrant consideration when interpreting acetabular morphology and discussing the relative indications for treatment or procedural options because they may lead clinicians to disagree about whether the same hip meets thresholds used in treatment planning. Future work should correlate measurements based on horizontal referencing and interteardrop referencing in patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity with clinical and surgical outcomes to (1) determine whether acetabular indices measured using the interteardrop line or floor-based horizontal reference confer superior clinical value and (2) define procedure-specific thresholds for relevant diagnostic subgroups. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: Combination Therapy of Injectables With Energy-Based Treatments for Facial Rejuvenation: An Updated Review.
abstract: Background Fillers are frequently combined with other injectables and energy-based devices to target volume loss, dynamic rhytides, and photodamage. Questions remain regarding optimal treatment sequencing, safety, and synergistic clinical efficacy.OBJECTIVETo evalute the current evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of combining injectable therapies with energy-based treatments for facial rejuvenation. Methods MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched using keywords on dermal fillers with neuromodulators, intense pulsed light (IPL), laser, microfocused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V), high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), or radiofrequency (RF). Studies reporting safety, efficacy, sequencing, or clinical outcomes were included. Results Combining fillers with neuromodulators produces synergistic improvements in facial rejuvenation by addressing volume loss and muscular hyperactivity with superior outcomes and longer treatment durability compared with monotherapy. Intense pulsed light, nonablative lasers, MFU-V, HIFU, and RF appear safe when used with fillers, with studies demonstrating no significant adverse interactions or compromise of filler integrity. Combination treatment may enhance optimize facial contouring, improve skin quality, and improve patient satisfaction and retention. Histologic and clinical studies suggest synergistic effects when MFU-V/RF are combined with biostimulatory fillers. Conclusion Combination treatment with fillers and complementary modalities offers a comprehensive approach to facial rejuvenation. Current evidence supports the safety of most nonablative combination protocols. Additional studies are needed to assess the safety and efficacy of combining fillers with more aggressive resurfacing procedures and novel devices.

title: MRI-based biomarkers for risk stratification and assessment of treatment response in Metabolic dysfunction-associated Steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects up to 38% of the population globally. Liver biopsy, the historical reference standard, is invasive, subject to sampling error and not scalable. MRI-based biomarkers provide non-invasive, quantitative whole liver assessment. MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) is the most accurate noninvasive measure of steatosis (thresholds of 6.4%, 17.4% and 22.1% for grades ≥1, ≥2 and 3), and a ≥30% relative reduction is associated with histologic response. Liver stiffness by magnetic resonance elastography (MRE-LS) is the most accurate imaging biomarker for fibrosis: MRE-LS of 3.1-4.4 kPa corresponds to F2-F3 and ≥5 kPa to cirrhosis, and each 1-kPa increase is associated with a 43% higher risk of hepatic decompensation. Iron-corrected T1 is a sensitive but nonspecific marker of disease activity whose prognostic value requires further study. Composite scores, MAST, MEFIB, and MASH Resolution Index, combine imaging and blood tests for advanced fibrosis diagnosis and response assessment. MRE is cost-effective compared with vibration-controlled transient elastography for detecting advanced fibrosis. Artificial intelligence may broaden access by automating analysis and enabling PDFF from routine MRI. We review the evidence supporting these biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and regulatory use, and their role in clinical trials and in treatment decisions for approved MASH therapies.

title: Repeated Exposure to Military Low-Level Blast Is Associated With Regionally Specific Reductions in Gray Matter Volume in Breachers and Snipers.
abstract: Objective To examine the association between duration of repeated exposure to low-level blast and alteration in brain structure. Setting Data were collected at 2 neuroimaging facilities. Participants Canadian Armed Forces breachers (n = 30) and snipers (n = 31) with a history of repeated exposure to low-level blast (average years = 9.70, SD = 4.57) and sex- and age-matched active military controls (n = 57). Design MRI and neurocognitive data from breachers and snipers were collected prospectively at baseline (time 1) and after a training exercise involving a concentrated regimen of blast exposure (time 2) (time gap = 80.56 days, SD = 36.90). Time 1 and time 2 data were used to assess the chronic and training-related effects of blast exposure, respectively. MRI and neurocognitive data from controls were collected twice with a comparable time gap. Main measures High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, plus neurocognitive measures. Results Voxel-based morphometry conducted on MRI data collected at time 1 demonstrated that compared with controls, there was lower regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers, and bilaterally in parahippocampal gyrus (bordering on amygdala) in breachers. Regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers predicted neurocognitive function. We did not observe any difference in regional white matter volume between groups at time 1, nor any changes in regional gray or white matter volume between time 1 and time 2. Conclusion Chronic but not training-related low-level blast exposure was associated with dissociable patterns of regional gray matter volume reduction in snipers and breachers, and regional gray matter volume predicted neurocognitive function in snipers. The differential pattern of structural alteration between breachers and snipers and its relationship with neurocognitive function in snipers can inform health monitoring programs for diagnosis and treatment of blast-exposed service members and Veterans.

title: From imaging to intelligence: AI applications in CT and MRI for hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, largely due to high recurrence rates after curative treatment and poor prognosis in advanced-stage disease. Multiphasic computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) play central roles in the noninvasive diagnosis and management of HCC; however, diagnostic variability and limited sensitivity for early-stage and atypical lesions continue to pose major clinical challenges. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing medical image analysis and improving clinical decision-making in liver oncology. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-based applications for HCC imaging using CT and MRI. We discuss the roles of AI in lesion detection and segmentation, differential diagnosis and tumor classification, imaging-based biological characterization, and prediction of treatment response and prognosis. In particular, radiomics and deep learning approaches have enabled automated extraction of high-dimensional imaging features, facilitating noninvasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and heterogeneity. The integration of multimodal data, including imaging, clinical, and molecular information, further enhances predictive performance and personalized risk stratification. Despite encouraging results, most existing studies are limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous methodologies, and insufficient external validation. Challenges related to model interpretability, data standardization, and clinical integration also remain unresolved. We highlight current limitations and future research directions, emphasizing the need for multi-center collaboration, prospective validation, and development of transparent and regulatory-compliant systems. With continued technological innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration, AI-driven imaging analysis is expected to play an increasingly important role in precision medicine and outcome optimization for patients with HCC.

title: In Vivo Detection of Ampullary T2 Hypointensity as a Marker of Vestibular Atelectasis.
abstract: Background and purpose Vestibular atelectasis (VA) is a histologically defined collapse of the membranous labyrinth, often accompanied by dense basophilic deposits. While delayed postcontrast 3D-FLAIR imaging allows indirect visualization of VA, no in vivo correlate of the basophilic deposits has been reported. This study describes a novel T2-weighted hypointense signal within the ampullae and utricle as a potential imaging biomarker of VA and explores its clinical relevance in patients with bilateral vestibular areflexia. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 47 patients with bilateral vestibular areflexia, confirmed by video Head Impulse Test and vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials. All underwent 3T MRI with delayed postcontrast 3D-FLAIR and high-resolution T2-weighted sequences. The presence and distribution of ampullary or utricular T2 hypointensities were evaluated and correlated with radiological VA, clinical presentation, and vestibular function. Results Among the 47 patients included, VA was identified in 32 (68.1%). A distinct T2 hypointense signal was observed in 25 patients (53.2%), exclusively within the VA group. These hypointensities were significantly more prevalent in the superior and posterior ampullae compared to the lateral (FDR-P<0.001). VA patients were significantly younger, had better hearing thresholds and more severe posterior canal dysfunction; short vertigo episodes were more frequent in this group without reaching statistical significance. In age-adjusted Firth logistic regression, ampullary hypointensity was the only variable independently associated with VA (odds ratio: 124.59, 95% CI: 5.35-2900.22; apparent area under the curve: 0.973, 95% CI: 0.890-0.994), although the estimate was imprecise owing to quasi-complete separation (FDR-P=0.0104). Conclusion A T2 hypointense signal within the ampullae and utricle was observed exclusively in patients with radiological vestibular atelectasis in this cohort. Its anatomical distribution is compatible with the basophilic deposits described in histopathological series, although this correspondence remains hypothetical in the absence of tissue analysis. This MRI sign may raise suspicion of VA when delayed postcontrast 3D-FLAIR imaging is unavailable or contraindicated, rather than replace it.

title: Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Versus Image-Guided Gastrostomy Placement in Patients With Cirrhosis: A Multi-Institutional Research Network Study.
abstract: Background The selection of an appropriate technique for placement of a gastrostomy tube in patients with cirrhosis remains controversial due to concerns about adverse events. We used real-world data to compare outcomes after percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) versus fluoroscopically guided gastrostomy by an interventional radiologist (IR G-tube) in patients with cirrhosis. Methods We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study of adults with cirrhosis who underwent gastrostomy tube placement from 2014 to 2023 using the TriNetX Research Network. Using relevant Current Procedural Terminology codes, patients were categorized into 2 groups: PEG (43246/0DH64UZ) or fluoroscopic IR G-tube (49440/0DH63UZ). Periprocedural adverse events were defined as short-term (14 d) or long-term (180 d). Propensity score matching was performed using demographic, clinical, and available laboratory covariates. Binary outcomes were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% CIs, whereas mortality was reported using adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) from Cox proportional hazards models. Survival was assessed with Kaplan-Meier analysis and log-rank testing. Results Of the 5028 patients meeting selection criteria, 1579 underwent PEG placement and 3449 underwent IR G-tube placement. Adjusted odds of periprocedural adverse events for PEG vs IR G-tube were as follows: aspiration pneumonia (aOR: 0.66, 95% CI: 0.51-0.85), hemorrhage (aOR: 0.79, CI: 0.59-1.06), blood transfusion (aOR: 0.99, CI: 0.78-1.27), and infection or peritonitis (aOR: 0.96, CI: 0.68-1.34). In the 6-month follow-up period, PEG placement was associated with lower odds of tube malfunction (aOR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.64-0.96) and tube replacement (aOR: 0.47, 95% CI: 0.36-0.63). At 6 months, PEG placement was also associated with lower mortality risk (aHR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.70-0.91; P=0.011). Conclusions In a large multicenter cohort of patients with cirrhosis, PEG and IR G-tube placement had similar short-term rates of bleeding and infectious adverse events, whereas PEG was associated with fewer tube malfunctions and replacements and lower observed mortality at 6 months.

title: State of the art: thoracic ultrasound.
abstract: Purpose of review Thoracic ultrasound has continued to expand beyond simple bedside triage into a quantitative, procedure-guiding and increasingly artificial intelligence-augmented tool across pleural and respiratory medicine. This review summarizes the literature published over the past year, highlighting developments in effusion characterization, pneumothorax diagnosis, image-guided pleural procedures, artificial intelligence, training standards, critical care applications, malignant pleural effusion management, and diaphragm/interstitial lung disease assessment. Recent findings Elastography and contrast-enhanced ultrasound have moved from exploratory to comparative and multicentre randomized evaluation for effusion characterization and biopsy guidance. Meta-analyses have reaffirmed the superiority of point-of-care ultrasound over chest radiography for both pneumothorax and thoracentesis guidance. Artificial intelligence tools have shown that they can close the acquisition-skill gap for novice operators, although automated interpretation (particularly B-line quantification) remains inconsistent against expert consensus. A new UK national training standard for pleural procedures has been published, alongside the first validated thoracic-specific competency assessment tool. A large multicentre randomized trial found that a point-of-care ultrasound-driven diagnostic pathway did not improve early discharge rates in emergency department patients with dyspnoea, an important negative finding. Diaphragm and quantitative lung ultrasound continue to accumulate evidence as noninvasive markers of interstitial lung disease severity and ventilator weaning readiness. Summary The past year's literature confirms thoracic ultrasound's trajectory from a purely diagnostic adjunct towards a quantitative, procedure-integrated and artificial intelligence-supported modality, while also delivering important cautionary and negative findings that temper enthusiasm and clarify where evidence remains immature.

title: Diagnostic value of multiparametric MRI radiomics combined with serum PSA and tissue P504S for prostate cancer.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic value of multiparametric MRI radiomics features combined with serum PSA-related indicators and tissue P504S expression for prostate cancer, and to develop a multimodal auxiliary diagnostic model in a retrospective cohort that was not restricted to early-stage disease. Clinical, imaging, and pathological data from 126 patients with suspected prostate cancer were retrospectively collected and divided into a prostate cancer group (69 cases) and a benign lesion group (57 cases). All patients underwent prostate MRI; radiomics features were extracted, and LASSO regression, with 10-fold cross-validation for tuning, was used to construct a Rad-score. Serum t-PSA, f-PSA, f/t-PSA ratio, and PSAD were measured. Tissue P504S expression was detected by immunohistochemistry and semi-quantitatively scored. A combined diagnostic model was constructed using multivariate logistic regression. ROC metrics were evaluated in the model-development cohort and are reported as apparent performance. AUC differences between models were compared using the DeLong test. The prostate cancer group had higher t-PSA and PSAD and a lower f/t-PSA ratio than the benign lesion group (all P < .001). P504S was positive in 64/69 cancer cases (92.8%) and 9/57 benign cases (15.8%; P < .001). Eight radiomics features were selected, and the median Rad-score was 0.86 in cancer cases and - 0.52 in benign cases (P < .001). The full model combining Rad-score, f/t-PSA, PSAD, and tissue P504S semiquantitative score achieved an apparent AUC of 0.956 (95% CI: 0.918-0.994), sensitivity of 92.8%, specificity of 91.2%, PPV of 92.8%, and NPV of 91.2%. The overall imaging + serum model had an apparent AUC of 0.912 (95% CI: 0.856-0.968). In exploratory location-based analyses, AUCs were 0.962 for peripheral zone lesions and 0.934 for transition zone lesions. The full model showed promising apparent discrimination for prostate cancer in this retrospective cohort and may represent a potential auxiliary diagnostic model after tissue sampling. The imaging + serum model could potentially support biopsy decision-making, whereas the full model requires tissue P504S assessment and may assist diagnostic confirmation or risk characterization. Neither incremental clinical benefit nor a reduction in unnecessary biopsies has been established. Internal and external validation and evaluation of the practical clinical workflow are required before routine use.

title: Synchronous hepatocellular carcinoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma in a patient with chronic hepatitis B: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale Synchronous double primary cancers involving hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) are exceptionally rare. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is an established cause of HCC, whereas Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is the major etiological factor for NPC. We report a patient with synchronous HCC and NPC and review the relevant literature. Patient concerns A 63-year-old Chinese man with chronic HBV presented with a liver mass detected on routine screening. He reported nasal obstruction. Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced imaging showed a 46 × 59 mm hepatic lesion with portal vein tumor thrombus and a 41 × 29 mm nasopharyngeal mass with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsies confirmed moderately differentiated HCC and EBV-associated non-keratinizing NPC. Final diagnoses were HCC Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer Stage C (CNLC IIIa, Child-Pugh A) and NPC T3N2M0 Stage III (AJCC 8th edition). Interventions He received hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC, mFOLFOX) combined with tislelizumab and donafenib; radiotherapy for NPC was deferred after shared decision-making. Entecavir was continued. Outcomes At 19-month follow-up, both tumors remained controlled; the NPC met radiographic complete response criteria. Lessons Synchronous HCC and EBV-associated NPC were controlled during treatment with a tislelizumab-containing multimodality regimen, and the NPC achieved a radiographic complete response. The contribution of each treatment component cannot be determined from a single case, and definitive radiotherapy remains the standard of care for locoregionally advanced NPC. Multidisciplinary management and close monitoring are essential.
originalAbstract:
Rationale

Synchronous double primary cancers involving hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) are exceptionally rare. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is an established cause of HCC, whereas Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is the major etiological factor for NPC. We report a patient with synchronous HCC and NPC and review the relevant literature.

Patient concerns

A 63-year-old Chinese man with chronic HBV presented with a liver mass detected on routine screening. He reported nasal obstruction.

Diagnoses

Contrast-enhanced imaging showed a 46 × 59 mm hepatic lesion with portal vein tumor thrombus and a 41 × 29 mm nasopharyngeal mass with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsies confirmed moderately differentiated HCC and EBV-associated non-keratinizing NPC. Final diagnoses were HCC Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer Stage C (CNLC IIIa, Child-Pugh A) and NPC T3N2M0 Stage III (AJCC 8th edition).

Interventions

He received hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC, mFOLFOX) combined with tislelizumab and donafenib; radiotherapy for NPC was deferred after shared decision-making. Entecavir was continued.

Outcomes

At 19-month follow-up, both tumors remained controlled; the NPC met radiographic complete response criteria.

Lessons

Synchronous HCC and EBV-associated NPC were controlled during treatment with a tislelizumab-containing multimodality regimen, and the NPC achieved a radiographic complete response. The contribution of each treatment component cannot be determined from a single case, and definitive radiotherapy remains the standard of care for locoregionally advanced NPC. Multidisciplinary management and close monitoring are essential.

title: Successful rechallenge with almonertinib and corticosteroids after gefitinib-induced interstitial lung disease: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale First-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are highly effective in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) remains a rare but potentially fatal adverse event. The safety and efficacy of EGFR-TKI rechallenge - either with the same agent or an alternative one - following ILD resolution are not established and represent a significant clinical knowledge gap. Patient concerns A 53-year-old never-smoking woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma - detected to harbor an L858R mutation in exon 21 of the EGFR gene - developed progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia after 2 months of first-line gefitinib therapy, despite confirmed initial radiographic and clinical response. Diagnoses The patient was diagnosed with grade 3 gefitinib-associated ILD. Interventions With the discontinuation of gefitinib, the patient was given methylprednisolone to resolve ILD. To control advanced lung adenocarcinoma progression, the patient was subjected to 6 cycles of treatment using pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab, with measurable tumor shrinkage, followed by maintenance therapy with bevacizumab. Furthermore, given the tumor progression 14 months later, the patient was prescribed docetaxel plus bevacizumab to restore control. Ten months later, the patient experienced disease progression and strongly requested to use EGFR-TKIs again given prior response to EGFR-TKI. The patient was rechallenged with almonertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, and methylprednisolone. Outcomes The patient had measurable tumor shrinkage, with sustained tumor control and no recurrence of pulmonary toxicity. As of last follow-up, she maintained progression-free survival for approximately 8 months on almonertinib. Lessons This case provides a hypothesis-generating observation, illustrating feasibility only in highly‑selected patients with EGFR‑mutant NSCLC and prior severe TKI‑related ILD. With prophylactic corticosteroids and rigorous surveillance, third‑generation EGFR‑TKI may represent a tentative clinical option for such patients, but general safety cannot be inferred from this single case.

title: Adrenal ganglioneuroma in an adolescent presenting as an incidentaloma: Imaging-pathology correlation and diagnostic challenges: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Adrenal ganglioneuroma (AGN) is a rare, benign, and usually nonfunctioning tumor arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic ganglion cells. Preoperative diagnosis is difficult because the clinical presentation is often nonspecific, and imaging findings overlap with those of other adrenal neoplasms. We describe an adolescent adrenal incidentaloma with detailed imaging-pathology correlation, adding to the small number of reported adolescent cases. Patient concerns A previously healthy 16-year-old male underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) after a bicycle accident. No traumatic injury was identified, but imaging incidentally revealed a well-circumscribed right adrenal mass measuring approximately 6.1 cm × 3.6 cm × 5.0 cm. Diagnoses CT and magnetic resonance imaging showed progressive, persistent enhancement across the arterial, venous, and delayed phases without demonstrable washout (attenuation increased from 20 Hounsfield units unenhanced to 55 Hounsfield units in the venous phase, with further qualitative enhancement on 15-minute delayed images) and no intralesional fat, suggesting a non-adenomatous lesion and raising suspicion for a neurogenic tumor. Biochemical evaluation showed no evidence of hormonal hypersecretion. Histopathological examination after resection established the diagnosis of AGN. Interventions The patient underwent right adrenalectomy because of the size and radiologically indeterminate nature of the mass. Outcomes The postoperative course was uneventful. Transient elevation of blood pressure noted during follow-up prompted biochemical reevaluation, which showed no evidence of excess catecholamine. Follow-up CT at 9 months showed no recurrence. Lessons Progressive delayed enhancement without washout and absence of signal loss on opposed-phase magnetic resonance imaging, a pattern previously described in ganglioneuroma, may suggest the diagnosis preoperatively, although definitive diagnosis requires histopathological confirmation. Complete surgical excision established the diagnosis and achieved a favorable short-term outcome; the excellent long-term prognosis of AGN is supported by the published literature, and our patient remains recurrence-free at 9 months.

title: Prediction of pathologic complete response in breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy using baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT-derived CT radiomics and clinicopathological biomarkers.
abstract: Objective The study aimed to assess whether baseline fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT)-derived CT radiomics adds predictive value to clinicopathological biomarkers and PET metabolic assessment for pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in breast cancer. Methods This retrospective study included 104 patients with stage I-III breast cancer who underwent baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT, NAC, and surgery. Clinicopathological variables and tumor maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) were recorded; 107 CT radiomic features were extracted using PyRadiomics. Clinical, Metabolic, Radiomics, and Combined models were developed using L2-regularized logistic regression and evaluated by nested five-fold cross-validation. Discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis were assessed; 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using 1000 bootstrap resamples of pooled out-of-fold predictions. Results Forty-six patients (44.2%) achieved pCR. Area under the curves (AUCs) were 0.784 (95% CI: 0.686-0.875) for Clinical, 0.595 (0.470-0.704) for Metabolic, and 0.636 (0.526-0.739) for Radiomics models. The Combined model had the highest numerical AUC (0.797; 95% CI: 0.705-0.880), with accuracy 0.731, sensitivity 0.630, specificity 0.810, and F1-score 0.674. Conclusion Combining CT radiomics and SUVmax with clinicopathological biomarkers yielded the highest numerical discrimination for pCR, but improvement over the Clinical model was modest. Larger multicenter external validation is needed before clinical implementation.

title: An Anatomy-Guided Frontal Sinus Setback Workflow Using Patient-Specific Cutting Guides and Resorbable Fixation in Chinese Transfeminine Patients.
abstract: Frontal sinus anterior-table setback is a technically demanding component of forehead feminization when simple burring is insufficient to achieve the desired contour. We describe a structured operative workflow in 4 Chinese transfeminine patients aged 20 to 32 years. Preoperative computed tomography (CT) and virtual surgical planning were performed with ProPlan CMF, and a patient-specific cutting guide was used to localize the frontal sinus boundaries and the anterior-table osteotomy line. After reduction of the brow and supraorbital region, the mobilized anterior-table was repositioned posteriorly according to its relationship with the adjacent reduced bony contour and stabilized with a RapidSorb 2.0 resorbable plate-and-screw system, avoiding permanent metallic hardware in this non-load-bearing region. The frontal sinus mucosa was preserved without curettage, sinus obliteration was not performed, and the nasofrontal outflow tract was preserved. All patients underwent postoperative day-5 CT to document the early anterior-table position and frontal bony contour and completed 6 months of clinical and photographic follow-up. Improvement in forehead contour was observed without major complications. Because concomitant facial procedures were performed in selected patients, overall facial appearance reflects the combined effects of these procedures. This report presents preliminary technical experience with resorbable rigid fixation for frontal sinus anterior-table reconstruction; larger series with longer clinical and radiographic follow-up are needed to assess long-term skeletal stability, frontal sinus-related outcomes, and fixation behavior after material resorption.
