title: High-power radiofrequency ablation with optimized pulsing algorithm for renal tumors: initial clinical experience and safety profile.
abstract: Incidental diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma is increasing. While surgery remains the standard treatment for localized T1b or larger lesions, image-guided percutaneous ablation represents a valid alternative for T1a cases. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is effective but limited by smaller ablation volumes and sensitivity to the heat-sink effect. Microwave ablation and cryoablation have emerged to address these limitations, although the first is susceptible to thermal injury to adjacent structures and the second requires multiple, larger probes and longer procedures. High-power RFA (HP-RFA) is a recent development that delivers higher energy (370 versus 200 W), enabling faster and larger ablations. This study evaluated the feasibility and safety of a novel HP-RFA system incorporating an impedance-controlled pulsed algorithm and internally cooled electrodes. Five patients with small renal tumors (mean diameter 2.3 cm) unsuitable for surgery underwent ultrasound- or computed tomography-guided HP-RFA. Technical success, safety, and early tumor control were assessed. All procedures were technically successful. No major complications occurred; one minor perirenal hematoma was managed conservatively. Follow-up imaging at 6 months demonstrated complete tumor ablation without local recurrence. These preliminary findings suggest that HP-RFA is feasible and safe for treating small renal tumors and may represent a promising evolution of RFA. Further studies are needed. KEY POINTS: Question Can HP-RFA provide feasible and safe minimally invasive treatment for small renal tumors while overcoming limitations of conventional RFA? Findings Technical success and efficacy of HP-RFA were achieved in 100% of cases. No major complications. Complete tumor ablation was accomplished. Relevance statement HP-RFA demonstrates feasibility, safety, and effective early tumor control in small renal tumors. By enabling larger, faster ablations, it may overcome limitations of conventional RFA and expand the employment of minimally invasive treatment options instead of surgical approaches.

title: MRI-based virtual radiographs of the pelvis for assessment of acetabular morphology.
abstract: Objectives We generated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based virtual radiographs (VRs) from hips with/without intra-articular contrast and compared them with conventional anteroposterior pelvic radiographs (CR) regarding measurement bias, interobserver and intraobserver agreement, and diagnosis of acetabular deformities; we also assessed hip deformity prevalence on VR in asymptomatic participants. Materials and methods Retrospective study of 50 patients (100 hips; mean age 34 years) with femoroacetabular impingement or hip dysplasia undergoing CR and unilateral magnetic resonance arthrography. Additionally, 53 asymptomatic participants underwent noncontrast MRI. Segmentation of the osseous pelvis was performed on T1-weighted volume interpolated breathhold examination (VIBE) Dixon MRI using 3D nnU-Net, pseudo-computed tomography generation, and cone-beam projection to generate VR. Acetabular coverage (lateral center edge angle (LCE), acetabular index (AI), anterior/posterior coverage, extrusion index (EI)), and acetabular version were compared between CR and VR. Interobserver agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and κ statistics; bias with Bland-Altman analysis. Results Interobserver agreement for VR ranged from moderate to almost perfect (ICC/κ 0.60-0.94), except for the AI. LCE showed no significant bias with ( - 0.2° ± 2.5, p = 0.663) or without contrast ( - 0.2° ± 2.2, p = 0.530). Systematic differences occurred for AI, EI, anterior/posterior coverage, and ischial spine sign; 57-75% of discrepancies were within CR interobserver variation. Diagnostic classification showed substantial agreement between CR and VR (κ = 0.62), comparable to CR interobserver agreement (κ = 0.70). In asymptomatic participants, 13% had acetabular dysplasia, 68% normal coverage, and 19% overcoverage. Conclusion MRI-based VR provides acetabular morphology assessment comparable to CR and enables radiation-free evaluation in symptomatic patients and asymptomatic populations. Key points Question Can MRI-based virtual radiographs reproduce conventional radiographic measurements of acetabular morphology, enabling radiation-free two-dimensional assessment in symptomatic patients and asymptomatic populations? Findings The lateral center-edge angle showed no significant bias between virtual and conventional radiographs; diagnostic classification of acetabular deformities agreed substantially (κ = 0.62), comparable to conventional radiograph interobserver agreement. Relevance Statement MRI-derived virtual radiographs can provide acetabular measurements comparable to conventional radiographs without ionizing radiation, supporting integration into three-dimensional surgical planning and enabling assessment in young patients and population-based cohorts where repeated radiographs are undesirable.

title: Oxygen-enhanced brain MRI using dynamic gradient-echo and MR fingerprinting.
abstract: Objectives Oxygen-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using dynamic three-dimensional (3D) gradient-echo and MR fingerprinting (MRF) was applied to evaluate oxygen transit from blood to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Materials and methods Twenty healthy participants, enrolled between December 2023 and March 2024, underwent 3-T MRI including Pre-oxygen inhalation 3D MRF (pre-O₂ MRF), dynamic 3D gradient-echo (volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination, VIBE) during oxygen inhalation, and post-oxygen inhalation 3D MRF (post-O₂ MRF). Pre-O₂ and post-O₂ MRF each consisted of two acquisitions. Signal intensity on dynamic VIBE and T1 relaxation times from MRF were evaluated in gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), surface CSF, and ventricles using volumes of interest (VOIs). Results Dynamic 3D VIBE demonstrated a rapid signal increase in surface CSF immediately after oxygen inhalation, with a smaller increase in GM. Post-oxygen inhalation VIBE signal was significantly higher than pre-oxygen inhalation signal in surface CSF (p < 0.001) and GM (p < 0.001). T1 relaxation times differed significantly across phases for GM, WM, and surface CSF (p < 0.001) as well as for ventricles (p = 0.024). Large effect sizes were observed for surface CSF (Cohen dz = 4.15) and GM (Cohen dz = 1.31) in dynamic 3D VIBE, as well as for surface CSF (Cohen f = 1.31) and GM (Cohen f = 0.73) in T1 relaxation time measurement, suggesting substantial physiological changes following oxygen inhalation. Conclusion Dynamic 3D VIBE images visualized oxygen inhalation-related signal change in the surface CSF, which were quantitatively validated by T1 relaxation time reductions derived from 3D MRF. Key points Question Can noninvasive oxygen-enhanced brain MRI visualize and quantify oxygen-related signal changes in cerebrospinal fluid using dynamic 3D gradient-echo and 3D MR fingerprinting? Findings Dynamic 3D gradient-echo showed rapid surface CSF signal increases after oxygen inhalation, accompanied by significant T1 reductions on 3D MR fingerprinting. Relevance statement This noninvasive oxygen-enhanced MR approach may provide a clinically feasible method for assessing oxygen transit into CSF and could support future investigations of human CSF dynamics. Dynamic 3D gradient-echo images visualized oxygen inhalation-related signal change in the surface CSF, which were quantitatively validated by T1 relaxation time reductions derived from 3D MRF.

title: Patient-specific biophysical AI-powered modeling for predicting RFA volumes in HCC.
abstract: Objectives To clinically evaluate a fully automated, artificial intelligence-powered, patient-specific biophysical model for predicting radiofrequency ablation (RFA) volumes in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and to compare its performance with manufacturer-provided ablation estimates. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 96 RFA procedures in 65 HCC patients treated using a single ablation with a cluster needle. Tumors, needle position, and postablation zone were manually segmented on periprocedural computed tomography. Liver parenchyma and vascular structures were automatically extracted using deep learning. A graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated biophysical model simulated heat transfer, vascular heat-sink effects, and tissue necrosis using patient-specific anatomy and procedural data. Correlations between ablation volume manually segmented and clinical or anatomical parameters (ablation time, ablation tip temperature, tumor-capsule distance, vessel proximity, type, and diameter) were assessed. Model-predicted volumes were compared with ground truth and manufacturer estimates using relative volume difference (RVD) and volume similarity. Results Final ablation volumes showed wide variability (7.9-78.8 cm³) and were not correlated with any individual clinical or anatomical parameter (Pearson r - 0.02 to 0.29). Across 94 evaluable cases, simulated and ground-truth volumes were similar (p = 0.165), while manufacturer estimates significantly overestimated ablation volume (p < 0.001). The model achieved a median RVD of 0.39 (interquartile range 0.24-0.57), significantly lower than the manufacturer's algorithm (1.04; 0.64-1.61). Incorporating patient-specific ablation time further improved accuracy. Simulation was fast (0.45 s per second of ablation on GPU). Conclusion A fully automated, patient-specific biophysical model substantially improves RFA ablation volume prediction in HCC compared with manufacturer approximations, supporting its potential role in personalized treatment planning and outcome standardization. Key points Question In patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, can a fully automated, AI-powered, patient-specific biophysical model predict radiofrequency ablation volume more accurately than manufacturer-provided estimates? Findings A fully automated, AI-powered biophysical model integrating patient-specific anatomy and vasculature predicted RFA volume significantly better than manufacturer estimates (median relative volume difference (RVD) 0.39 versus 1.04). Relevance statement Accurate ablation volume prediction could support personalized radiofrequency ablation (RFA) planning, reduce reliance on operator experience, and standardize treatment margins in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), potentially improving local tumor control and reducing recurrence in cirrhotic patients undergoing thermal ablation.
